• Tortni. A'SONG OF THE ROAD. The Gauger walked with willing foot, And aye the Gauger played the flute; And what should Master Gauger play But Over the Hills and jar Away? Whenerer I buckle on my pack, r And foot it gaily in the track, •• 0 pleasant Gauger long since dead, I hear you -fluting on ahead. 6 You go with me the self-same way— The self-same air for me tyou play. For I do think, and so do you, .f," It is the tune to travel to. • • . For who would gravely set his face • e• 1 To go to this and tiother place? There's nothing under heaven so blue 1 That's fairly worth the travelling to. On every hand the roads begin, And people walk with real therein; But wheresoe'er the high4.ays tend, Be sure there's nothing at the end-! 7 . Then follow, you, wherever hie The travelling-mountains of the sky, e Or let the streams in civil mode • Direct your choice upon a road. ; For one and all, or high or low, .1 Will bring you where you wish to ; ' And one and all go night and day • Over the Hills and far Away. The Magazine of Art. R. L. STEPHENSON. YOUTH AND AGE. With eager feet that have no dread of wrong, And eyes that hold no prophecy of tears, Youth steps across the meeting place of years, And bids the Future welcome with a song. To childhood's vision, fetterless and strong,. The path Way through the unknown year appears 'A broad highway of hope, untouched by fears, Where flowers unfold and birds sing all day long. Azul the same simple faith that reckons all The years as summers—all whose dreams of love Are dreams of constancy and stainless truth, In the dark days when cares and sorrows fall, Still finding sunshine on the heights above, Shall keep within the heart petipetual youth. But, to the Aged, boreed with weight of days, Whose dreams confuse the living with the dead, The New Year brings a gift of peace instead Of joyous hope; by steep and chequered ways, 0 3r mountains climbed with prayer and crowned with praise, god's loving-kindness hath his pilgrim led: Ad still his promise cheers the hoary head, And feeble hands new Ebenezers raise. Sweet is the faith in youth's far-rvaching eye, But better far, -when the long track is past, And sight is dim and feet no more may roam, The trust that sees unmoved the end draw nigh, Apd welcomes each New Year with joy at last, As the bright vestibule of heaven and home ! —Mary Retries in "Sunday at How."

When alone we have our thoughts to watch, in our families our tempers, in society our tongues. . Robie, a Border character, carrying a chair and a kail- pet ,on his head, was met by an acquaintance one morn- ing. " What are ye efter the day, Robie? " "Oh, I'm ! faittin' !" " What are you flittin' for?" " Oh, to be ' near ma worn," "Where are ye workin'? " " Oh, I Wena eotten a job vet." A descendant of the Marquis of Montrose being taunted by a Campbell for the long time his ancestor's 1 head was stuck upon the Tolbooth at Edinburgh, "Mont- rose," said lie, "was too good a soldier to quit his post till he was relieved," alluding to the Marquis ofsAreyll's head having been placed in its stead, atter the Restora- tion. White (rushing in): "Is Brown here?' Green: "No." White:, "Has he been here any time within the Last henr ?" Green: "No." White: "Confound him! He said be would meet me here at five o'clock, and here it is 5 30. If you see him now, 'tell him I got tired of waiting around here for him, and went off. Tell him I've no patience with men who don't keep their appoint- ments." " Do you ever think, George dear," she said, and her voice was soft'and low, as befitted the perfect beauty of the night, "how closely true happiness is allied with tears ?" "I don't believe I ever do," replied George. "Yes," she went on, looking up into his face, "when one is truly and wholly happy, there is but little to di- vide a smile and a tear." " That's a fact," said George, "but I never thought of it before. There's nothing but the nose." CARLYTR AS A SCHOOLMASTER.—Mr. Jonathan Findlay, ' a civil engineer, resident in Montreal, Canada, was more than sixty years ago, says an American paper, a pupil of Carlyle's. Mr. Findlay was born and brought up at Kirkcaldy, a small town on the Firth of Forth, eight miles from Edinburgh. In his early boyhood the Rev. Edward Irving kept a school there, which young Find- lay attended. After a time Mr. Irving formed a part- nership with Thomas Carlyle, and a more extended plan of instruction was undertaken, the school being re- named an "academy." Mr. Findlay describes Carlyle, ' when a schoolmaster, as resembling a labourer in the roughness and uncouthness of his appearance. He did not have the power to interest his scholars in their les- sons, and he punished them without pity or mercy. Car- lyle used often to occupy himself in writing at his desk, and woeful was that boy's fate who dared to interrupt him. The tavrse would be thrown at the culprit's head, and he would be required to present himself for a sound thrashing, with the means thereof humbly carried to his teacher. No perception of Carlyle's great merits as a writer have been sufficient to efface from Mr. Findlav's memory the impression of his tyranny and cruelty the ill-nature and arbitrary disposition which mark the author equally distinguished him as a young school- master ruling a class of trembling little boys. But, in • judging Carlyle at this time, much allowance must be imade for the manners and customs of the day, when severity in school discipline was considered the only 1 proper way of educating youth. 'TO MAKE FARMING PAT.—That is the question of the day.' Some men teenage to answer it successfully. They know how to buy and feed and sell, as well auhow to manage land. How can that business yield a profit when the cheese or butter is not sought but avoided in the market? A good-looking cheese, ap- parently from Derbyshire or Leicestershire, was brought into the railway carriage where we sat the Other day, by a man who said he had jtest bought it in a shop for 2d. a , pound! We wishedl him out soon after he got in. and , told him he had better use-it in his poultry-yard. He had thrown away his money even at that low piece. MILEALINIL—A new substitute for milk, which is now being extensively used in rearing calves, foals, lambs, and young pigs, is thus spoken of in the columns of the 'French Journal Agrieole :—" The means employed to Increase dairy produce, in order to augment the neces- sary quantity of milk for the development of this trade, have been not only to seek good milking qualities in cows of all kinds, by raising the standards of the breeds, but (atteation has also been directed to discover in chemicals a composition for an artificial milk, for rear- ing and also for fattening calves. The nutritive proper- ties of the natural milk being discovered, it was not difficult to arrive at the composition of a substance con- taining in proper proportions an equivalent to these nutritive elements, and it was necessary to establish the normal combination in a manner to insure assimilation by the digestive organs of the young animals which in their first and imperfect development demand a very delicate apportionment of these properties—an appor- tionment which, to be effective, must be analagous to that which exists in the natural milk. It is evident that here lies the difficulty. By means of deep thought, great perseverance, and at, a very great cost, it is at last overcome. But it is to an Englishman that we owe the work of bringing this production to perfection, and which is now in great favour with dairymen under the name of ' Milkaline.' The writer of this article is an old agriculturist, having an experience of nearly half a con- wry in the rearing of cattle. From the commencement of the discovery of this new production, I was struck with the practical advantages that must arise from its use, and I hastened to try it, and I have obtained the most happy results. PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDLRE.—The Daily News says the Government have framed a complete scheme for deal- ing with Parliamentary procedure. Mr. Gladstone on Wed- nesday received a copy of it from Sir Michael Hicks- Beach. A copy has also been submitted to the Speaker, who, we believe, has expressed his favourable opinion of the proposals.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly fleeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday, the chair being oc- cupied by the Rev. G, F. Roberts. There were also presept Messrs. Harrison, Brown Derbyshire, Broad- bent, Greening, Blackhurst, Brown, Gibson, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Ratcliffe, and J. C. Sutton (clerk.) TUB CHRISTMAS DINNER : THE MASTER'S REPORT. The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported that, in accordance with the order of the Board about tie fruit and beer for the inmates' Christmas dinner, he begged to say that there were two half barrels of beer ordered, supposed to contain 144 quarts, as would be seen by the order book. There were over 400 people who had dinner, 291 of them having beer, and the total consumption, including a little given to the helpers, who sat up the previous night preparing pud- ding, loss in stillaging, serving, dm, was 145 quarts, being under a pint to each of the recipients. There was 136 lbs. of currants and 186 lbs. of raisins ordered, making 30 lbs. of fruit, 384 i lbs. of fruit was made into mince meat, pud- dings, kc , leaving 7i lbs. in store. Well knowing that many of the poor people were half starved before their ad- mission, and being on a restricted diet while there, he thought it was the wish of everyone that they should have a good dinner on Christmas lay, and plenty of it. There- fore he gave it tbem without weighing to each one, as many of them were served a second and third time. Con- sequently, be must apologise for being unable to comply with that part of the Board's order. In conclusion per- haps he might be alio Red to say that neither the matron nor himself had any dinner on that day, neither did they taste the beer. On January 13th Mr. Reynolds' family gave the inmates a musical entertainment, which was very much appreciated by them, and in their name and on their behalf he begged to offer them his best thanks for such consideration and kindaess.—Mr. GREENING said that he felt perfectly satisfied with the use that had been made of the beer, and that the quantity consumed had not been excessive.—Mr. BLecxann.s.r said that a deal of trouble would have been saved if they had had that information at first. He was perfectly satisfied with the information. although at the same time he thought that they ha 4 been rather extravagant.—Mr. Ginsox said that he thought the quantity excessive. It did not seem likely that they would get more explanation, but he should make it his business to attend the audit and call the attention of the auditor to the excessive amount.—Mr. HARRISON : Do you think it excessive when you consider the large number of people fed here ?—Mr. GIBSON : Yes.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that he also thought it was excessive. Tha fruit should have made puddings for 1,000 people, according to the returns for other unions. He did not see why that Union should require three times as much fruit for puddings as ether unions. He did not think the explanation a satisfactory one.—Mr. GIB- SON : Everyone that I have mentioned it to say that it is unreasonable.—The CHAirOnAN We voted a Christmas dinner.—Mr. GissoN : We did not vote a Christmas dinner for the whole week —Mr. BROWN said that ne more fruit was ordered this year than last. He was perfectly sure that there had not been a pennyworth of waste or extravagance. (Hear, bear.) A full explanation might not have been given, but the members had a right to attend the committee meetings, and it WAS there that quastions should be asked. They should not ask the questions at the Board meeting for the purpose of figuring in the newspapers as though they were the greatest economists under the sun. He was mire that the House was worked economically, and that the total cost would oompare very well indeed with the cost in other unions.—The discussion then dropped. SCHOOL COMMITTEE.

The report of Mr. Mines, superintendent of the schools, stated that, notwithstanding the severity of the weather, the children generally continued healthy and cheerful. The annual Christmas tree and prize distribution took place in the schools on the sth inst. The prizes were distributed by the Rev. G. F. Roberts, chairman of the Board of Guardian;, who, together with Mr. Darbyshire, addressed the children. A large number of friends from Warrington, were present to witness the distribution. At the close of the prize giving a tnusical programme was gone through by several friends, who gave their serviCes gratuitously, among whom he especially had to thank Mr. A. E. Maisey And Mr. Nebo- field. who came from Manchester for the sole benefit of the children. He had also to thank Miss Edie Bennell, Miss L. Horton, Miss Perry, Mrs. Schofield, Mr. Peers Brimelow, Mr. Gflo. Fairhurst, cad Mr. I'. London for the part they took in the programme. Mr. Henley, Governtnent Inspec- tor, visited the schools on the previous Friday, and after going through the homes and hospital, expressed himself pleased with their clean and tidy appearance, and the im- provements which were being made in the lavatories and playgrounds. On behalf of the children he had to thank Mrs. Sheridan for her invitation to the pantomime on Satur- day last, which they much enjoyed, and also Mr. Hill, of Howley, for several volumes of the "Christian Miscellany." A deputation of Guardians from the Ormskirk Union. to- gether with their chairman and clerk, visited the schools for the purpose of ascertaining the mode of furnishing and general management prior to opening their new schools at Ormskirk. The chairman was in attendance to meet the deputation.—The report was adopted on the motion of the CHAIRMiN, seconded by Mr. W. Hourarrosr. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee reported that fees had been allostfed in 159 cases, of which 129 were old cases.—The Chairman said he supposed that the large number of appli- cations was still due to the distress in the fustian cutting trade.—Mr. BROWN: Yes, that is so.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. BLACKHURST, seconded by Mr. BROWN. This was all the business of interest.

div.head: SPOOPENDYKES GO CLAM
div.p: THE SPOOPENDYKES GO CLAM
DIGGING.

TM Now, my dear," said Mr. Spoopendyke, appearing before his wife one July morning, in a pair of top boots, canvass pants, and a son' wester hat. "Now, ray dear, look alive. I'm going to the beach to dig clams, and you may go along if you want to." _ _

Have you got a shdvel for me?' a.sked Mrs. Spoopen- dyke, jumping up and arranging her toilet. "Well, no," rejoined Mr. Spoopendyke, eyeing her gloomily. "There's an old steam reaper out back of the hotel, and I saw a man yesterday with an improved stamp machine. You may hire either of those, but I'm going to dig clams with a hoe." _
"Then I'll dig with a hoe, too," smiled Mrs. Spoopendyke, pleasantly, as she looped up her skirt. "Say, dear, I have never been at the seaside before, and don't know how clams grow."

They don't grow old fixing their frocks, anyway," re- plied Mr. Spoodendyke, impatiently. If you are going clamming with me, you'd better begin to think it over, because the clams along this shore go to bed at dark and they haven't any night bell. Hurry up, will ye r r m ready," fluttered Mrs. Spoopendyke, casting a glance at the mirror and pulling her basque down behthd "Is that my hoe ?" she inquired, as her husband handed her a short-handled implement with a broad blade. " What.do I do with it?' "You begin by taking it out of my earl" growled Mr. Spoopendyke, dodging the flying utensil. "And if you succeed in getting it out alive, you put it under your arm. Now, if you've got through drilling with that koe, we'll start." "Do the clams bite at this hoe, like fish 7' she asked, as they walked over the sands toward the sea. "I suppose, when they take hold and begin to wiggle, I jerk 'em up quick, don't I ? " "Not too quick," grinned Mr. Spoopendyke, sarcastically. "If you are too sudden you're apt to make the clam mad, and he'll pull you into the hole, hoe and all. Now, look here," he continued, stopping near the water's edge and pointing to some little holes about the size of a lead pencil. "There's a clam in each one of those and they've got to come out." " Pooh! " ejaculated Mrs. Spoopendyke, stoutly, "I'm not afraid of any clam that can get into that hole! But how am lever to poke this hoe in there?"

You dig here, and I'll go over yonder," replied Mr. Spoopendyke, moving a little way off. "You watch how I do it, and then you begin." Mrs. Spoopendyke eyed him as he chopped away at the sand a few minutes, and thinking she had the hang of it, she started in. "Hi ! Hold' on there, will ye? What ye doing, any. how ? " he roared as the sand and water from his wife's energetic hoe flew all over him. "What d'ye think ye are, anyway, a dredging machine? Whoop, there! quit, I tell ye!" asked Mrs. Spoopendyke, redoubling 1. oho els, ggo iaround.e t away,"There's t ohnee nhere,,t, ha en 'rde eGlffogotar teoss:sewithout e dear?" and Mrs. Spoopendyke, though considerably out of breath, went to business with renewed vigour. "Graciorta, how ea thinksr ? :" fast they must run!" she added, fairly filling the air with more water and sand. "Whoop, there! Wall!" yelled Mr. Spoopendyke, drenched through, and his eyes plugged up with sections of the sea beach. "Stop it, can't ye?" "I will ifll can," sobbed Mrs. Spoopendyke, hysterically. "He hasn't come out yet, and I think he must .be going down deeper. But I'll get him !" and she put all her strength into the operations until a howl of pain from her husband induced her to look around, when she saw him stretched on the shore, kicking at the zenith with prodigious energy. "Did be bite you, dear ?" she exclaimed, dropping the hoe and rushing to Mr. Spoopendyke's side. No, he didn't bite me !" squealed Mr. Spoopendyke, dodging his head, under the impression that more clams Were after him. "Re only knocked ray mouth off and stove an eye in! Couldn't ye tell they were clams when ye saw 'ere coming out of the holes? Think ye can tell the difference between a clam and a court-house another time? If I didn't know any more than you do, I'd wrap myself in shells, dig a hole in the mud, and crawl in and study until I improved my mind some !" "I don't care," murmured Mrs. Spoopendyke, as she pre- pared to follow her husband home. "I didn't know these things were clams; I thought they were rocks. Anyway, -it was lucky he was where he could catch 'em, or they'd all been lost through my ignoranoe," and with this mental con- fession she put the clams in the sou' wester hat and started off, wondering if thev were good to eat, or only used to fire at cats.—Drake's Magazine.

• THE LIBERALS OF WIDNES. DINNER TO MR. E. K. MUSPRATT. On Monday night, a complimentary dinner was given at the Reform Club, Dale.street, Liverpool, to Mr. E. K. Mus- pratt, by the members of the Liberal Association for the Widnes Parliamentary Division ; Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, chairman of the association, presiding. About 150 guests sat do rrn to a capital dinner, served up in excellent style under the direction of Mr. A. Stacheli' house-steward. Amongst other guests were Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, A. Eccles, T. S. Timmis, J. A. Doughan, T. Brocklebank, J. L. Muspratt, F. H. Gossage, Colonel Mewburn, Rev. G. Beau- mont, Rev. W. Davies, J. K. Muspratt, J. Speakman, R. H. Davis, J. Clarkson, T. J. Peters. P. Handley, B: Brown, R. Craig, E. Carey, H. Brunner, H. Wide Deacon, C. Aldrich. EP B. Shores, &c.
Letters of apology were received from Sir Thomas Brocklebank, Messrs. W. B. Bowring, W. Oalton, and others.

The Chairman proposed the toast of "The Queen," and afterwards, in proposing "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Reyal Family," said they had all been looking forward with .interest to the intended visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to Liverpool in the course of the present week, and they must all have shared the general regret of the nation at the cause which had prevented the Princess of Wales from attending with her illustrious con- sort. He trusted elle would be speedily restored to her ac- customed health, and that at some future time they would have the pleasure of seeing her in that city. (Ap- plauee.) The Chairman then proposed the toast of "Our late can- didate, Mr. E. K. Muspratt," and in doing so said that when he looked round that large and cheerful company he found it somewhat diffieult to believe that they all were that night the representatives of a party which was so badly beaten at the poll on a recent occasion ; but he knew they all felt, as he did hinself, that they were beaten under very excep- tional circumstances. (Applause.) But, nevertheless, they' were the strongest party in the Widnes Division—(applanse) —and they had no doubt that before long they would see a great change. (Applause.) They had lost the last elec- tion not from the strength of their opponents, but because of the unexpected secession of one wing of the Liberal party, which, acting in obedience to commands from their leaders, felt constrained to go against their own sympathies and their own wishes and to vote for that party to which they had been opposed, and which had opposed them from time immemorial. He was free to confess that when he saw their Irish friends, in obedience to a compact which had been made with what he might almost call their natural enemies, turn their backs upon their old friends, he was deeply grieved. But that compact had already apparently fallen to pieoes—(applause)—and he could not but think that Mr. Parnell, for whom on many points he had a great respect, as an able man and a patriot—(applause)— must see and feel the mistake which he had made in parting company with his old friends and the friends of Ireland. (Applause.) The lory member for Widnes was now, accord- ing to his (the speaker's) political view of matters, in a state of instability—(applause and laughter)—and he thought that when next Mr. Moss had to appear before his constituents they would see that " Humpty Dampty will have a great fall." (Laughter and applause.) Lord Salis- bury and his colleagues had denied that they had entered into any understanding or made any compact with the Irish party. Well, the human conscience sometimes indulged in extraordinary vagaries, and he could only suppose that Lord Salisbury reconciled that denial to his conscience something in the same manner as the two Scotah farmers, of whom they might perhaps have heard, who satisfied their con- sciences with relation to a breach of the Sabbath day. These two farmers were 'walking together "from kirk" on a Sun- day, when Sandy said to Donald: "Donald, my man, it's no good to talk business on the Sabbath day'; but, Donold, sup- posing this were Monday what would you tak' for your coo?" Says Donald: "Oh, supposing this were no' Sunday I would tak' six pun ten." "Oh, mon," says Sandy, "You want a enickle lot o' siller ; but supposing this were Monday would you tak' six pun? " " Weel," said Donald. " suppos- ing it were Monday I would tak' six pun'." (Loud laughter.) He thought Lord Salisbury, Lord R. Churchill, and their friends, must have taken a lesson in casuistry from the Scotch farmers. (Applause.) But, be that as it might, he believed the day was not far distant when what would probably be a short and tronblous session would come to an abrupt termination, and he expected they would be able to meet again in that room for the purpose of paying another compliment to Mr. Muspratt and wishing him all success. (Loud applause.) He did not know whether all the circumstances connected with Mr. Muspratt's coming forward were known to them, but he might tell them that, though doubtless Mr. Muspratt felt, as every man must have felt

, —honoured by the invitation from a constituency such as Widnes—yet there were many private and personal con- siderations which weighed so mach with him that he did not feel, in justice to himself and to others, that he could accept that flattering invitation; and it was only when they assured Mr. Muspratt that of all men known he was the fittest—(applause)—and the most likely to be acceptable to the various sections of the great Liberal party in the divi- sion, and that they considered the Irish party, which was so strong and numerous in the division, were entitled to-have a candidate who would be reasonably acceptable to them— (applause)—that Mr. Muspratt consented to come forward to contest the division, on condition that his candidature was acceptable to the bulk of his constituents. (Applause.) They had had a complimer t paid to Mr. Muspratt which, in his (the chairman's) pxoerience, had not been paid to any man before. His name was brought before the four separ- ate districts in the division and was unanimously accepted by all the four. (Applause.) MrS`Muspratt had come before them under peculiar circumstances, amongst ,which was the sudden and unexpected death of his brother, and he stipu- lated that he should therefore be excused from anything be- yond an address to be given to each of the four dietricta of the division: but they all knew how he had warmed to his work and how thoroughly he had done it. (Applause.) If eVer they had had an honest and earnest candidate they had one in Mr. Muspratt. (Applause.) Mr. Muspratt was an able man, not one who took up opinions simply for the purpose of a canvass, but one who from youth to manhood had been slowly forming his opinions, until his opinions became convictions, which ha laid before his constituents with per- fect frankness, and with an ability and logical power which was seldom met with. (Applause.) He would not enter into any question of Mr. Muspratt's opinions. Be did not always agree with the opinions which Mr. Muspratt bad pat forth in the course of his late campaign; but he did say that the Liberal party and Liberal opinions covered a large and wide area, and so long as the members of that party were within that area, and moving in the same direction as the rest of the party, they must be welcomed into their body. (Applause.) The only point they had to look to as members of the Liberal party was that there should be a large and generous liberality shown one towards another in the expreseion of political opinion. (Cheers.) Mr. T. Brocklebank, in supporting the toast, said he had been asked by the chairman to do so as representing another section of the Liberal party. As regarded their late candi- date, he coeld only say, as the chairman bad said, that a better candidate than Mr. Muspratt, who expressed the opinions ef the majority of the Liberals of the Widnes Division, could not possibly have been found. (Applause.) Without wishing to enter into any political discuesion, he might say that he was present at many meetings where Mr. Muepratt addressed the electors, and he had been pleased and struck by the very able manner in which be handled the subject of trade. (Hear, bear.) They all knew the very bad state of trade in Ws country, and all of them wished tkey knew the remedy to be proposed and carried oat.. Mr. Muspratt, in many of his speeches, threw more light on the cause of trade depression and made more sug- gestions on this subject than he (Mr. Brocklebank) had had the Pleasure of listening to before in other speeches. He had observed that Mr. Muspratt bad been mentioned on the toast list as their late candidate, and he hoped most sincerely that Mr. Miispratt would not only be 'their late candidate but their future candidate. (Loud ' applause.) The toast was then drank with much enthusiasm. Mr. E. K. Muspratt received a most flattering reception in rising to acknowledge the toast. He said the terms in which the chairman had proposed his health were far too Mattering to him—(cries of "No, no," and "Not a bit of it "),—and the fact a so large a number of the Widnes electors assembling together after an electoral defeat to celebrate—or rather to dine together—was certainly re- ceived by him as a great compliment—(hear, hear, and ap- Plause,)—because dining together was supposed to be a matter for rejoicing, and he thought there was hardly any- thing to rejoice over in one sense over the late election ; but he might assume by their presence that they considered their c andidate had deserved success. (Hear, hear, and anplause.) During the late election they were oppoeed in the first instance by that party which took to itself the title of the patriotic, the religious, and the constitutional Party. (Laughter.) The Tories spoke very much about religion during the past contest, and they dubbed every- body throughout the country who said he was in favour of the Affirmation Bill an Atheist. They used the name of Mr. Bradlaugh during the late Parliament as an electioneer- ing deriee—(hear, hear); Lord Randolph Churchill was the man who first suggested that, If they would take their minds back to the beginning of the last Parliament, when Mr. Bradlaugh first presented himself and asked to affirm, and afterwards asked to take the oatb, Sir Stafford North- cote desired to allow him to affirm. (Hear, hear.) It was Lord Randelph Churchill and the Fourth Party who thought it would serve their party's interests if they prevented Mr. 'Bradlaugh affirming. They opposed Mr. Bradlaugh in every way, and Lord Randolph Churchill was the principal man who forced on that style of opposition—a man who had not the first basis of religious feeling in his composition. The Tory party called themselves the patriotic party, and when- ever delicate negotiations with other Poweat were going on they worried and opposed the Government inces- santly by questions which could do no good even after they were answered. They urged on the Government to send an army to rescue General Gordon, and did everything in their power to lessen the reputation of that great hero, while they did everything in their power to raise the reputation of Mr. Bradlaugh. (Hear, hear.) Then they claimed to be the constitutional party. But he would like to show how they merited that name. During the last Parliament, whenever they spoke of Ireland their cry was coercion and more ; coercion. But no sooner did they see office in sight, and find or think that an alliance or compact with Mr. Par- nell and an Irish policy would gain them the seals of office, than they threw over coercion. In dealing with this question of the relation of Ireland and England, did they send over a man to carry out a definite policy P No ! They simply sent oat a stop-gap, a man who by their own

showing, and by the correspondence published two daYg ago, was admittedly sent there for the purpose of carrying the Tory Government over the elections. And now that that had served their purpose the Tcries were going back to their old cry of coercion and more coercion for Ireland. If that was constitutional policy, arid if what he had shown was their religious and patriotic policy, then he would have nothing to do either with religious, or patriotic, or consti- tutional government. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Liberal party had got highereeiews of what were religion, patriot. lam, and constitutionalism. Why did he allude to will! the Tory Government had done and the Tory Parry ha" done? It was because he held it up as a lesson to the Liberal party and the Liberals 'in the Widnes Division guide their conduct in the future. Let them, at any rate' new that they were in Opposition, not follow the tactics of the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) They as Liberals, he hoped, would abide by their principles. They bad great principles, which united them: and they had all the same end in view, although some of them liked to ape proach that end perhaps somewhat slower than others. Sc) long as they remained true to Liberal principles, so long would they find that they would be respected ultimately by the country, and ultimately they would gain their ends. (Hear hear.) Through the miserable tactics of the Tory party during the last election, the question of Ireland had been placed under conditions which were extremely diffi- cult. Mr. Gladstone appealed to the country to give bins a majority large enough to do justice to Ireland, but the Tor? patty and the party of Mr. Parnell together prevented that, and they were now face to face with this Irish question, which was one extremely difficult to deal with, and it wag one which required the experience of a statesman like 311 r. Gladstone. He believed at the present time there was no statesman who had more experience than Mr. Glad* stone. The Irish question was so fraught with difficulties when they came to look at it in detail, that he thought they must wait until they heard what Mr. Gladstone with his experience would do under these circum- stances. He (Mr. Muspratt) was not afraid during the election campaign to speak upon this question, and he was not afraid now. He thought it desirable that each one of the Liberal party should give some expeession of their own honest convictions, and let them see how far they could act together. They were all agreed in this, that any man who belonged to the Liberal party was better fitted to guide this country than one who held Tory princi- ples. Their policy in the future was to organise them- selves for the purposes of an election, and secondly, be educate the people into Liberal principles. They had other difficulties to face besides the Irish question, aed he did not know that that comfortable country gentleman who was now Chancellor of the Exchequer would have a very easy task in dealing with the budget. The late Government were thrown out of office upon that matter, and he would like that they should allow the present Government to re- main in power until they present the country with their budget. (Laughter.) Another question they would have to deal with was county government. He expected that the Tory Government would do whet they had done before, and that was to ransack the pigeonholes of the Local Gov- ernment Board and find a scheme of Sir Charles Dilke and appropriate it. (Laughter and hear, bear.) Among the questions which the Liberals should educate their party upon was that of education. (Hear, hear.) There had been, he was glad to say, a very strong committee formed. and he trusted they would inquire into the subject of education, with the view of improving the education of the people. There was no doubt the Catholics were quite right from their point of view in desiring to keep up their own schools, and he thought—and he had said so during the campaign —they ought to be placed upon a perfect-equality with other schools. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had not the slightest doubt the committee would recommend that ; but he had also not the slightest doubt that they would have to abolish school fees. He noticed the other day that the late chairman of the London School Board (Mr. Bux- ton) stated that there was an increasing difficulty in getting the fees in London on account of the distress Of the people. Now be thought when they found that to be the ease they should have that whisk he advocated, and which, he dared say, lost him some fow votes—free edncatim. He had

re-ally pointed out to them what he thought should be their policy now that they were in orrposition. With regard to the suggestions thrown out by the chairman and Mr. Brock- lebankohat he should be their future candidate, all be could say was that that must depend upon circurnstanees. It was as their chairman stated that be came forward with very great reluctance owing to private circumstances, and It would depend upon those circumstances whether be should be able, if they honoured him in the future by ask- ing bite to be their candidate, to accept it. He had not the slightest doubt that they would find another candidate in the division. (Cries of "No, no.") He hoped he would be a man connected with Widnes, and he hoped that they would find many others batter fitted to represent them-- (loud cries of "No ")—thanshe might be able to de. He thanked them very heartily for the compliments they had bestowed upon him, and for the great cordiality with which they had received the toast. (Loud cheers.) Mr. A. Eccles next proposed the toast, Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party," and in doing so said that they must look to the future, and without doubt the greatest question before the country at the present time—and which would have to be dealt with in the future—was the question of Ireland. He asked them to which party could the settlement of that auestion be properly and most safely left? Certainly not to the Conservative party, whose policy with reward to Ireland had been one of coercion—for the policy they had accepted before the late elections was an election dodge, for by no other means could they have got the support of the Nationalist party. What they wanted at the present time was a party determined to do pieties to Ireland for the sake of justice, and not for the sake of snatching some small party advantage, and the only statesman able to do that was their great leader, Mr. Gladstone, who bad devoted the greater part of his life to the amelioration of the Irish people. (Applause.) Colonel Mewburn also supported the toast, and in doing Po said that Mr. Gladstone of all others was the man moat fitted to deal with the Irish question, for he would go into the question with a mind fully able and anxious to meet the difficulties of the question. They only felt grieved that after all Mr. Gladstone had done for the sister isle, Irishmen could not out their confidence in him. (Ap- plause.) When Mr. Gladstone proposed his plans for the settlement of the Irish difficulty be was sure that they would receive the united approbation and support of the Liberal party, and would carry all before them. (Applause.) Mr. F. H. Gossage, in responding to the toast, said he was a most sincere supporter of Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party. (Applause.) He thought they ought to place great confidence in a statesman like Mr. Gladstone, who was able to go back to a record fifty-three years ago tx) refute a ml•-statement. (Hear, hear.) By their belief in themselves they constituted the great Liberal party, so that when they drank the health of Mr. Gladstone they were all the time drinking to their -noble selves. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He hoped that the Liberal party would not be divided on small difficulties, so that if the time should come again when Mr. Gladstone would be in ' the opposi- tion they would find all Liberals true, and the party would not long remain in opposition. When that party was not is Opposition the advancement of the country would be secured. (Applause.) Mr. Doughan also replied to the toast. Mr. E. Carey afterwards proposed "The Widnes Division Liberal Association," and in doing co said tbat that aseocia- tion had done good work. They had a successful revision, and they had had a quiet and well-conducted election. With regard to the important question of registration, he thought they ought to have great additional facilities pro- vided in that respect, and he hoped that would be effected before long. With regard to the association's work he thought they were top apt to rely on the mere righteoasness of their cause, and left it toe much to that, whereas they ought to use argument and show their friends and neigh. boars that their cause was righteous and jast, and thereby gain the support of those people. In conclusion, he wished they had in the other three districts of the division so useful and vigorous a club as they had in Widnes. (Ap- plause._

Mr. Aldrich (Elnyton) and Mr. Beaumont (WooIton) also spoke in reply to the roast. Mr. T. S. Timmis' in propoeing the toast of the "Liberal Prem." paid a tribute to the service which the Liberal Press had rendered to the Liberal party in the past, and said that be believed in the future it would exercise a very Yiluable moderating influence. Mr. Farrie having responded to the toast, the proceedings terminated.

WRECK AND LOSS, OF 21 LIVBS.—The North German Lloyd steamer Berlin, which has arrived in the Weser, from the Brazils, landed 14 men of the crew of the Hamburg steamer Feronia (Paulsen). whi.th sank near er- schelling. The Ferona left Cuxhaven OR January 11th for the East Indies, China, and Japan, and during a heavy north-westerly gale on the same night became leaky when near Tose!, in conaequence of which the steamer sank about eight o'clock on the morning of January 12th. Thirteen men of the crew and one passenger were,picked up at 1-30 p.m. on the 13th, E half N, 14 nautical miles from Ter- schelling, by the Berlin. They had been five and a half hours in an open boat, and were thoroughly wet through. N-thing is yet known as to the fate of the captain and the rest of the persons who were on beard.—Ancther account, from Bremerhaven, states :—The Feronia (steamer), Paul- sen, left Hamburg on Monday morning, and encountered a gale from north-north-west the same evening, with a terrific sea, which smashed everything, and extinguished the fires. In the night the rudder broke, and the vessel-sank about eight a.m., 24 miles from Terscbel ling. Only one boat could be lowered, which drifted in the North SC'A for six hours with 14 persons in it, until the steamer Berlin picked them up- Twenty-one persons were drowned.

div.head: MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

A meeting was held in Bewsev-road Wesleyan Chapel on Monetay evening in connection with the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society. There was a good congregation. The chair was occupied by the Rev. James McTurk, who WAS supported by the Revs. E. Salt, J H. Jones, G. E. Cut- ting, Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., and Mr. Wright, secretary. The meeting commenced with singing and prayer.—After- wards the Sumawrany (Mr. Wright) read the annual report. which stated that the work from the first bad grown, the area of its operations had become enlarged, and the mis- sionary stations had multiplied. The report gave a digest of the work being, carried on in India, China, Wostern Africa, and other foreign parts, and referred to the efforts of Methodist ladies to alleviate the condition of the women of India. The report asked for renewed support.—The Rev. G. M. CIITTOTG then gave as interesting address, which was principally designed for the juvenile portion of the csn- gregation. His remarks he interspersed with short anec- dotes, some of them telling of events which hail come un- der the personal notice of the narrator, which were of interest alike to young and old. In spreading the gospel in foreign parts, Mr. Cutting remarked, there WAS a great deal of hard work to be done. It might be very well to come home again and address public meetings, but the work abroad demanded heroismsand more than that, it required the help of Gods—The Rev. ENOCH SALT, the deputation, in the course of an address, said that the question then be- fore them was one of profound interest, and he did not think that the interest taken in missionary work was in any way fes.gging. It seamed to him that the great questions which underlay that enterprise had an interest which could not pass away and which would not diminish. The question whether there was a dod, whether there was anything beyond the vale, and whether they were responsible in a world to come for the course that they pursued in this world, must ever be present in the human mind in one form or another, aud would continue to engage earnest attention from generation to generation. The subject of missions. as well as religion, he held to be one of great interest. Reli- gion must be missionary if it were to be in any real sense of the word enduring. He trusted that there was no doubt in the mind of any religious man as to the necessity of the Christian church being missionary, and extending and en- couraging missionary work.. Latterly their attention had been called to the condition of the people at home—the masses of people congregated is the large towns and cities of this country—and there had been brought to their knowledge such revelations of poverty. wretchedness, and irreligion as had deeply impressed, and in some cases deeply disheartened the Christian mind. But they must not say, as some people were doing, that it was their duty to concentrate their forces upon that state of their own country to the extent of withdrawing them from miesionary enterprise abroad, the fact being that unlers they encouraged missionary enterprise abroad there was no like- lihood ',that they would see their work prosper much at home. Every since Christianity was founded it had sought to spread itself far and wide. Supposing that Christianity had refused to leave Jerusalem until everyone there had re- ceived it, and had come to live in harmony with it, he ven- tured to say that the greatest missionary career on record would have had no place in history or in fact, and in that case the greatest Christian document ever penned would have had no existence. He referred to the missionary career and Christian writings of the apostle St. Paul. He believed, although it might seem paradoxical, that Christianity could not stay at home without it went abroad, for if it was attempted to confine it to one place until all the people were converted he did not think it would even prosper there. It was the religion of humanity, and must aim at embracing humanity, and only so far as it tried to realise that object would it be healthy in any district or amongst any people. Instancing the effect of missionary work. he said that fifty years ago, when it was commenced in Figi, the people were cannibals; but to-day there was not a cannibal in the island, and the people were "clothed and in their right mind." He also spoke of the civilising effect of the work in the Sandwich Isles.—A hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Salt on the motion of the Rev. J. H. JONES, seconded by Mr. HEYWOOD, and supported by the Rev. U. K. CurrlNG.—Prior to the meeting a successful juvenile collectors' tea p trty was held, and a coffee supper was par- taken of afterwards.—On Sunday missionary sermons were preached, in the morning by the Rev'. J. IL Jones, and in the evening by the Rev. G. 'F. Cutting.—Collections were made in aid of the foreign missions.
