div.head: YJREIGN NEWS,
div.p: YJREIGN NEWS,

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAINT. ACTIVITY OF THE ARABS. Stmear.--The rebels again show signs of ac- tivity, occasionally firing upon the British cavalry patrols. Two thousand two hundred rebels are reported to be between Tamai and Hendoub. A body of 100 camel loads "of am- munition. ae well as a number of rifles, are stated to have reached the rebels from Kassala. The report of guns has been heard from the direction of Tamai. General Hud- son has been appoiated to the command of a brigade in India. CAIRO, SllNDAL—lnformation has been received from the commandant of the Ghirrek garrison. He reports that the garrison are well taken care of and fed by the Abyssinians. They number more than 1,000, including women and chil- dren, and are marching across King John's country: Rumours are current that Ras Aloula is preparing to attack the rebels. Osman Digma is said to be alive and is credited with the intention of attacking Massowah. and with intend- ing to co-operate with the rebels who are hovering about Swaim, and are causing considerable uneastness to the gar- rison. On thts account, and also owing to the suepicious attitude of the inhabitants' the Seakim garrison is to be reinforced. Numbers of the enemy are reported to have been seen mar Wady Halts, upon which place the British force is strongly concentrating. THE EASTERN CRISIS. REFUSAL OF SERVIA. TO DISARM BELGRADE, SA'TIIIIDAY.—M. Garashanine has rejected the proposal of the Powers for disarmainent, on the ground that no commencement whatever having yet been made with the peace negotiations Servia desires to be protected against surprises. As another reason for refusing to comply with the BRUM:GODS of the Powers, the Servian Premier, referring to Article 1 of the armistice protocol, which fixes a term within which notice may be given to terminate the arrange- ment, points out that the Collective Note of the Powers offers no guarantees for the simultaneous disarmament of all the States concerned. Sone, SATURDAY.—It is believed that the Bulgarian Government in its reply to the Collective Note of the Powers will express its readiness to disarm as soon as the Servians do the same, or the Powers guarantee the Princi- pality against invasion. The proposal made by Servia and supported by Austria, that the delegates for the peace nego- tiations should meet at Bucharest, is objected to by the Bulgarian Government, who point cut that the International Military Commission, in its fifth sittiag, designated Sofia as the place of meeting. ATHENS, SUNDAY.—The Greek Government declines to accede to the request of the Great Powers to disarm. Other classes of the army and navy reserves will shortly be called Out. ST. PETERSBURG, WEDNESDA.Y.—The semi-official Journal de St. Petersburg, referring to the refusal of Greece and Servirtodemebilise, says : The Powers will redouble their efforts to attain the end in view. Such a course is called for, not only from regard for the dignity of Europe, but also by the necessity of preventing calamities the extent and issue of wirch none can foresee. The Servian, Greek, and Bul- garian Governments should therefore demobilise under the conditions desired by Europe. EXTENSIVE TURKISH ARMAMENTS. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDLY.—The Porte has iLISt or- dared 500 pieces of field artillery from Messrs. Krupp, and 14 canon of 24 centimetres for batteries. It is maintained In Russian Armenian circles, but denied by the Porte, that M. de Nelidoff has recommended the Ottoman Government to carry into effect Article 61 of the Berlin Treaty relating to reforms in Armenia

THE CIROLINES QUE6TION. Roam, SUNDAY.—The Latin text of the Allocution pro- nounced by Leo XIII. clearly shows that the main object for which the Consistory on Friday was held was to afford the Pope an opportunity for giving the College of Car- dinals and the world fuller information regarding the reasons on which his proposals as mediator were based. and expressing his conviction that the fact of the refer- ence of the Caroline Islands difficulty to the Pontiff is a proof of the necessity for a full restoration of his liberty and rights. He expressed his satisfactidn that his proposals had been accepted. PRINCE BISMARCK AND THE POPE. BOMB, MONDAY.—Prince Bismarck's reply to the Pope's Inquiry as to when it would be convenient to the Imperial Chancellor to receive the Papal Envoys deputed to invest him with the insignia of the Order of Christ, is published to-day by the Vatican organs. The reply, whieb is written in French, addresses the Pope as "Sire," and "Your Holi- ness."' The Prince expressed deep gratitude for the decora- tion and the Pope's letter accompanying it, and says that the mark of approval has afforded him all the more pleasure as being connected with a work of peace, in which he was able to co-operate. The Imperial Chancellor's letter con- cludes by declaring that so far as he is concerned, he will always and readily take any opportunity, consistent with the fulfilment of his duty towards his Master and his country, to testify his gratitude to the Pope. . FRANCE.—MINISTERIAL DECLARATION. Penis, SATURDAY.—The Ministerial declaration was read to-day in the Senate and Chamber of Deputies. It states that the composition of the Cabinet indicates the line of conduct which it is intended to pursue. A policy of con- ciliation will be adopted towards the various Republican sections, each being required to make certain sacrifices in return for the sacrifices agreed to by the others. Such a course, it is added, must result in'a gradual advance, pru- dent but continuous. towards the reforms demanded by the democracy. Reference ist then made to the necessity of effecting changes among certain officials who, while serving the Government, consider them selves at liberty to openly oppose it. The intervention of the clergy in politi- cal contests is also condemned. Rigid economy is promised, and some adjustment of taxation not affecting the price of food; in order to restore the equilibrium of the finances. The country being tired of distant enterprises which entail many sacrifices without adequate compensation, the Government will try to restrict those sacrifices, while endeavourinc to obtain the greatest advantages from the possessions already acquired. PA.RIS, MONDAY.—General de Ceurcy Lae been recalled to France, and will be replaced in Tonquin by General Warnet.

ANOTHER TRAGEDY IN PARIS. An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris states : Yet another tragedy has to be added to the list of crimes which have lately occurred here. A painter named Bel- lingert fired a revolver at his mistress, lodging the bullet in her head. He then tried to blow his brains out, but failed. • THE UNITED STATES.—STRONG LA/fGUA.GE TOWARDS ENGLAND. NEW YORK, MONDAY —The Irish in this city continue to display considerable activity in raising funds to assist Mr. Parnell. WASHINGTON, tolmenev.—ln the Senate to-day. Mr. Frye. senator for Maine, called attention to the fact that the treaty with Great Britain relating to Canadian fisheries had been prolonged, and moved a resolution pointing out the unfair position in which American fishermen had been placed hitherto, and declaring that, in the 'opinion of the Senate, Congress ought to appoint a Commission to adjust the question. Speaking in support of this resolution, Mr. Frye inveighed against the course pursued by Great Britain in this pestion. Several Republican Senators afterwards joined in the debate calling attention to the action taken by President Cleveland' in consenting to the indefinite exten- sion of the fishing treaty, and intimating that the Preeident had exceeded his powers. The Committee of the Senate has reported in favour of the appointment of a Commis- sion to regulate international commerce. A united States war vessel attached•to the Pacific squadron has been ordered to Same*. THE PROPOSED RAILWAY BETWEEN WINNIPEG AND HUDSON'S BAY. WINNIPEG, MONDAY.—The English and Canadian en- gineers who were sent out in Ostober last by the British capitalists and Canadian contractors to survey the route of the proposed railway from Winnipeg to Hudson's Bay have returned here. They report that the road will not only be practicable but can be easily constructed. THE NIHILISTS IN RUSSIA. BERLIN, TUEEDAY.— Intelligence from St. Petersburg announces the discovery by the police of a Nihilist resort opposite the Annitchkin Palace. A quantity of bombs and explosive material, a secret printing press, and documents of a compromising character were seized, and several Nihi- lists were arrested on the premises. • THE CONDITION OF BURMAH. MANDALAY, JANUARY 15.—The flying columns lately sent out have returned here. In a skirmish with a party of dacoits; the Madras Infantry lest one man killed and three wounded. The enemy's loss was unknown. Great satis- faction is expressed by the civil and military authorities at Lord Dufferin's approaching visit to Burmah, when it is hoped that a firm policy will be announced, as the present political situation inspires uneasiness. A troop of cavalry and a Bombay mountain battery have been deepatched to reinforce the garrison at Moutshobo. A large number ef Burmess from Upper Burmah are coming into Lower Burtnab.

TROOPS FOR BURMAH. CALCCrTTA, WEDNESDAY.--Ia consequence of the repre- sentations of the Rangoon Chamber of Commerce the Indian Government has decided to immediately despatch the 18th Bengal Native Infantry to Burmah. DELHI, TcESDA.Y.—the Viceroy to-day inspected the first and second army corps, comprising 35,000 men of all arms The troops then marched past, the cavalry and artillery afterwards repassing the saluting point at a trot. The whole programme could not be carried out owing to heavy rain. FIGHTING IN BURMA.H. • 31YINGYAN, TimaSDAY.—ColOnel Ornmannev attacked Kumnah,on Monday. The rebel princes took. to flight. Thirty of the enemy were killed and six guns captured. One Sepoy was captured. THE AFGHAN FRONTIER. MERY TUESDAY.—Aocording OS later intelligence frem the Russian Delimitation Commission, dated Meruchak, Saturday, the weather had improved and the topographical surveys were being continued. The British Commissioners had commenced the survey of the frontier district from Davletabad, proceeding by way of the Sangalik river to the Amu Dania. On the 13th inst., New Year's Day (0.5.), the Khan of Penjdeb, accompanied by all the Sank chiefs, came to the Russian camp to offer his congratulations. M. Le•sar and Captain Komaroff went to Le.itcbak yesterday to make a prelimiaary survey in Connection with the fron- tier line to be traced between Karen' Khan and Khoja- Bales.

div.head: 11 E I,X4MINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 23, 1886.
div.p: 11 E I,X4MINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 23, 1886.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. •Mr. Gladstone states that no deputation will be re- ceived by him on the Irish question, as announced in the newspapers. Tie Duke of Devonshire's Irish tenantry have accepted the 20 per cent abatement offered to them, and are now freely paying their rents. The tenants on Lord Antrim's estate, in Antrim, have re- fused to pay any rent unless a reduction of 50 per cent is granted. At Feries Chapel, on Sunday, the family of Mr. O'Con- nell Curtin, who was shot by moonlighters. were jeered and howled at as they entered the place of worship. They re- mained until the close of the service, and, on leaving, there was a still greater disturbance, the police, over a dozen in number, having to charge the people to make way for the Curtin family. EXECUTION OF SILEEFILN.—WiIIiarn Sheehan, the man who to get possession of the family effects murdered his mother, sister, and brother at Castletownroche, about seven years ago, and afterwards concealed their bodies in a well, ahere they lay undiscovered till a few- months ago, was hanged at Cork on Wednesday. He is said to have expres- sed great penitence for his crime. BLACK Mait.—lt was recently reported that the National League party at Mitchelstown had decidei to levy a rate of is in the pound on the tenants of the Kingston estate to suppoit such of the tenants as might be proceeded against for refusing to pay their rents. A circular now issued from the offices of the League instructs certain persons to get in the rate, and says that the names of contributors and de- faulters will be printed and posted at the church and chapel gates, and at various public places in the neighbour-

hood. - STARTATION IN IRBLAND.—" An Irish High Sheriff " writes to a London contemporary t,) express the far that famine is approaching in Ireland. "Along the roads," he says, lam struck by the hungry and dejected look, when bad whiskey has not eoddened the faculties. A. few days ago my agent asked a number of small farmers what per- centage would enable them to pay a year and a half's rent. 'Sir,' said they, not 100 per cent; we're starving.' I be- lieve this is perfectly true. There is nothing to be found , on their homesteads." No KENT.—The Killarney correspondent of the Irish Times says that on Monday night about 20 men, armed and , disguised, visited several farmers' houses at &sheen, Knock- nahoe, and ether townlatads to the east of Killarney, and cautioned the tenants on no account whatever to pay their rents, as otherwise " their fate Wie sealed." They fired j shots outside each house they visited. Several of the far- I mers thus visited acquainted their landlord, Mr. D. C. Colts- man, of the circumstances, but though the police have in- vestigated the ,matter, none of the armel party could be identified DV any of the farmers or. any members of their families. LANDLORDS' DEIVNCE.—At a meeting of the Landlord's Defence Uaion in Cork, on Saturday, it was decided to pre- pare a memorial making "a strong representation a' to 1 Government regarding the state of the country. To add I to the force of this appeal the officials of the Union have forwarded for publication a series of ". outrages" reported , 'by members at the meeting of the Union on Saturday. In ; no case is the name of the district given where the outrages 1 are alleged to have taken place, and in One Case it was sta- ted that a school was boycotted because legal documents directed against tenants passed through the hands of the locii postmaster, who was father of the young lady who presided over the echooL In another case the family of a I deceased man experienced difficulty in getting a coffin, I hearse, Jec., for the purpose of burial. Burnt. 11,1ruhsto..—A. well-to-do farmer, named Edmund I Allen, was shot dead within three miles of the town of Tip- perary on Saturday. A. few days ago the land steward of Mr. Chadwick, a boycotted landlord, load lent him a horse, and'he went to Damerville House on Saturday afternoon to return it. He arrived at Damerville House at half-past four, and walked away down the avenue. Soon after pass- ing out at the entrance gate his way lay along a narrow road with a high wall at each side. Hera his dead body, still warm, was found etretched on the road a few minutes after five o'clock. Three farmers, who found the body, took it on a cart to the house of one of them and summoned a doctor, who found three bullet wounds in the back. Dee ceased had been for some time in litigation with neighbours about a right of passage, and on Thursday a man was fined £2 or a month's imprisonment in a case in which the de- ceased was the complainant. On a previous occasion ano,her man prosecuted •bY the deceased was sent to prison for three menthe. Deceased was a Pretestant, and is stated that he was a cousin of Allea, one of the " Manchester

martyrs." DEPUTATION TO LORD HARTINGTON.—A deputation waited on Lord Hartington in London, on Wednesday, from the trading and commercial classes of Ireland, as re- presented by the Belfast and Dublin Chambers of Com- merce and other commercial organisations, to suggest action regarding the state of affairs in Ireland. After addresses from several speakers, who alluded in more or less strong terms to the evils under which the commercial classes of Ireland laboured by reason of the prevalence of the law of the National League and its system of boycotting, and who called upon his lordship as a representative of the Liberal party to use his influence to stop such a state of things, Lord Hartington said that while haying listened to them with deep attention he should hardly think it right, on the eye of the opening of Parliament, to express any opinion, nor had he any authority to express any opinion on behalf of the Liberal party. In the course of a few hours they would learn the intentions of the Government in regard to the Irish question. and until they had heard what those in- tentions were he would refrain from attempting to define the policy of the Liberal party. PROTEST AGAINST HOI.Vie RCLIL—A meeting of the City and County Constitutional Club was held at Limerick on Saturday for consideration of the several Irish questions which are likely to become prominent, and for the drawing up of resolutions to be presented to Lord Salisbury, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Lord-Lieutenant, and the Irish Chief Secretary. The Knight of.Glin, who presided, in opening the proceedings, referred to the proposed county boards as in his opinion just as dangerous to the country as a Home Rule Parliament sitting in'College Green. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. James Spaight proposed a series of re- solutions protesting against the formation of any separ- ate legislative body for Ireland, declaring their firm COM- viction that legislation must lead to the loss of public credit, the destruction of ' property of all sorts and a reign of terror in which crime must go unpunished and life and property be unprotected ; and protesting most strongly against the abandonment of the Loyalists of Ireland. The fourth and last resolution declared that " owing to an or- ganise4 resistance of the law by an association making use of coercion And terrorism to gain its ends, the state of Ire- land is unbecoming a civilised country, and requires imme- diate and firm action on the part of the Government to pro- tect life, liberty, and order, and restore the supremacy of the law." Mr. Spaight, in supporting the resolutions, ac- cus€d Earl Spencer and Mr. Trevelyan of being responsible for the rise of the National League. He held toat they were not living under the law of England. but under the law of the National League. The speaker also condemned the pro- posal to establish county boards as a slow and painful way of extinguishing the loyal minority.—Viscount Guillamore seconded the resolutions which were nnanimously adopted. —A resolution was then proposed and unanimously carried condemning the proposal to establish county boards in Ire-

land. LORD SALISBraT AND IRISH DayrTATioNs.—Lord Salis- bury, replying on Tuesday evening to deputations from various Irish Loyalist associations, said it was impossible that the Government should not be deeply impressed with the number, character, and weight of the arguments of the deputations, whose statements indicated how grave was the crisis that brought them together. The information they had laid before him was most valuable, very striking, and very painful. It was painful to hear of an aesociation overshadowing the law and superseding ordinary tribunals. I was painful to heir of works that were done by the tremendous engine of intimidation, and of the certainty of power with which it penetrates into the most intimate relations of social life, add of the difficnlty there appears to be on the part of any class in resisting its effects. It was painful and instructive to hear that the machinery of local government in Ireland was used for as- sisting, those combinations of whose existence and power the deputation bad given so many instances. It would" not be seemly two days before the opening of Parliament for him to go into the question of the Government's policy, but he assured them that Government would not be untrue to the responsibilities which rested at such a moment on the Government of the United Kingdom. INGENDIARY SPEECHES OF PUSH MEMBERS OF PARLIA- MENT.—On Tuesday, at the National League meeting, Mr. Deasy, M.P. (presiding), said the Nationalists disregarded coercionovell knowing that they would before the year's end make their own laws. The landlords were the real criminals, and the vengeance of heaven would yet fall upon them. In spite ef their cry, the rents would come down to one half what they were at preseet. Mr. William Redmond, vt.r., said the Irish party would get liberty for the frisk

nation. or, once for all, tear the mask of constitutionalism from the face of England. They only asked for their just rights, and, if refused, let England take the consequences* Would the Government punish Viscount Cole for urgir:a ' that the Roman Catholics should be hunted out of Ferman- agh? Lord Carnarvon had been a very soft, old womanish sort of man since he came to Ireland, but what•w'as he going , to del with this fellow ? The Nationalists ought to redouble their efforts for Horne Rule, as he did not believe landlord- ' ism would be abolished until they got their own Parlii- ntent.—Mr. Edward Harrington, M.P.. said that if the Brit- ish Government wanted to put down crime and outrage, let I them remove the cause. (Applause.) Kerry, one of the most disturbed counties, was also one of the most rack-rented.—Mr. M. J. Kenny, M.P., did not apprehend the interference with the National League, as it was too arduous aa undertaking, and involved the overthrow in a few weeks of any Government that would attempt it. The English would have to eonsider whether to accept the Irish members as the constitutional spokesmen of the Irish people and accede to their demands, or fight the question out with moonlighters, who would bind themselves together like the Whiteboys of old to save their homes from feloni- ' eus landlordism. (Applause.)

THE MERSEY TUNNEL. OPENING BY THE PRINCE Ole WILES. The formal ceremony of opening the Mersey Tun- nel was performed at Liverpool, on Wednesday, by ! the Prince of Wales. Punctually at the appointed ' time, ten minutes past noon, the train conveying the Prince of Wales and suite from Chester entered the central station of Birkenhead. The long street behind the railway station known as Argyll-street South was . all a-flutter with bunting. Small boys kept them- , selves warm by pelting each other with 'snowballs, and shouting " Three cheers for the Prince of ! Wales 1" and a large crowd of soberly attired, quietly- demeanonred people stood patiently behind the im- provised barricades beyond which they must pass; but for the rest, the town wore its usual humdrum as- pect. Down below, seated on a kind of improvised I gallery flanking the platform, were hundreds of the Birkenheak folk, a good many even of the prettiest I among them looking somewhat pinched and blue With 1 the cold. They would have been colder still but for the forethought of some people, who stretched a can- vass awning overhead, and of others who scraped away from the deal benches the snow which lay two or three inches deep. On the right awl left plat- forms a guard of honour of Cheshire Volunteers— namely, the Ist Rifles and Ist Engineers—was drawn up. Most of the spectators had been waiting there since eleven or even half-past ten o'clock, offering in their exhibition of endurance a striking spectacle of British loyalty. It was a real relief to everybody when the Royal visitor, wrapped from head to foot in a dark greatcoat, stepped from his carriage on to the red carpeted platform, and with the least possible de- lay proceeded to the business of receiving and reply- ing to addresses, first from the directors and other officials of the Mersey Railway Company, and se- eondly, from the Corporation of Birkenhead. Mr. Knight, the secretary, read an address of welcome, given under the common seal of the company, which after gratefully acknowledging the interest which his Royal Highness takes in all enterprises appertaining to the well- being of the people, pointed out the great importance of the tunnel as a connecting link between great railway systems, and its value as a great engineering achievement. His Royal Highness, who was in excelleqt voice, said, in reply, that it was at all times a sincere pleasure to him to asso- ciate his name with any undertaking tending to promote the general welfare of the community. He did so on the present occasion with the liveliest satisfaction, for the present work was one which deserved the warmest support and encourage- ment, for it could not fail to afford material benefit not only to the important communities of Liverpool and Birkenhead, but to many millions of the industrial classes in addition. Admirable skill, indomitable patience, and incessant and unwearied energy had been displayed by all who had been engaged in bringing the work to a successiul issue. The Princess of Wales greatly regretted that she was unavoid- ably prevented from taking part in these proceedings. The Recorder of Birkenhead then read an address from the Corporation, which his Royal Highness suitably acknow- tedged. These necessary preliminaries finished, the Royal party re-entered the train, and in a minute or two reached the Hamilton-square station, where the tunnel really begins, an where the Prince spent a few minutes more in inspect- ing the magnificent machinery by which the tunnel is ven- tilated. Unless told ot it one would never guess that over- head there rolled a great istuary with gigantic steam ferry- boats churning their way across, and fleets of merchant ships of all lands from China to Peru. There was, however, just a trifling difference between this special trip and ordi- nary ones—the tunnel was lighted on both sides—gas-jets on one side, lamps on the other—and the effect as the train stormed and pounded on its way was rather pretty. It would have teen a hundred times better for the Prince bad he traversed the distance on foot, with a cigar to assist contemplation, and somebody to tell him all about the hie- tory of the enterprise, but instead of having a quiet half- hour by himself he bad to submit to being rushed through at high speed and in a crowd. This is one of the disadvant- ages of being a prince. What the Prince did not do some hundreds of people did shortly after the train plunged into, the tunnel and the line was pronounced "clear." Five ' thousand tickets were issued for the walk through, and the perambulation of the tunnel went on until seven o'clock in the evening. Three minutes' run from Hamilton-square Station brought the party to James-street Station on the Liverpool side, and here the Prince of Wales had the op- portunity of testing the splendid lifts with which this station is furnished. There are three of them, and they are eapable of raising 24.0 passengers in about 32 seconds from the platform below to the street level above, and of course lowering them from the street to the plettorm in the same brief space of time. Counting the hydraulic lifts oa the Birkenhead side, there are five in all. It was at this station that the Prince of Wades, amidst great cheering, de- clared the tunnel open. But, notwitbstanding the announce- ment, the tunnel will not be open for public traffic until the let of February. With its enormous crowds of people lining the pavement, and every window crammed with sightseers, James-street presented a very striking spectacle ; but Castle-street, just round the corner, excelled it in this respect. All the way along jams-street, and round by Castle-street to the Town Hall, the path was kept clear by strong wooden barricades, behind which at least twenty thousand people were wedged as tightly as they could stand. Order was admirably main- tained, although when at the corner where the two streets join a portion of the wooden barricade gave way with a crash, it took a squad of muscular policemen all their time to prevent a deluge of curious and ebulently loyal humanity from overflowing the open way and obstructing the Royal progress. Arrived at the Town Hall, the Prince wos pre- sented with and replied to' an address from the Mayor of Liverpool in the name of the Corporation. His Royal High- ness, in reply, said "I thank you most cordially for your address, and for the hearty welcome which you have given me in Liverpool. I appreciate very highly the loyal words in which you allude to the Queen and the members of my family ; and I can assure you that it affords me much gratification to visit once more your loyal and prosperous city. The Princess of Wales begs me to express her unfeigned and sincere re- gret at finding that 'she is tenable to fulfil her engagement here to-day, and to be thus deprived of the pleasure which she would have experienced in paying a second visit to your town, which gave her so cordial a reception on a pre- vious occasion. You rightly observe that lam deeply in- terested in every movement that is calculated to tend to the advantage and well-being of the people of this country, and it is a great satisfaction to me to think that my name will be associated with the memorable enterprise which, by completing a connecting link in our railway system, supplies a want that has long been felt in this part of the kingdom. This terminated the proceedings in the Council Chamber. The Royal party, together with a company of guests num- bering about two hundred and sixty, were next entertained by the Mayor at luncheon in the ball-room of the Town Hall. The Mayor presided at luncheon, with the Prince at his right. Auiong the guests at the head table were Lady Sefton, the Mayoress, Prince Albert Victor and the Duchess of Westminster, Prince George of Wales and the March- ioness of Ornionde, Mr. Raikes and the Princess Hohenlohe, the Earl of Sefton and the Marchioneis of Ailesbury, the Marquis of Ormonde and the Countess of Leicester. the Duke of Westminster and the Countess Spencer, Lord Claud Hamilton and Lady Lat,iom, Viscount Weymouth and the Countess Theadoree Holenlohe, Lord Alwyne Compton and Lady Cheshane, Lord Clark and Lady Alice Wilbraham, the Bishop of Liverpool and Mrs. Reikes, the Bishop of Chester and Mrs. Byte, Viscount Molyneux and Miss Harris, Lord R. Grosvenor, Sir Thomas Edwards. Loss, Oiir Thomas Earle, Sir Thomas Brocklebenk, Sir Andrew Walker, Sir James Picton, and Sir W. B. For- Wood. The brief speech in which, after the usual loyal toasts, the Prince of Wales proposed the prosperity of the Mersey Railway was frequently applauded, and especially in those passages in which he spoke of the valuable services of Major Isaac, to whom, more than to any other man, the success of the railway is doe. Ihe Prince of Wales, in the course of his reply to the toast ot his health and that of the Princess of Wales, said : I have been engaged to-day, Mr. Mayor, on an interesting and important work, a work which I feel convinced will be a very great benefit, not only to the town of Liverpool, but which will improve the vast commercial reseurces of the surrounding towns. (Applause) The difficulties in mak- ing a subterranean or subaqueousr railway are only too clear. You have hitherto bad means of taking passengers and goods over the river by steam ferries. lam aware that this right has existed a long time—l believe as far back as the eleventh century. But it is a remarkable fact that in the last year you conveyed across the Mersey from Birkenhead to Livert,ool on the steam ferries 26 million passengers and 750,000 tons of goods. (Applause.) You may say, such being the case, why do you require this tunnel, and to have your railway to connect Liverpool and Birkenhead ? The answer is that you have to encounter storms, yoa have to encounter fogs, and you bare to encounter ice. Both your passengers and your goods are very frequently imperilled. Therefore, a great engineering scheme of this kind, which will be a very great boon, is one deserving the praise of all

for those who have started it, and is quite sure to prosper. (Applause.) Not only, wilt it greatly benefit the commerce of the north-west of England, but also it will open up a rail- way system to Welee--to that beautiful, picture:nue coun- try with all ha health-giving resorts. (Hear, hear.) Ibis scheme might have taken place twenty years ago, but at that time there were difficulties, There was an idea of coil- , structing a pneumatic railway, so that we may say that the ' railway which to-day has been opened has not exceeded more than six or seven years. Great praise is due to Major Isaao—(applause)—lor the indefatigable manner in which he has carried out this work, and in finding the capi- tal; and as well as to him is due also recognition for the indomitable energies of Mr. Brunlees and .Mr. Fox, the engineers; and I must not forget to allude :to the name of Mr. Waddell, the contractor. At the head of this company we find my right hon. friend Mr. Cecil Ra.ikes, who laas had a long experience in railways. Before sitting down, as I know time is short, and there is Le time for long speeches, I wish most cordially to drink prosperity to the Mersey Railway, which I am sure you will drink most heartily, and connect with this toast the name of its chairman, Mr. Cecil Raikes. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with great cordiality. Mr. H. Cecil Rallies having replied, the Prince of Wales proposed the health of the Mayer. He said: "You are aware of the Mayor's great popularity, and his deserved popularity, for have you not elected him for a second term of office as your Mayor? As for myself, this ; is not my first visit to Liverpool, and I hope by no means it may be my last. I have always been received with the greatest kindness, and I have always looked back to my different visits with the greatest pleasure and satisfaction. When I think that 100 years ago this town numbered only 40,000 people, and that now with your suburbs it is close on 700.000, it epeaks-for its prosperity. Most cordially do 1 propose this toast, Mr. Mayor, and most sincerely do 1 wish long life and proeperity to Nit- sown. (Cheers)"

The Mayor:briefly responded. Just before luncheon an interesting ceremony took inane on the balcony of the central window of the ball-room. Ac- ccrding to long-established custom the Royalty of England, represented on this occasion by the Prince, presented itself to the gaze of the thousands of spectators who filled the streets below. A roar of cheering arose from the dense mass the moment he appeared. It seemed as if all Liverpool had poured itself into the streets. By four o'clock, the time at which the Prince of Wales started from Limehouse Station for Chester, every waggoner, every cabman, every owner of a donkey-cart, everybody who owned anything upon which anybody could stand and see over his neighbour's shoulders, made the most of an opportunitv which occurs only once or twice in one's lifetime. The 4th Dragoons went pact at a walking pace, the Prince, seated with the Mayor, following in an open carriage. Along the five streets through which the procession passed, and in the large open space which is bounded on one side by Lime-street Railway Citation and on the other by that noble building, St. George's Hall, there must have been at least 40,000 persons congregated. Toe Prince of Wales may well feel flattered by the warmth of his reception, and the Corporation of Liverpool by the excellent behaviour of the enormous multitude which swarmed the thorongh- fares. In the evening a barquet was given at the Adelphi Hotel, at which the Right Hon. H. C. Raikes, M.P., pre- sided, and which was attended by a large number of guests, amongst whom where Sir W. Forwooa, Sir F. Bramwell, President 1.C.E., Major Isaac, Messrs. Brunlees and Fox, and a number of the principal citizens of Liverpool. Sir William Forwood proposed the toast of the evening," Suc- cess to the Mersey Railway," to which Mr. Raikes re- sponded. The proceedings were very succe,sful. ln the evening also the Mayor gave an At Home and dance at St. George's Hall. Which was attended by about 1,500 guests.

div.head: NEW BISHOP OF MANCHESTER.
div.p: THE NEW BISHOP OF MANCHESTER.
(rnoic A. SHEFFIELD CORESPONDENT.)

Dr. Moorhouse ie a Sheffielder by birth and by parentage. He is the only son of Mr. James Moorhouse, cutlery manu- facturer, Devonshire-street, Sheffield, who was Master Cutler in 184-0. Dr. Moorhouse, who was born in 1826, early showed a predilection for the Church. It is elated that his father tried to dissuade him, on the ground that he had a good business to his hands and he would never do anything at college. His career has shown that his father's predic- tion, shrewd man as he was, was not verified. Young Moor- house, being allowtd his own way, entered St. John's Col- lege, Cambridge, where be took mathematical honours in the final examination for degrees. He was ordained by the Bishop of Ely to the curacy of St. Neots, where his minis- trations were so acceptable that the parishioners were anxious to retain him as vicar. But in this they were dis- appointed, for the young clergyman returned to his native town as curate of the parish church, under Dr. Sale, vicar of Sheffield. This was in 1855, and he remained in Snef- field until 1861. Many persons may yet remember his able and energetic pulpit ministrations, and his marked success with classes of young men, whilst at the meetings of the ruridecanal chapter the remarks that fell from his lips always had great weight with his clerical brethren. His efforts resulted in -the establishment of the Church Institute. The classes held at that time in Queen-street schools were in a very lagging condition. He threw his whole energy into the movement and inf deed fresh life into the work, and as a result the premises in St. James-row were erected. In 1861 Moorhouse left Sheffield. lie married Lydia, the eldest daughter of the late Dr. Sale, vicar of Sheffield. His last visit to the town in 1876 was of a very interesting character, taking place a few days after the announcement of his appointment to the Bishopric of Melbourne. It was on the occasion of the foundation stone laying of the Dyer's Hill Church, erected as a memorial of the late Canon Sale. Mrs. Moorhouse, the wife of the Bishop and daughter of Dr. Sale, laid the stone, her hasband being present as well as the Archbishop of York. After the ceremony a meeting , was held, at which Dr. Moarhouse delivered an address, some portions of which are of great interest at the present moment. Speaking of his departure for Australia he said : I cannot feel that I should otne to see you again, although you have hoped as much in my hearing. I feel that it is not right for colonial bishops to be appointed to distant Sees and then come back and air their aprons in St. James's-street. I think that it is not a right thing, and if Gad spares me I don't think my friends will often see me in in St. James's-street. It is for a colonial bishop to go to his diocese and devote himself to his work there. Perhaps seine time hence, as an old man, I may come back to Eng- land to die. _ _

Fortunately, after nine years' arduous work in his Anstra- Han diocese, Bishop Moorhouse returns to England in full health and vigour to undertake still moro responsible la. boars. Two years ago, on a rumour that the Bishop was returning to England, the secretary of the Sheffield Church Lecture Society invitid him to lecture in the town. He re- received a reply stating that the rumour was incorrect, but his Lordship added :—"I hepe some day before many years have passed to see you and dear old England once again." For many years it was the custom of the Bishop to visit his father-in-law in Sheffield at New Year, and his eveni..g ser- mon on the first &May in the year always attracted a crowded congregation to the parish church. Dr. Moorhouse is a man of scholarly distinction, a Broad Churchman, an indefatigable worker, and an unostentatious man. Tbe aop)intrnent has given the greatest satisfaction in Shef- field, and it is believed that the Manchester people will find him a most suitable successor even • to the much-lamented Dr. Fraser.

Evidence with regard to the Sheffield industries was Oven on Wednesday at a tneeting in London of the Royal Com- mission on the Depression of Trade. SHOCKIN6 AFFAIR. AT LIVERPOOL WORKHOUSE. A shocking discovery was made on Thursday morning in the Liverpool Workhouse. One of the officers perceiving a smell of fire in the lunatic department made a search, and on entering the room of a female official, Miss M'Curdy, was horrified to find her lying in front of the fire dead, her head and upper part of body being shockingly burnt. She had been suffering from neuralgia,•but was seen in bed all right about an hour previously. THE NETILERBY HALL ROBEERY.—The trial of Anthony B. Rudge. Jan. Martin, and James Baker for the Netherby robbery ana subsequent murderous outrages in Cumberland, began at Carlisle Assizes on Monday. The prisoners were arraigned upon the charge of murder, and each in turn pleaded "Not guilty." Servants at Netherby proved the robbery of £250 worth of jewelry from Lady Graham's bedroem, to which access was gained by a ladder through an open window.—Ladv Graham identified as the stolen property the jewelry -found in the river at Teebay, where Rudge and Martin were captured. The robbery was com- mitted while the family were at dinner.—Sergoant Roche identified Baker and Radge as two of the four who shut him and Johnstone at Kingstown.—Evidence followed at the attack upon Constable Fortune. As he was pursuing four men along the railway Fertune was struck on the head, ap- parently.with a jemmy. He sustained nineteen wounds, and was left bleeding and insensible at the foot of the rail- way embenkmeut.—The case was at journed.—On Tuesday the trial was resumed before Mr. Justice Day. The first evidence taken was to complete the branch of the case re- lating to the attack upon P.C. Fortune.—Dr. Walker described Fortune's wounds as such as might have been in- fi;cted by a jemmy. The wounded officer had been in a dangerous condition for a long time, but was new bett,,r, though weak.—Evidence was called to trace the progress of the prisoners from Carlisle to Plumpton.—The case was ad- journed.—Further evidence was given as to the apprehen- sion ef Rudge and Martain at Tehay with revolvers in their pockets.—The learned Judge then summed up, and the jury retired at a quarter pest seven o'clock to consider their ver- dict. After deliberating for over an hour they returned into court with a verdict of guilty against all the prisoners, upon whom sentence of death was passed. The prisoner Rudge made a remarkable speech. He seems to have ad- mitted the murder, but protested that Martin and Baker were innocent of that crime. Mr. Justice Day has awarded the police officers and railway men engaged in the capture ef the prisoners sentenced for the Netherby robbery and murder the 'urn of £177. Of this Superintendent Ssmpill receives £25 for his vigilance and efficiency; Inspector Roche, £2O; Sergeant Johnstone, £2O; and Police•constable Fortune £2O, for bravery. Tne remaining portion is divided amongst 11 railway men. THOMPSON CO.'S SPECIAL CHRISTMAS OFFER let column of page 6.—Adet. An alarmi g outbreak of disease among pigs occurred on two farms close to Canterbury en Sunday. Forty animals' were slaughtered on Monday by order. At Plymouth. on Tuesday, Mr. Welch, the eldest son of the station-master of Plymouth, was found hanging from a door of his residence. ihe suicide is attributed to disap- pointment in !eve. CHLORO-LV.SRED CouGn LOZENGES, a medicated linseed ex- tract. 6d ; postage, 2d. Kay Bros., Stockport, and all Chemists. —Advt. On Saturday, at the High Park Colliery, Greasley, near Nottingham, Ed. Rowley, a collier, 'WAS repairing the con- ductors in the shafts when he fell a distance of 300 feet. He was dashed to pieces. Wan MATIRIAL.—A • Leeds firm h..s received a large number of orders for small arms and other war material from the Italian and other foreign Governments, and dsuble sets of workmen are executing the orders. A CROWN OF GOLD OR A. CORONET OF PEARLS is the privi- lege of few to have, but all can rejoice in having their grey, white, or faded hair restored to its natural colour by the use of Mrs. B. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer.—Advt. FROZEN TO DELTIL—Mr. Mark Gibson, farmer, Thornton, near York, has been frozen to death in a ditch near his home. Deceased, who was returning home from a neigh- bouring village, fell into the stream when attempting to cross a rude bridge, and, being benumbed with the exces- sive cold, was unable to extricate himself, and was quite dead when his son, some hours afterwards, discovered where he was. LORD TOLLEMACHE AND THE PRIMITIVE 'METHODISTS.— , Responding to an application by the superintending minis- ter of the Northwich Primitive Methodist Circuit, Lord Tolleroache stated that although he can ill afford to reduce- his income in view of the agricultural depression which presses so fearfully upon his Suffolk tenantry, he will con- sent to relinquish the ground rent of the Primitive Metho- dist Chapel at Castle, Northwich. FrnEs.--.—Early on Tuesday morning a fire was discovered in the furniture warehouse of Mr. Bradley, Cheapside, Bolton. A large quantity of furnitute was destroyed. Damage was done to the amount of £5OO, which is not covered by insurance. Inceadiarism is suspected.—A fire broke out in the joinery workshops of Messrs. Brooks, Thomas, and Company, Dublin, and was extinguished on Tuesday morning. The damage is estimated at £2,000, which is covered by insurance. It is not known how the fire originated. AOCIDENTALLY HUNG.—On Saturday afternoon George Henry Gibson, Strood, aged si years, was discovered to have hanged himself by a piece of clothes line which was attached to a staple outside the back door. When found he was quite dead. He was playing cheerfully only a few minutes before, and its is supposed that he must, naving hung the cord round his neck in several twists, have acci- dentally fallen off the side of the steps upon which he had been standing, and so became suspended and ucab.e to re- gain his footing. FronTufG IxrezTeow.—Dr. W. S. Saunders says :—" I have often limited infectious diseases to the room occupied by the sufferer by nailing a sheet saturated with dilute Coady's Fluid over the doorway." Caution i—Condy's Fluid bears the name of Condy and Mitchell at foot of every label. Beware of worthless colourable imitations.—. Advt. MR. MUNDELLA AND RICRRATIV-11 EDUCATION.— Mr. illundella spoke at a meeting held at the London Mansion • House. on Saturday, to promote the establishment of re- creative and practical evening classes in School Board and other schools. He drew a contrast—to our own disadvan- tage—between the training given in day schools in this country and on the Continent, and said it was a remarkable fact that the higher and the more complete the education given in the public elementary schools the greater was the demand for the work of the night school. Tina GOVERNMENT AND DOGS.—Sir R. Cross has issued a circular from the Home Office, stating that it is hi. illy desirable that all local authorities, under the Dogs Act of 1871, should rigorously endeavour to stamp out rabies in dogs by following the directions which Professor Brown, the professional officer of the Agricultural Department, has sub- mitted to the Privy Council. The gist of the proposal of Professor Brown is that all dogs should be put under re- straint, as they are in the Metropolitan Police District. The circular has been forwarded to all the courts of general sessions. MINERS' RIOT.—A serious riot occurred on Sunday after- noon at Brotherton, near Fryston Colliery, where the miners have been on strike for more than a year The new miners, who have been harassed by the strike hands, marched to Brotherton, armed with sticks and rifles, and made an attack npon the pitmen residing there. A serious conflict resulted. One policeman was shot in the arm, another had his helmet struck, and three of the strike men were shot. Others were injured. Only one of the attacking party was eeri, nsly in- jored. No arrests were made. Most of the men who took the offensive in the riot have absconded. AN ABSCONDING BANERTIPP.—LIABILITIES £02,000.—A a meeting in Edinburgh, on Monday, of the creditors of Robert Girdwood, for many years a wool broker in Scot- land, it was reported that the bankrupt (who has ab- sconded) received from farmers and sheep breeders wool to the value of £40,000, which he had disposed of and ap- propriated the proceeds. He appeared to have been specu- lating largely in lead mines and quarries in \Vales, on which he had spent more than £120,000, and at the data of his Iflight his total liabilities were £91500. The creditors ex- pect to receive a dividend of is 2d in the pound. I DEATH OF THE "RAILWAY KINGS" WIDOW. Tse death is announced, at the age of ninety, of the widow of a man who once filled a prominent plac in English society, Mr. George Hudson, the "Railway King." Mr. Hudson was a Yorkshireman. After the collapse of the great spec- ulative fabric which he reared, be lived in retirement until his death, which took place a few years ago. The residence of his widow at the time of her decease on Friday was Pitt- street, Kensington—a striking contrast to the glories of the palatial edifice which the "Railway King " raised for him- self, in the days of his prosperity, at Albert Gate. RELEASE OF MR. STEAD.—Mr. Stead, editor of the Pall Mall Gazette, who was convicted for the abduction of Eliza Armstrong, and sentenced to three months' imprisonment, Ws liberated from Holloway Gaol on Monday morning. About 30 persons assembled outside the gates, including several of both sexes, weariag the garb of the Salvation Army. There was no demonstration, and Mr. Stead drove laway in a four-wheeler to the Pall Mail Gazette Office. In the evening a public meeting was held in the Exeter Hall, under the presidency of Mr. Stansfeld, M.P. A resolution wits passed expressing confidence in Mr. Stead, and testi- moniele were presented to him. RAILWAY COLLISION AT CHORLT.—Oia Wednesday , morning, shortly before six o'clock, an alarming collision lbetween two luggage trains occurred at the junction just outside Chorley station. It appears that a goods train, mostly laden with broken stone, from Cbatburn to Chorleyt I was signalled to stop, but owing to the steep incline of the Blackburn line and the slippery condition of the metals the train went beyond the junction, and at the moment toe goods express from Preston to Manchester came up and dashed into the Chatburn train. Three wagons were smashed, and the engine of the Preston train was badly ' damaged. Fortunately no one was hurt, though tbe driver and the stoker of the Preston train narrowly escaped. Traffic was impeded for over four hours, the passenger trains Pe- ing worked on a single line. MINERS' CONFERENCE—The annual National Miners' Conference was opened at Birmingham, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. Burt, M.P. The questions for con- sideration include responsibility of chief managers and others in charge of mines, extra shafts, prohibition of blast- ing powder in dangerous mines, check weighing of coal, Improvements in organisation, and legislation to provide against danger arising from coal dust. There was a large attendance of delegates. The Conference was resumed at Birmingham on Wednesday morning, when Mr. Burt, M.P., delivered the presidential address. He congratulated the miners on their increase of political power, and an- nounced his intention of re-introducing'at the earliest pos- sible moment the Employers Liability Amendment Bill, *o render the law compulsory instead of permissive. TH.E Swowsrones.—Early in the week a severe snow-

storm prevailed in different parts of the country, in some places being accompanied with strong winds. On Monday, in Liverpool. "all sorts of weather " was experience-CI. Incoming vessels report very strong weather in the Channel. The pilot boats were uuable, in some cases, to get alongside vessels to take off the Liverpool pilots. In Manchester during Sunday— night and Monday morning snow fell heavily, interfering considerably with vehicular traffic. From several of the suburbs the tram service was entirely suspended, whilst from others it was only worked by the aid of additional horses. In some of the couutry districts around Crews the roads are almost impassable. The trains had difficulty in running to time on account of the slippery state of the rails on Sunday. Vivid and continuous sheet lightning was seen in the Channel between the Isle of Man and the Scotch coast.on Saturday night, and the barometer • fell rapidly on Sunday. Snow i•ell heavily in North Wales on Sunday night and at intervals on Monday. There are drifts of great depth in many of the country roads, and the mountain ranges are all thickly covered. The Caledonian line was blocked between Glaseem and Beattock. At Scar- borough, sleighing was freely iteltilged in. Both telephonic and telegraphic communication was interrupted, the weight of snow hiving caused six telephone and twe telegraph wires to break down. The snowstorm continued in the north-west of Ireland on Monday night. The fall is the most severe experienced for many years. ISCHOOL BOARD.—The ordinary monthly meeting of the members of this Board was held on Monday evening in the Board Offices, Prescot. Mr. W. L. Evans presided, and there were also present Messrs. C. Spencely, W. Golds- worth, J. T. Hall, T. P. Hewitt, J. B. Sanders, and Mr. H. Cross (clerk.)—lhe Clerk said he had received a letter signed by all the teachers, in which they denied haying instructed Mr. Baylis to ask on their behalf at the last meeting why the buns had not been distributed this year. He had also a letter from Mr. Baylis stating that he had not meant to ask on behalf of the teachers, and expressed hie apology, as it was a misunderstanding.—Mr. Baylis submitted the following. report :—" Gentlemen,—During the quarter ending this day, 31 children living in your dis- trict have reached the age of Itve years, and are Pow with one exception absent through illness, attending school as follows: Church Schools 12, Board Sckools 7, Yew Tree Schools 6, private school 6. Three families have come to reside in Prescot whose 9 children are attending Board School 6, Yew Tree School 8. One family have left the town whose four children attended Board School 2, and private school 2. Minimum temperature at your schoe last week 42 dogs." It was decided that the Chairman and Mr. Hall should go and look at the stoves and see what could be done to improve the heating of the schleols,— The following statement was submitted, showing receipts and expenditure for quarter ending 25th December, 1884, as compared with receipts and expenditure for quarter end- ing 25th Dec“mber, 1885 :—Receipts, 1884—Rates, £lOO ; school fees, £54 8s Id ; sale of books, Ace, £1 is 10e1 ; total, £159 lOs 61. 1885—Rates, £150; school fees, £44 10s 54 ; sale ef books, £1 6a id ; total, £195 16s 6d. Expenditure, 1864—Books, apparatus, and stationery, £ll 17s 31; fuel, light, cleaning, and replacement of furniture, repairs to buildings and furniture for schools, £l2 13s; expenses of administration, £5 Os 64 ; officers' salaries, £ll 5s ; other expenses of maintenance of schools, 8s 24 ; prosecutions, £4 5s 10d ; teachers' salaries, £ll5 16s 104 ; total, £l6l Os 7d. 1885-Books, apparatus, and stationery, £lll7 7d; fuel, light,'cleaning, and replacement of furniture, repairs to build- ings and furniture for schools, £22 6s 104 ; expenses of administration, £3 ; officers' salaries, £2l 5s ; other ex- penses of maintenance of schools, £1 15s 44 ; prosecutions, ss; teachers' salaries, £lO2 16s 7d; total, £163 6s 4d.— The Clem said there were .8129 in the bank. £lOO was still due to them, and cheques for £3O would be signed that night. —This was all the business.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The forteightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday at the Workhouse, Wlistoo, near Prescot. There were present Mr. J. Leatherbarrow (chairman), the Revs. T. Chambers, and J. Barnacle ; Messrs. J. Jackson, W. Birchali, J. Lowe, J. T. Hall, W. Tyrer, W. Newsome, James Fisher, W. J. Ashton, E. Sider, J. Ellison, T. Heald, P. Longton, W. Swift, and J. Kenwright. MASTER'S REPORT. The Workhouse Master reported that there were 485 inmates this week against 495 last w,ek, and 460 in the corresponding period of last year. Vagran's relieved 36, against 4.6 in the corresponding week of last year.

THE WATER SZTPPIX TO THE HOUSE. - A letter w.is read from the Local Government Board, asking if the Guardians had arrived at a decision with regard to the sink- ing of a well on the Workhouse premises—The Clerk said they were waiting for a report from Mr. Timmins an,/ it was decided to inform the Local Government Board that the matter was still under consideration.

TIIN GUARDIANS AND THE ST. HELENS CORPORATION.— A letter was read from Mr. Brewis (Town Clerk of S,-. Helens), a copy of which had been sent to the Local Gov- ernment Board, conveying the ratified opinion of the Health Committee that the charge they had decided to make for the maintenance of paupers in the Borough Infectious Diseases Hospital, viz., 6s per patient per day, was fair and proper; and they saw no reasou to alter their resolution. The Clerk was instructed to further communicate with the Local Government Board, and forward the letter sera to the Town Clark Of St. Helens before the reply was framed. • Cosr or PAUPER leceeencs.—The Clerk stated that he L had received notice from various county asylunss of the re- ' ductien of the rate- of maintenance for pauper lunatics. Rainhill was reduced from 9s 4d to 8s 9d per patient te Prestwich from 8s 9d to Sc 2d; and Lancaster from Sc 93. to 8s 91 . THE RECENT INQUEST AT THE WOREHOUSE.—Regardiii-- the recent coroner's inquiry at Whiston into the circum- stances attending the death of a Widnes woman who had broken her leg and been conveyed to the workhouse Hos- pital, Mr. Newsome said he was not satisfied with the re- sult of the inquiry, and did not think the conduct of some of the Union officials had met with approval.—lt was de- cided to hold an inquiry on Monday next. AN INVITATION .TO THE INMATES.—An invitation from Mr. Wallace Revill, of the Theatre Royal, St. Helens. for the whole of the inmates to witness the pantomime was de- clined with thanks, on the ground that it was not possible • to convey them to and from the theatre. THE FUNERALS OF ROMAN CATHOLYCS. —The following, letter was read by the Clerk :—.' 12, West-street, Prescot, Jan. 18, 1886.—Gentletnen,—I beg to inform you that I shall diecontinue reading the funeral service over the de- ceased Catholic poor of the Workhouse in the Catholic Church, Prescot, as there is now a chapel at the Workhouse and e paid Catholic clergyman. The funeral service can be read over the deceased Catholic poor quite as will if not better at the Workhouse as at the Catholic Church at Prescot.—Believe me, yours sincerely, R. BRINDLE."—Mr. J. T. Hall considered it a very proper letter.—The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) thought it required consideration. It became a question whether they would grant the chapel for the use of the burial service being read over dead bodies in it.-,Mr. Newsame pronesed that the letter be referred to the Rev. Mr. Winkler, of Por- tico, who lead been appointed Catholic instructor.—Tne Clerk said that Mr. Winkler lad no right to use the chapel at the Werkhoune for such a purpose. It was not erected to read the burial service over bodies in.—Mr. Swift thought the burial service ought to be read without goine, into the chapel.—The Clerk thought so too.—The Rev. T. Chamb,rs thought if even the letter was referred to Mr. Winkler and be said he would read 1,6 e service in the chapel it would be A matter of consideration for the Guardians as to whether his determination at his willtngaess to do it should he entertained.—The Chairman said the matter would then come again before the Board.—The Rev. T. Chambers aeked where the services were read before the chanel vas built? ' —The answer he received was that so far as Catholics were . I concerned they were read at Prescot Church.

Mr. Newsome said he would rather there was no discussion on the subject at present.—The Chairman said as a matter of fact no burial service had been read on ,anv part of the Workhouse premises.—Rev. 'l'. Chambers thought it ought to be so now —Mr. Newiome said it eeemel to him as if the chapel was going to be a bone of contention.—Rev. Thomas Chambers: No; not at all.—The Cliai-man said the two Catholic clergymen=-Mr. Brindle and Mr. Winkler —would arrange the matter between themselves and then it would come More the Board.—Mr. Longton thought it would be unnatural to bury paupers without having the burial service read —Mr. Newsome said it was a case •of more pay.—Mr. Chambers: I think not.—Mr. Newsome : I am afraid it is ; it looks very much like it.— The Chairman said in. the case of Protestants the burial service was read over them in the church yard.— The Clerk said if the Guardians determined that they would net permit the burial service in their chapel they would have no need to ask Mr. Winkler. He (the clerk) thought it was for the Guardians to say whether Mr. Winkler should use the chapel or not.—Mr. Chambers distinctly objected to- services being read in the chapel. He thought Mr. New- some should withdraw his proposition.—Mr. Newsome said his object was to get the rev, gentlemen to make some amicable arrangement. He should not withdraw. If the ehapel was used for the living it might also be used for the dead—Mr. Chambers objected on sanitary grounds to its being used for the dead. In order to bring the matter to a conclusion he would move an amendment that the letter be not entertained, but that the custom which prevailed should lee continued.—Mr. Fisher seconded.—On being put to the vote nine Guardians heist up their hands out of the 16 pre- sent.—Mr. Newsome said it would be useless to put his resolution, but the matter would not stop there.

Seam CHIEF :SECRETARY FOR IRELAND.---The Gls3e says: Lord Salisbury has lost no time in placing the precticat administration of Ireland in the capable hends of Mr. W. H. Smith. With regard to Mr. Smith's successor at the War Office, it is felt that no better appointment could be made than that of Viscount Cranbroolf, upon whose accept- ance of the post the Government would be enabled to meet Parliament with the administrative offices. completely filled. The office of Lord President now held by Lord Cranbrook dees net demand equal urgency. We are glad to believe that there is no truth is the idle gossip about Lerd Salisbury retiring from the Foreign Office, and the country will hope that the state of Lord Carnarvon's health, which was the chief reason why he would only accept the Lord Lieutenancy for a limited period, will by-and-by render his return to the Cabinet more likely than we should believe it to be at present. Therrien TO MR. ARCH, M.P.—Mr. Chamberlain presided' at the baequet given in London on Saturday evening in honour of Mr. Arch. He said he observed that the defeated Tory candidates were explaining their discomfiture by as- cettainin4 that their epponents had offered bribes. To this he replied that if the Liberals bad gone to the electors ad- mitting that they had nothing to offer which promised any hope of improvement in the condition of the most.namer- ous and least fortunate class of the population, then they would have tFduced the contest to a barren controversy. The franchise which was given to the latourers was only valuable and was only intended to be valuable as a Dever by which they coeld obtain reforms in legislatton which would recognise the responsibility of all classes in the community. The claims of the labourers cluld not now be ignored. Speaking of a reference to advanced politicians, the right hon. gentleman said it seemed to him absolutely impossible that the leader of the Liberal party should not be an advanced politician. No one was willing to make greater sacrifices than he himself was in order to secure the unity of the Liberal party ; but there was one thing he would not sacrifice, an that was the union and integrity of the empire. 011EAPEST Housi in the city for Glass. div.head: EXAMINEk.
div.p: THE EXAMINEk.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 23, 1386

LORD SALISBURY was on Tuesday inunda- I ted, at the Foreign Office, with deputations- There were present representatives of the Irish Defence Union, the Irish Patriotic Union, the commercial men of the south- west of Ireland, the commercial men of Belfast, and the London branch of the : Orange Institution of England. They had a I terrible tale to tell of boycotting, intimida- tion, and outrage in the sister isle. The Earl of PEMBROKE presented a memorial in the following terms : "My LoRD„—We wait upon your lordship as at deputation from the Irish Defence Union, a body (); gentlemen English, Scotch, and Irish, whom we fee". warranted in describing as of great weight and ink- . portance, and whose names we hand to your lord- ship. Our object is to call your lordship's attention to the condition of Ireland, to point out the illegal" ity that reigns there, and to pray your lordship t° find a remedy. Earl eEmsktoKE proceeded to urge that at that moment "the law was powerless in the larger part of Ireland " ; and he said "the deplorable condition of things they had to describe was duo to the uncertainty which hangs over Ireland in the public mind, to a feeling that no Government will dare to observe a strict observance of the law, and to a general belief that th - party of lawlessness are on the winning side, and will become at no distant time the governing power of the country," Other speakers v.T.nt into detail by way of enforcing these statements, all of which go to prove that so far from the pre- sent Government having m nded matters by coming into power they have all but lost control over the government of Ireland, Lord SALIS- BURY was studiously careful in his reply, but he was evidently wincing under the represen- tations that were made to him. He admitted that the crisis was a grave one and added :--
L

"I have listened with great attention—it is my- business on this occasion to listen, to hear what you. have to say—and most valuable is the information which you have laid before me; most valuable, very striking, very painful. It was painful to hear, as I did from one speaker, that an association over- 'shadowing the law and superseding the ordinary tribunal of the country exists and exercises power in every parish in the south of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) It was painful to hear the list of works which are done by that tremendous instrument of intimidation, of the certainty and the power with which it penetrates into the most intimate rela- tions of social life, and of the difficulty there ap- pears to be on the part of any class of resisting its effects. (Hear, hear.) It was painful and instruc- tive to hear that the machinery of local government in Ireland is used, not for its primary purpose, not for the purpose of transacting the local business and superintending the local welfare of the people of the country, but for the purpose of assisting those combinations of whose existence and whost power you gave me so many instances, (Cheers). He was not in a position, he said, to indicate the policy of the Governmentseeing that they were so near the opening of Parliament; and with an intimation that the Government duly appreciated " the sorrowful facts he bowed the deputations out. It must be hard for "proud SALISBURY " to have it thus made patent to the world that, after a six months' trial, his new departure on the Irish question is an utter failure. As he is not over-s.crupulous, he. above all others, will feel that so far as the Tories are concerned the alliance with the Parnellites has been worse thana crime ;it has been a blunder. What makes the situation a hopeless one for him is that, he cannot expect to succeed by a change 91 front. The Tories, standing alone, are 111 a hopeless minority in the House of Co mons. They are not strong enough to repair the error they have made. When the Liberals took office in 1880 they sought to govern Ireland by the ordinary law, but soon found that if they were to be masters of the situa- tion they must have larger powers. ?II.: GLADSTONE had a large majority behind hira: the House gave him what be asked for; an a

div.p: gradually—remedial legislation following on —order was restored in Ireland. Lord SALISBURY is not in a position to "go and do likewise ; " he is not in a majority; and, besides that, the supporters that he com- mands are not of the kind to press for such reforms in the administiation of Ire- land as are admitted to be necessary by the Liberal party. Lord SALISBURY is in office When he has no right to be; he is weak, and must go to the wall. We have no sym- pathy with the proposal put forward in some !quarters that it is the duty of the Liberals, in a crisis of this kind, to " ptace patriotism , before party," and help Lord SALISBURY out of the difficulty in which he finds himself. It is a law of life which applies to lords as well as labourers that men must bear the consequences of their own misdeeds. Lord SALISBURY has doubly failed; he has failed to get a majority to support him; and he has failed to preserve order in Ireland. The ; Patriotism which is before party demands that he should resign a position which he has no just title to hold. This is not the tune to attempt to govern by shifts and stratagems —by a policy of legerdemain. The Tories are secondary as to numbers; let them take a secondary position; and, if they are so full of zeal for the State as they' Profess to be, they will be legitimately em- 1 ployed in helping the Liberals to set crooked things straight. It would, of course, serve the Party interests of the Liberals if the Conser- vatives were to hold on to office for some Months longer; the longer they remain on the Treasury Benches, incapable and dis-1 or.edited as they are, the stronger in the end I Will be the tide of feeling against them. But 1 "eantime England suffers; abroad, a con- tinental war is imminent, but the great Powers have no regard for the s views of a rime Minister whose political life is not Worth a month's purchase; at home, there is, a lack of confidence in the commercial world, trade is more and more depressed, and Wages are being reduced; while as to Ire- land 'chaos is come again." The out- look for the Liberals who may be asked to take office is indeed stormy; but they must be ready, if need be, to face the worst. That, -as it seems to us, is what true patriotism demands of them.

THE speeches at the Complimentary Din- ner to Mr. E. K. MUSPRATT show that the Liberals of the Widnes Division of South- West Lancashire are by no means dishear- iened by their defeat. They have faith in Their cause, and such strong faith in Mr. MUSPRATT as a candidate that they will not hear of anyone else being suggested for the next contest. It is well known that for cer- tain personal considerations, which still weigh with him, Mr. MUSPRATT was reluc- tant to allow his name to be brought forward -as a candidate. But it became apparent that he was the unanimous choice of the Party; that he was the man most likely to Win the seat; and, having consented to enter the lists, we know how stoutly he fought the battle. That he did not come off the victor was no fault of his; it was due tb the , folly of the Irish electors in voting, at the bidding of Mr. PARNELL, for the Tory can- didate. They went wrong, and everything , seems to have gone wrong with the Irish since. So far from putting themselves in a position to command the situation, they have made it more than ever difficult for such men as 111 r. MUSPRATT to advocate their cause. The Tories have turned their backs upon them, and there are many Liberals who are riot unnaturally less anxious than they were to consider the question of Home Rule for i Ireland. It was morally wrong for the Irish , electors to ally themselves with the Tories, • and the result bas shown how far it was from being politically right. But it is never too late to mend. The time cannot be far dis- tant when the electors of the United King- dom will be again appealed to. If the Irish- men of Widnes think they did a good thing for themselves in voting for Mr. T. C. ErivrAßDs-Moss, they will, of course, vote for him again; but, on the other hand, if they have come to see the error of their ways, they will show themselves anxious to have an °Dl>ortunity of supporting Mr. MUSPRATTp 'hose failing, if he has a failing, is in lean- ing to Ireland's side.

THE Duke of liticHmoND, as Secretary for I Scotch Affairs, has caused a circular letter to be sent to the School Boards of Scotland which is in its way a strong argument in favour of Free Education. It seems that the starving crofters of the Island of Skye have of late been thinking more of food .for the body than food for the mind. Thew. have felt that the first claim on them was to keep body and soul together, and, having found that a difficult task, they have been compelled to neglect "demand notes" for school rates. The consequence IS that "the School Boards foresee great difficulty in maintaining their schools, and even fear that this may become impossible.' The Education Department have no power to enforce the payment of school rates; all they can do is to call attention, as they are doing, to the fact that, if grants are not earned under the ordinary conditions they Cannot be paid, and a "serious loss must fall upon the ratepayers of each district." Thus the poor will become poorer, and there Will be a deadlock as to education. It is needless to say that there would be no diffi- culty of this kind under a system of Free Education.
"TOUCH AND GO."

The inhabitants of Widnes are getting tired of going to St. Helens to try their County Court cases. Now that they find themselves the centre of a Parliamentary division they think they should have a County Court judge to themselves at least once a fortnight. Who knows—their county-courting might become pleasant, if done nearer home ?

More light is wanted on the gas question. At Widnes and Golborne there have been strong complaints as to the escape of unpurt- ied gas. The other evening the inhabitant* of the latter place resolved to take to petro- leum lamps if there wasn't a speedy change for the better in the gas—both as to price and quality.

At Warrington there are some who say that they get biz gas bills whether they burn much or little. The suggestion of one Town Coun- cillor is that "atmospheric air" is forced thrpugh the pipes and sold for gas.

A bright idea; how would it be to get up an "Atmospheric Air Company ? " No need to mind its being called a bubble company_ it would float." There is a good deal of the raw thaterial about; it can be had dirt Cheap.

div.p: points as an actress ; but she needs in one respect to begin at the beginning : Learn to speak slow; all other graces Will follow in their proper places."

The Schoolmaster of Trinity School, Run- corn, would be master, too, of the School Board. Because he has not got the attention he thinks he should have, he has declined, in very offensive terms, to supply lists of absentee scholars. What are his school managers doing? Are they asleep?

The Workmen's Peace Society, 9, Bucking- ham-st., Strand, London, has issued a dia- gram showing "How the taxes have been spent during the last half century." It gives an appalling account of the cost of war. It should be in the hands of every workman.

*. At Dartford, on Saturday, a magistrate (Air. Fooks, Q.C.) commented on tne injustice of costs of 7s following upon a fine of is. Some brother magistrates thought his beha- viour unseemly, and retired. They had no sympathy with a justice who desired above all things to be just.

The Government of the United States are beginning to deal with the Mormans. Lorenzo Snow, an apostle, has been found guilty of being over-married. He has seven wives, and twenty-three children. Has he not been sufficiently punished?

"The British Medical Journal" says 'Sir William Roberts, of Manchester, has" proved by a series of carefully conducted experi- ments that the effect of stimulants is power- fully to retard the action of the various diges- tive ferments in the foods." What will the tipplers say to this who feel that they "must have a glass in order to help digestion ?"
The Bishop of Liverpool prououncs for a Radical reform of the church ; he would do away with deans. This is shocking—for a bishop. The church, he says, provides no work for a dean to do.

We have heard something like this before. There was a Dean of Carlisle who became Archbishop of Canterbury. He ws a dean, he said, for three years before he knew what were his duties as a dean. And £ ,000 a year all the time.
"Plenty of pay and nothing to do "—that has always been regarded as a perfect " situ- ation " Why not leave the church alone and make us all deans?

Mr. W. T. Stead came out of prison on Monday. where he has been "serving three months" for excess of zeal in the cause of humanity. If he had been released after the first day, the justice of the case would have been met, but Sir Richard Cross re- fused to interfere. A ruffian who has com- mitted an abominable assault on a girl of ten has just been sentenced by the Common Serjeant to one month's imprisonment only. What will Sir Rich ird do now? Perhaps as Home Secretary he will make the short sen- tence still shorter.

Disraeli, when he first came out as a poli- tician, was a Liberal—a Radical even; but Conservatives have written volumes to prove that he never was anything of the kind. They are answered at last by the late lord himself. In a second volume of " Home Letters "just published, there is a record in his own hand of his dining with Peel, in which he says :—" I reminded him by my dignified familiarity both that he was ex- minister and I a present Radical." There! that should suffice. unless the Tories take to showing that " Dizzy 'S himself never knew what he was.
