EmiuRATIoN FROM WIDNES.—Mr. James Hargreaves has , this week despatched to Pennsylvania, U.S„ nine of the ' destitute unemployed of Widnes. Employment has been provided for the men, who have promised to refund their passage money. RuNCORbT Boast]) OF GCARDIANS.—A fortnightly meet- ing of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Weir presided, and there were also present the Rev. .1. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Whittle, Parr, Whit- low, Speakman, Forster, Smith, Baguley, Mclntyre, Hall, and H. Linaker (clerk). There was only relief business before the Board. THE WEATHER AT WIDNES AND RUNCORIC—A heavy fall of snow took place at these towns on Sunday night and Monday morning. The roads were covered to a depth of several inches, rendering traffic of all kinds very difficult. A farther fall of snow took place on Wednesday night, fol- lowed by a rapid thaw, which made the thoroughfares in a most uncomfortable condition for pedestrians. On Tnesday afternoon a man named Critehley wasmalkinc, on the kerb- stone opposite Mr. Itnison's shop in Waterloo-road, when a portion of the cave of the roof fell owing to the weight -if snow upon it. Critchley was struck on the forehead by the falling mass, and received a serious wound which ren- dered him unconscious for a short time. Upon recovering he was able to walk home. A NEw RUNCORN STEAMER.—The large fleet of vessels hailing from the port of Runcorn has just received a valu- able addition in the shape of a large iron screw steamer of large carrying capacity, and in every way suitable for ocean purposes. The neer steamer left the stocks at Northwich a short time ago, having been built to the order of Mr. Ed- mund Finlay by Mr. Edwin Foden, of Sandbach. The vessel, which is named Confidence, sailed down the Weaver on Friday, and was docked the same day at Weston Point. She is entirely constructed of iron, and is 120 feet in length on the keel, 24 feet in breadth, and 10 feet 6 inches depth of hold. The carrying capacity of the vessel is upwards of SOO tons. The Confidence tool; is a cargo of salt on Satur- day, and on Monday morning left Weston Point for Irvine. The Confidence is commanded by Captain Joseph Shaw, for- merly of the schooner Three Brothers; the first mate being Mr. James Abrams. Mr. James mole, of Liverpool, acts as chief engineer. RrNeuRN RCRAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The nsual fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Whitlow. There were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Parr, Weir, Forster, Smith, and H. Linaker (clerk).—A letter was re- ceived from the Local Government Board, giving formal sanction to the borrowing by the Authority of the sum of £6713 for sewerage works in the township of Weston. The Board also sanctioned the communication of the sewers of that township with those of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. A second letter was read in whicta it was stated that the Board had recommended the advancing of a loan of the amount in question by the Public Works Loan Commissioners. A third letter, which had been received from the Commissioners, contained a number of questions tO elicit the information required before granting the ben. —Ort the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Weir, it was decided to advertise for tenders for the sewerage works at Weston, according to the plans and specifications pro. duced.—Dr. Adams, medical officer of health to the kuthority. wrote saving that no spread of scarlet fever was ',ported. THE WATERBURY WA:I:CII.—We learn that the turn-out of this watch at the American factory is now so great as to have reached 350,000 for 1885, or over 1,200 per working day. In giving the turn-out as 600 per day, we had no later return before us , than that of 1884. The demand for the Waterbury is still rapidly increasing. LOCAL BILL IN PARLIAMENT.—In the House of Commons on Wednesday, the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Bill canie before Mr. Examiner Campion on Standing Orders without opposition. It empowers the company to make new railways in the townships of Lowton, Haydock, Windle, Walton- on-the-Hill, and West Derby • the works to be com- pleted within five years. The company propose to raise additional capital to the amount of £340,0Q0, with borrowing powers to the extent of £113,000, and to enter into working agreements with neigh- bouring companies. The necessary proofs of com- pliance with the rules of the House were given, and the Bill passed its preliminary stage. THE PRINCE OF WALES IN IT:SCORN. The saloon train conveying H.R.H. the Prince of Wales and his two sons froth Liverpool to London passed across Rnncorn Bridge about 4-20 on Wednesday afternoon. Elaborate precautions were taken for the safety of the structure. On the Cheshire side the viaduct and bridge were protected by a cordon of constables under the command of Superintendent Leah and Inspector .Millington. Colonel Hamersly, the Chief Constabie of Cheshire, was present. The arches on the Lancashire side were guarded by a large staff of police in charge of Inspector Wood. One half of the footway over the bridge was occu- pied by the Cheshire constabulary, and the other by the members of the Lancashire force. WHITLEY PAROCHIAL TEA PARTY AND ENTER-. TAINMENT.—On Friday evening, a congregational tea party, followed by an entertainment, in connec- tion with the above parish, was had in the Sunday school. There was a large attendance. The follow- ing ladies assisted at tea ;—Mrs. Rowlands, Mrs. Cliffe, Mrs. Rutter, Mrs. Bate, Mrs. Fletcher, Mrs. Moreton, Mrs. Owen, Miss Highfield, and Miss Smith. After tea the chair was taken by the Vicar, when a pleasing and varied programme was gone through, including a pianoforte Let by Mrs. Bryant and Miss Barclay, also one by Miss Rowlands and Miss Okell ; two songs by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, ' two by Miss Jones, and the following (in character): "Santa Claus," by A. Houghton ; "The Zingari," by Miss Hampson ; the " A.8.C." duet, by Miss Howard and C. Clarke; and "The awkward squad" and "Stump oration" by Mr. A. Hawkins; the five last- named persons having come from Runcorn to assist. The various songs, B,:c.,were well rendered and much applauded. LOCAL CASES AT LI‘ERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS. —At these sessions on Tuesday. Mary Ann Woods, 39, of no occupation, pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of elastic side boots at Warrington, on the Bth inst., and was sentenced to nine months' imprison- ment.—Thomas Holden, 46, a labourer, pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing a coat, hat, and other property belonging to Luke Rogers, at Cuerdley, on the 16th November, and was sent to gaol for six months. James Woods, 39, grocer's assistant, pleaded guilty to breaking into the shop of William Whittaker, at Sutton, on or about the 18th ult., and stealing three keys. He was ordered to be im- prisoned for 12 months.—John Timmins, 27, labourer, and Philip Hughes, 22, painter, pleaded guilty to stealing 14 shawls, several remnants of cloth, one skirt, and two bedticks, the property of William Jones, Newton, on the 7th November, and Sarah Timmins, 39, of no occupation, was found guilty of receiving the property, well knowing it to have been stolen. They were each sent to gaol far six months. —Ellen Rush, a charwoman, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for steal- ing .£7 125.mthe moneys of her employer, Margaret Turton, Huyton, on the 14th November. CLAIM AGAINST A M/LIMEA.LER.—At the Liver- pool County Court, on Thursday the 14th inst. be- fore His Honour Judge Collier, a case was heard in which the executor of Thomas Basnett, deceased, of New ',;on-by-Daresbury, .sued Joseph Simkin, of ' Edge Hill, Liverpool, milkdealer, for 'zi."23 18s 10(1, balance owing for milk supplied. • Mr. Arthur Browne, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Wm. Lowe, Liverpool, for the defendant.—At the opening of the case Mr. Lowe admitted that the goods had been supplied and that the amount sued for was owing, but that the testator had for- given the debt, as he had guaranteed that the milk supplied should contain ten per cent. of cream, or yielik4lbs. of butter to the twelve gallons of milk, and that the milk when supplied only contained five per cent. of cream, and only yielded 21bs. of butter—His- Honour said that as the defence was of such a character he would order a jury tO,be sum- monsd to try the case, and he adjourned the case until Tuesday the 19th inst:—When the case was , called on the adjournment and the jury sworn, the defendant did not appear but his solicitor did, and after bearing the plaintiff, his Honour told the jury that their serv:ces would be very short as the defendant did not appear. On the previous j hearing it was such an extraordinary defence that he thought a jury ought to hear the case. He directed to give a verdict for plaintiff for the amount claimed, and the jury were then discharged.—Mr. Browne told his Honour that he had several wit- nesses to prove that such a guarantee was impos- sible, and his Honour allowed costs. THE LIBERAL REGISTRATION AGENT FOR NEW- TON DIVISION.—The post of Secretary and Regis- tration Agent to the Liberal Association (the "300") of the Newton Division having become vacant, the Executive Committee recently advertised for a suit- able person to fill the vacancy. In reply there were 40 applications received, and these were considered by the Executive at a meeting on the 14th inst. They were reduced to nine, and these were ulti- mately reduced to five, namely, Mr. M. H. Birkhead and Mr. Thomas Ormand (Earlestown), Mr. F. Murr- ray (Warrington), Mr. P. M. Campbell (Manches- ter), and Mr. J. W. McCoomb (Liverpool). Each of these candidates personally attended a further meeting of the Executive held at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-street, Earles-. town, on Wednesday last, when their claims were finally considered and the appointment made. The chair was occupied by Mr., Charles Pilkington, J.P. (vice-president), and about 30 members were present, including Mess:l-s. G. W. Rawlins and D. Maitland (Rainhill), Beilby (Haydock), John Adams and C. A. Luffman (Newton.) The candi- dates were called in and were questioned as to their abilities, qualifications, and past' experience. After they had retired the Executive decided to appoint Mr. P. M. Campbell, of Manchester, at a salary of £l5O per annum. Mr. Campbell, who received the votes of about two-thirds of those present, is well- known in this district. He resided at.Wargrave for some years, but left about three years ago. tip to his removal he manifested earnest interest in the Liberal cause, and was very active in its behalf. He was also a cordial and persevering worker in connection with the Liberal Club.

WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.— Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., has hecoeie a vice-presideat of this society, and forwarded £1 as a subscription. THE WIDNES Scuoon BOARD Vecetecv.—The Noncon- formists are about to bold a meeting to suggest who shell fill up the vacancy on the .e.ciaool Board caused by the resignation of Mr. &Shaw. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.—On Thursday, before Mr. J. C. Gamble and Mr. F. H. Gossage, Robert Boest was charged with not having proper control over his horse, and fined 2e 6d and costs, 44 6d. A fine of se, including costs, was imposed upon Michael Dodd tor allowing the chinewey of ' his dwelling-house, Oxtord-street, to be on fire. LECTURE AT WIDNES.—On Sunday the Rev. W. J. Chis- holm, of Liverpool, preached two sermons to good congre- gations at Zion Chapel. Oakland-street, Widnes. On Mon- day evening Mr. Chisholm delivered a lecture on " The three Hebrew children." There was a large audience, and Me T. S. Swale presided. £5 was collected for the circuit and trust funds. ROBBERY FROM DITTTON WORSHOUSE.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. J. Brundrit, William Bezley, a young man, pleaded guilty to having, on the Ist January, absconded from Dutton Workhouse, taking with him a suit of best clothing. The prisoner wee apprehended on the previous day by P.C.Barber, and Superintendent Leah haying narrated the circumstances, the prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' bard labour. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—At the last monthly meeting Mr. F. A. Lake presiding, the librarian (Mr. J. D. Jones) reported iliac 1,526 books had been issued from the Lending Library during December. During the some period 44 volumes were consulted in the reference deportment. A number of books had been presented. It was decided to add the Manchester Guardian to the list of newspapers taken daily for the reading-room. A WIDNES COAL DEALER AND HIS SCALES. William Steveus, coal dealer, Marsu-street, was summoned to W id- nes Petty Sessibes on Thursday to answer a charge of hav• lug unjust scales On Wednesday, the 13th inst., Superin- tendent Barker visited the diefendaut's c-al yard, and 'found the scales 21b. out of balance against the purchaser. Under• neath the weight end of the scale he found a large quantity of lead. When this was removed the scales were slbs. against the purchaser. Half cwts. and cwts. would be mostly weighed upon this scale. A fine Of £1 and 12s costs was imposed. MEETING AT FRODSHAM.—The third annual meeting of the Frodshem auxiliary of the Religious Tract Society was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. F. F. Edmonds. Mr. Butcher, of Bury, one of the association secretaries, at- tended as a deputation to advocate the society's interests, which he did in a very interesting speech. The meeting was also addressed by the Rev. Edwin Mosscrop. Tne report was read by Mr. Ormrod, the local secretary, from which it appeared that the sum of £l9. 3s 9d had been con- tributed by the auxiliary to the society's funds during the year. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Coort on Monday, Michael Carr was charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding John Riley.— Joseph Collier, a watchman, said on the previous Thursday afternoon, about two o'clock, he was patting the prisoner and three other young fellows off that part of the Widnes Alkali Company's Works, called "the extension," when the prisoner threw a piece of coal at him. He was struck upon the leg. The prisoner also sent a piece of brick which struck Riley. who was working on a wagon, on the back of the head. He now sufered from an ugly wound, and Was unable to appear at the court.—On the application of Inspector Wood, the prisoner was remanded for a week. MARRIAGE OF MR. TALBOT.—The marriage of Mr. Al- gernon Charles Talbot, of Aston Hall, near Runcorn, with Miss Edith E. Greenfield, second dauehter of Mr. W. B. Greenfield, Beechwood Park, [lets, took place at St. John's Church, Southwick-crescent, London, on Tuesday. The bridesmaids were Misses Mabel, Evelyn. Margarette, and Beatrice Greenfield, Miss Telbot, Miss Muriel Talbot, and Miss Granshaw. Mr. Charles A. Tatbot, the brother of the bridegroom, was best man. The officiating clergy were the Hon. and Rev. %V. Chetwynd Talbot, uncle of the bride- groom, assisted by the Rev. Sir Ernilius Bayley, Bart., the Rev. R. W. Forrest, D.D., and the Rev. Arthur Chetwynd Talbot. After the marriage there was a reception at 35, Gloucester-square. Later in the afternoon the couple star- ted for the continent, en route for Algiers. STREET ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —About eight o'clock on Thursday evening a serious accident occurred in Victoria- road. John Mooney, who carries on the trade of a butcher, &c, in Ann-street, was in company with his son and a man in his employ, wheeling a barrow from the London and North-Western Railway Station, when the horse in a lurry passing along the road at the time was startled by the noise made by the Salvation Army. The animal swerved, and reared and plunged in affright, overturned the barrow, and knocked down and trampled the three men. They were taken into Dr. Booth's surgery, which was at hand, and their injuries were attended to by Mr. Saul, aseistant to Dr. Booth. All had suffered a severe shock to the system, and had bruises upon legs, head, and body. No 'bones were broken, fortunately. The elder Mooney was the worst suf- ferer, and had to he conveyed home in a cab. THE FLAT ROBBERIES AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossaee and Mr. J. Brock, at.Widues Police Court on Mon- day, Thomas Keeling was charged with stealing a pair of boots and a singlet, worth 10s, the property of Stephen Themes Heath, mate of the flat Clarence. The prisoner pleaded guilty to stealing the boots.—John Heyee was charged with stealing from the flat Mira one jacket, two shirts, one pair of shoes, a scarf, a cep, a pair of stockings, two pairs of trousers, a vest, a pair of clogs, and a knife, valued at 3Ss. the property of George Hartley, the captain, and Arthur Claire, the mate. He pleaded guilty to stealing the trousers and knife. Heves was also charged, in con- junetion with John •Carroll, with stealing a variety of clothing from the flat Washington, the property of the cap- tain, William Webb. The circumstances of the robberies have been previously reported.—lnspector Wood informed the Bench that the prisoners were. three of the worst char- acters in Widnes.—Carroll, Heyes, and Keeling were each sentenced to three months' hard labour. THE BOYS' PLOT AT RMICORN: ALLEGED THE-Fr.—At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday. Richard Green, 12 years of age,was charged with stealing half-a-sovereign from Robert Harrison, aged 9. Green's parents live at 41. Blan- tyre-street, and Harrison's in the next house. On Tuesday Harrison was sent by his mother to get half a sovereign changed at Mr. Mellor's shop, Church-street. When he was returning home the prisoner met him and persuaded him to let him hide the money, and they agreed to spend it when they had 'a day from school. The prisoner told Harrison to 01 his mother that be had lost the money. Harrison, when he arrived at home, told his mother this story, and she went to school and asked Gillen for the money. He, however, denied having taken it, and was subsequently apprehended by Police Clerk Wallace, to whom he made a number of Statements. He said he put the money back in the basket. Mr. Lake, who represented the prisoner, pointed out that Harrison had not been sworn in consequence of his youth, and his statement, which was not corroborated, must be taken for what it was worth.— The Bench considered there was a doubt in the case, and discharged the prisoner. • ROEB2RY FROM THE WIDNES ORANGE BALL. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Jones and Ann Jones, his wife, who keep a common lodging-house in Lngsdale-road, were charged with stealing an overcoat, worth £l, the property of Thomas Chantler, a labourer, of 6, Eleanor-street, Widnes. Michael Doyle, a tramp, was charged with receiving the coat, well knew-mg it to have been stolen. On the night of the sth November Chantler was at the Orange ball held in the Drill Hall, where be hung up his top coat. About one o'clock, having had a glass or two of beer, he went home in the rain without hat or coat, and fell asleep on the sofa. At five o'clock in the morning of the 6th he awoke and went down to the ball, but found it locked up. He Afterwards could not find his coat, and told the prisoner Jones of his loss. Information was: also conveyed to the pawnbrokers, and on Tuesday night Doyle attempted to pledge the stolen coat at Mr. Neil's pawnbroker's shop in Albert-road. He was appre- hended by P.S. Strickland, and stated that Mrs. Jones had sent him. Jones and his wife were then taken into custody. They alleged that a plumber who had lodged at the house a few weeks had gone away owing a few shillings, and left the coat. Mr. J. W. Knowles, selicitor, appeared for the prisoners Jones. Doyle was discharged, and each of the other prisoners was fined 40s, or a month. "LARKING" WITH DR. MCDOUGALL AT EUNCORN.—At Riencorn Police Court, on Thursclay, before Captain Miele- burst and Mr. G. L. Davies, a man named Samuel Hurst, ' was charged with stealing three silver spoons and two forks. 'the property et Dr. MacDougall. It appeared that the pri- soner had been in the habit of calling at Dr. MacDougall's surgery to consult the doctor respecting some imaginary ailment. On Wednesday afternoon he called and the ser- vant told him the doctor was just going out and could not see him. The doctor departed and the prisoner entered the surgery, and wilfully damaged several pictures on the walls. He then entered the kitchen, frightened the servants, and took the teaspoons and forks from a basket on the table. P.S's. Smith and Barber afterwards apprehended him in the surgery. and the articles were found upon him.—The prisoner argued that he only took the articles for a lark, and on the application ef the prosecutor the charge of larceny was withdrawn and one of wilful damage substituted. In 44efault of paying a fine of 10s, and costs Os 4.1, he was sen- tenced to 14 days' hard labour.—Hurst was then charged with stealing 3s from a till of the Boathouse Inn, Mersey' street, kept by Samuel Spann. OR Wednesday afternoon , the prisoner went into the bar and asked the girl if there were any packet men in. Whilst the girl was away ascer- taining the prisoner left the bar, and on Mrs Spann entering found the draw slightly open and 3s short. When prisoner was apprehended the prisoner had only is 3d upon him, and the Bench gave him the benefit of the doubt and dis- miesed the case.

WARRINGTON DISTRICT HIGHWAY BOAHD.—A meeting of this body was held at the Board-room, Sankey-street. Warrington, on Wednesday after- noon, under the presidency of Mr. R. Houghton. There were also present Messrs. J. Hartley (vice- chairman), T. E. Withington (ex-officio), J. Fair- dough, W. Royston, R. Owen, John Grounds, George Lawton, S. Bent, W. Kerfoot, 11. B. White (clerk), and Thompson (surveyor).— The Clerk stated that he had written to Mr. D. Sankey in re- ference to the encroachment at Holl,ins Green, in compliance with the directions of the Board. He receivedsa reply from Mr. Sankey stating that he certainly gave no instructions for an encroachment, but left the matter entirely with the architect and builder. No doubt they thought that an improve- ment would be effected. If the Board would allow it to remain he should be glad, but if not he was willing to put back the encroachment. The Board resolved that he be asked to put back the encroach- ment.—The Clerk reported that there was a balance in hand of £1,350 6s 6d, and accounts amounting to £BB9 19s id were passed for payment:—Mr. Ker- foot drew attention to a dangerous crossing at San- bey Bridges—he would rather call it Sankey planks. The crossing was about the width of a cart. The traffic between Warrington and Widnes, St. Helens, and neighbouring places was heavy, and he thought some steps should be taken to endeavour to get the Railway Company to make an alteration. He also referred to a footpath near the Coach and Horses as being dangerous, as there was a drop of about eighteen inches. He believed it belonged to the Corporation. After a short discussion, it was agreed that the Clerk ascertain who was liable for the state of the bridge and footpath.—This was all the business.

I have also made inquiries from the head teacher of the Roman Catholic Sghool, and she in- forms me that during the time the girl was attending school, when it is alleged that she was suffering from fever, that she did not see that the child was at all unwell or appeared to be suffering from any complaint. She else states that I 1 the mother on the Ist of December came to her residence and asked permission for her children to attend school with- out school fees, as they were unable to pay them that week. Permission was granted, and the children attended six times ; each. I also beg further to state that always in visiting ' cases of sickness reported of a contagious character great I care is taken; and that the benefit of any doubt is given to the parents when they alleged sickness of that character, but I may say that we are often imposed upon, and it is exceed- ingly difficult to ascertain the real nature of the sickness alleged, as a great majority oi parents never employ the services of a medical man until they are really compelled to I do so, although it is often explainei to them by the visitors 1 where gratuitous medical advice and medicine may be ob- tained." The Clerk said as regarded the application in respect to the parish doctor, he might say that the relieving officer permitted him to inspect his books, and had stated that up to the 9th January Mrs Walton, never since her arrival in Runcorn from Widnes six months ago, made application to him for an order for medical relief and medi- cal advice. When the child died it was neces- sary, before it could be buried at the public expense, that there should be described accurately and truthfully to the relieving officer the woman's true status. The woman stated that that her husband, William Waltosi, three years ago, was committed to gaol for seven years for an indecent assault at Widnes. At the present time, and for POMP time past, Mrs Walton had been living with a man named John Stokes, a carter for Mr John Morris, Widnes. The Clerk remarked that all the dates in the reports he had verified from the Board's hooks, and found they were per- fectly accurate. The child was never forced into school, and Mrs. Byrne laad no reason up to two or three daysthe- fore its death of knowing that it was suffering from scarlet fever. The statement that a diagnosis of the case was taken .0v Inglesfield, and that he repudiated the statement of the doctor, was absolutely without foundation. He bad every reason to believe Inglesfield's report. Then there was an independent witness. The rent collector, who had been in the habit of going to Walton's house once a week, and fre- quently twice and occasionally three times a week, bad I stated to him that during the whole time that it was alleged ' to be obvious that the child had scarlet fever, the mother never once suggested such a thing to him. Father Fennelly said he had carefully examined the case with Mrs Byrne and he was satisfied that the statements , made by legieetield were qeite correct and that the state- ments of the woman were false, and that she was unworthy of credit , Mr. Handler said he did not think it was exactly the duty of the School Board to inquire into the matter. He moved that the reports of the School Visitors be sent to the secretary of the Commissioners, with a request that they will inquire fully into the case of Mrs Wahou's daughter in the presence of the reporters, and that they also be re- spectfully requested to report the result of their icquiry to this Board. Father Fennelley seconded the motion. The Chairman retnat ked that the best course would be to forward the reports with the statement that the Board after due inquiry found there was no around whatever for the charge, and that they had every confidence in their visitors. This would leave the Commissioners at liberty to make any I tuiry thst they might choose. Mr. Handley said that fixed the responsibility upon the School Board, and he thought it was only fair the Commis- sioners should make a full inquiry. They were satisfied there was no ground for the charge. But the Commissioners should give as much attention as possible to the case, and then publicly deny by their own body that they had been misled in the case. Father Fennell : Let them institute an inquiry if they thought proper. Mr. Handley : There would be no publicity given to it. The Clerk asked, woald it not qe more convenient to con- fine themselves to the Commissioners' communication and simply forward the visitor's reports, and repudiate the charge. Mr. Handley said perhaps after that discussion it would be wise to do that. The following resolution was then passed :—" That the , Clerk be and is he: eby directed to acknowledge receipt of the cemmunication of the Improvement Commissioners. dated the 7th January, and to state that the case has been thoroughly investigated; and to add that in the opinion of this board the charges brought agaiast the assistant visitor are entirely without foundation." INSULTING THE BOARD : HOLY TRINITY SCHOOLS AGAIN The Clerk said this week the returns of non-attenders and irregulars had been returned blank from Trinity infant girls' and boys' schools. The following memorandum had been written on the back of the Trinity boys' school sheet :—"As it has been to much trouble for either yourself or assistant to bastow upon us so much as your shadow this week—one of the most important and critical in the school year—(L assume you have been too much engrossed with the new toy)-we feel that it is too much trouble for us to furnish lists. We further have decided to cease the supply =less we have a guarantee that some attention should be paid to them." The Clerk asked if in the face of that letter the visitors were still to send in sheets, and still continue to render any assistance in the Trinity Schools. There was a time, be be- lieved it extended to two years, that the Board was entirely cast adrift from Trinity Boys' School. They would not supply returns, and they seemed to have reverted to that policy. It was settled by the Board at that time that as they would afford no information the Board's responsibility ceased. The question Bowyer wanted to have settled was this—was he to be relieved from the obligation of attending to these schools or not. The Chairman: If they furnish the returns in the usual way they will he attended to. Mr. 'Handley : I think that note is worthy of print and T ehould feel inclined to take no notice whatever of the school. The Clerk: So should I. Mr. Handley said if Holy Trinity did not want the as- sistance of the Board's visitors, let the Board look and see that chilren were educatri in other schools. They had paid sufficient out of the rates for the visitation of denomi- national schools. It might not be known that they bad paid about £3 a week on purpose to drive children into de- nominational schools, and to be insulted by a letter of that kind from three schools in the town which had been be- nefitted to the extent of hundreds of pounds by the Board's action—he thought it needed taking notice of in its proper light, and that they need 'a ot trouble the schools with any returns. If they lay a complaint the Board would have a complete justification. The Clerk : Tkat is what the Board did before. Father Fennelley said if they would not till the returns, do not notice the schools. The subject then dropped, that being the understanding. There was no other business of interest.
EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT WESTON.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, on Monday afternoon held an inquest at the Rival Oak Inn, Weston, upon the body of John Spruce. 30 years of age, who was killed at Weston Works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company on Satur- day. Mr. John Aeliton. solicitor, was present on behalf of the company. and superintendent Leeh represented the Police. Mr. J. W. Kirkham also represented the company. From the evidence it appeared that Mr. Wlliam Norman, of Ford's-terrace, Weston, who is one of the chemists at the works, had for several weeks past been engaged in an experiment to extract .sulphur from black ash waste. For his operations he had a tank filled with the waste, which he boiled with steam. The tank was on a platform. Below were four large puncheons in wbich the black ash was de- composed, and the eoxious gas sulphur•tted hydrogen was given off, but not in large quantities. On Saturday the de- ceased was assisting Mr. Norman, his only duties, however, being to fetch water and hydroc eloric acid when required. Mr. Norman, about ten o'clock in the morniiig, left the place for about ten minutes. and during his absence T e deceased was seen by Thomas Kineton, an engine driver, who lives in Shaw-street, Runcorn, to stir up the chemical ccitnpound in one of the puncheons with a stick, and then step back- ward as though about to leave the stage. He then pitched forward, and fell with his bead against the edge of a cask. He was immediately picked up, And was foumd to be com- pletely insensible. Dr. McDougall was telephened for, and that gentleman upon his arrival at the works strortly after- wards had the deceased removed home in A ceb, and. every- thing posiible was done far his recovery. He, however, never regained consciousness, and died aCont seven o'cleck on Saturday eveninf.—Mr. Norman said he had worked at the experiment at all hours of the day awl night, and there was no danger about it. The deceesed and the other men who lied assistsd him (witness) had instructiens not to in- terfere with the operatiens, and the deceased bad no right to stir up the contents of the puncheon. The deceased was a weak man, and had had to be taken away from wheeling salt. He took an interest in the experiments.—Dr. Mc- Dougall stated that cases of this description were of an ex- tremely rare occurrence, and be thought the deceased must have'acted very injudiciously in stirring up the liquid, be- Cause the gas wee one that always gave notice of its pro- sence. even in the smallest quantities. He considered the ' experiments of Mr. Nernran ware conductud with proper care. - It was work which none but an expert should per- form. Death was calls d by the inhalation of sulphuretted hydrogen.—The Co,orier having rimmed up, the jury de- liberated in private for some minutes. Mr. T. C. Price, the foreman. said the jury had arrived at a verdict of " Acci- dental death," and they did not consider there was any blame attached to the company in any way. Several of the jurymen had suggested that a printed notice should be posted at the placr warning persons not to go near the casks.—The Coroner: No doubt your clients will see to that, Mr. Ashton.—Mr. Ashton : Yes.
A COUNTY COURT FOR WIDNES,

On Wednesday afternoon a meeting of tradesmen and other business men was held in the large room of the Cen- tral Hotel for the purpose of taking action to have a County Court at Widnes. Mr. James White was voted to the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. F. Lawrinson, C. H. Lewin, 5. Matthews, W. T. Husband, J. Goff, T. Sadler, T. J. Peters, J. W. Knowles, S. Owens, Saul, Farrant, Beach, F. Parkes, &c. The Chairman said they would all be agreed that it was absolutely necessary there should be a County Court in Widnes. (Hear, hear.) They had put up with the incon- venience quit long enough. Fortunately he did not re- quire the court very often, but when he had done so he had found it very inconvenient to go out of Widnes, and in many cases he had lost the account rather than be put to the trouble of going to St. Helens. What was good in his case tradesmen and others must have expe- rienced in hundreds of cases.

I Mr. Husband, at the call of the Chairman, made a few / remarks. He described the steps previously taken in order to get t Counts, Court established in Widnes. A petition signed by the magistrates and other gentlemen who it w.s thought wow(' be influ-ntial in the matter, was duly pr,-sented by one of the mernli-rs of Parliament for South- West Lancashire to the Lord Chancellor. The Lord Chan- cellor, be believed, forwarded the tp,tition to His Honour Judge Thompson, of the St. Lielons County Court, and the result was that they did not succeed in getting a court held at Widnes. He thought they ought to make this more a tradesmen's and workingimen's petition. It would hare more influence with the judge, and there was no doubt in his (Mr. Husband's) mind that he would be willing to hold a court in Widnes once a month if be thought it would be a saying of time and money to poor people. Many poor ptople had to spend money in railway fares, and hise a day's work in addition to attend the court at St. Helens. Through the bad train service they were obliged to stop in St. Helens longer tban tkere was any need, mid consequently they spent more money than they ou4ht to do, and frequently in drink. The result was that Widnes was a great deal poorer than it ought to he—(hear, hear)—and the County Court instead of doing all the good it should sometimes did d great deal of harm amongst poor people. If they could get up a poor man's petition be bad no doubt his Honour Judge Thompson would concede what they had to Ofik. Ha pointed out that this matter did not affect the solicitors, who got their fees whether the court was at Widnes or St. Helens. r. C. H. Lewin observed that it was the tradesmen and shopkeepers woo were anxious for this court, and he should not like it to appear that the solicitors of W:does were asking for the court to be established for their own benefit.
Mr. Husband said if the tradesfnen did not move he would not.

Mr. Knowles said he had frequently met with instances in thea course of his practice whet e tradesmen had had small acnounts owing to them, but in consequence of tbe trouble and expense of koing to St. Helens, bad allowed them to become bad debts in preference to prosecuting the persons. He expressed his readiness to give all the aid in his power to establish a court at Widnes.
Mr. T. J. Peters spoke in the same strain. Mr. PArkts moved that it was expedient to have a county' court in Widnes.
Mr. F. Lawrinson seconded the motion.
Mr. Davies slid he bad locit several hundreds of pounds rather than be put to the expense and trouble of going to St. Helens.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A special ine-eting of this board was held on Tuesday at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Mr.-J. Pritchard prksideti, and there were present the Rev. Famer Fennelly, Mr. W. Handley, and Mr. F. Rigby (clerk).
ELECTION OP MR. IMISON.

Owing to an informality in the previous election of Mr. E. Imison to the vacancy caused by the retirement of Mr. P. Briscoe, it was necessary tbat he should be reappointed. The Chairman said as the representatives of the Church party were not present he begged to propose that Mr. Imissm be elected a member of the board. Mr. Handley seconded the motion with pleasure. He had no doubt that Mr. Imison would prove a very useful arbd active member. He might mention that he wished those words about Church party were not mentioned. They were met there, and ought to be met as representatives of rate- payers. and the sooner they tried to have that feeling on the board the better it would be.
The motion was carried unanimously. THE SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A VISITOR: INVESTIGATION

AND RESULT. The Clerk read the following letter : Town Hall, Runcorn, 7th January, 1886. Dear Sir,— I am directed by the Runcorn Improvement Commissiouers to furnish you with the following extract from the report of the Medical Officer of Health submitted to the board to- day. "The mother of one of the children whose death is re- ported as due to dropsy after scarlet fever, made the fol- lowing statement to me on the 4th of the present month in the presence of the nuisance inspector. " My daughter, Martha Walton, aged 5 years, lived with me in Back Brunswick•street. She was taken ill about the latter end of '.the first week in November last, and remained in bed until Sunday, the 15th. On the Monday the child went to school ; no inquiry was made by the teacher as to the cause of her absence during the previous we. k. On the Monday in question the School Board officer" Inglesfield " called and dirdeted me to send the child, Martha, to school. The child, Martha, continued attending school for three weeks. On Friday, the 4th of December the child came home from the school, ill again. On the following Mon4av her elder sister aged eight years attended at the school, but the teacher refused her admittance. On the same day the School Board officer called again and wanted to know the reason why the children were not sent to school. I told him that the elder child bad been to the school that day but that the teacher refused her admission; lie then examined the sick child in bed, and felt at the lumps in her throat, and said she had only a cold, and ifstructed me to send the elder child to school in the morning, and the teacher was to be told that the child must go to school and must be admitted, and that the School Board officer said so, and if I did net send her to school I would be summoned before the magistrates. I did not obey the instructions of the officer. On the Tues- day evening following I took the sick child to a doctor. Ihe doctor told me that the child must have had scarlet fever, and was now suffering from dropsy. The doctor gave instructions as to what I was to do for the child, and he saw her again on the following Thursday at my own house. On the Wednesday the School Board officer called again. I then told him that I had taken the child to a doctor; he wanted to know what the doctor said. I replied that the doctor said that she was suffering from dropsy after scarlet fever. He said that he did not believe that I had had a doctor, but desired me to ask the doctor when I saw him again whether her sister might go to school. My poor child died on Sunday morning the 13th of December last." I would merely observe that the above is a plain unvarnished history of a truly sad case. This child along with her elder sister attended school during the period of the greatest activity of infection, and most probably her own death was hastemi if not entirely due to exposure during the peeling stage ot the disease. It is impossible to exaggerate the misery and sorrow which this humble victim of a cruel fate may be the ineocent cause of spreading to other happy homes. (Signed F. McDougall), yours faithfully, E. MARSHALL. F. Rigby, Esq., clerk to the Runcorn School Board.' The Clerk then read the following report from Inglee- field :—" Gentlemen,—ln my report in reference to the Walton case I have to inform you that I first found the family on the leith of August last. I could not get the mother to send the children to school till September. They were first rep red to the office week ending Friday Sept. 4th. I visited on the 7th of September and the mother alleged want of means. I told her she must get the children to eceotd or she would be brought before the Hoard to give her statetnent there. On the week ending Friday September 11th they were reported again. I visited on the 14th Sept. and I cautioned her again. She alleged fees. On the week end- ing Friday October 2nd, Selina was reported alone. I visited on the 5q3. October. Alleged fees. On the week ending Friday, October 9th Selina was reported. I visited October 12th, and asked if Martha was attending school, and the mother said no ; she had no proper clothing to go in. I told her to try to get her some at once and send her to school. On the week ending Friday, October 30th, they were both reported. I visited on the 2nd of November. Then the mother told site Martha was unwell. I asked her what was to do with her, and she said "I think it is a bad Cold." I told her to send Selina to echool if it was only a

div.head: SINGULAR FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SINGULAR FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday, in consequence of the rapid thaw that then set in, considerable danger was incurred by pedestrians through large accumulations of snow sliding oft the roofs of buildings. One very singu- lar accident occurred, and unfortunately proved fatal. A woman named Bate, the wife of a labourer, living at 18, Appleton-street, was standing on the pavement close to her own house, holding in her arms a child of five months old, when a length of wood spouting, measuring 36 feet and 6 inches, accompanied GT an avalanche of snow, fell with a tremendous crash from the roofs of three of the houses. The child was struck on the head, and knocked out of its mother's arms. Its skull was smashed, and it died shortly afterwards. The mother, who was unhurt, had a miraculous es- cape.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

WEDDING AT CADISHEAD —On Thuraday week, a wed- ding took place in the Wesley Chapel, Cadishead, the bride- groom being Mr. Osborne, of Portsmouth, and the bride Miss Duey, daughter of the Rev. Thomas Dory, resi- dent Wesleyan minister. The ceremony was a very impres- sive one. Sacrament was administered, and the service was conducted by the father, and assisted by the brother of the bride and the bridegroom's brother, the Rev. E. Osborne. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—The annual tea party took place on Monday, when there was a good attendance. After tea a public meeting was held, when the Rev. J. Yonge, of Warrington, occupied the chair. He spoke chiefly- on the growth of the Congregational Church in Cadishead., and ex- pressed great hepes of the future from what bad been achieved in the short time they had had a place or worship at Cadishead. The Rev. Thomas Willis, of &Iv Chapel, Manchester, also gave some very good advice. The building fund treasurer, Mr. Garland, of Warrington, then read the balance sheet for the past year, which showed a slight balance. He hoped before long they would be in posi•ion to wipe off the debt on the building, some £l6O. The Paster, Rev. D. Clegg, also addressed the meeting. He trusted they would continue to be united, and show them- selves in right good earnest. He would strive to do his part if they would only do theirs. The meeting was en- livened by the choir, by dialogues, and by a solo from Miss S. Shaw. A vote of thanks to the chairman and the ladies was given, and the meeting terminated.—Ou Tuesday there was a tea for the scholars and friends. After tea there were recitations and singing. As many as 79 prizes were given to the Sunday school scholars who had made their required punctual attendances. Mr. Robinson gave a ealecti,,e on the hand bells. A cordial vote of thanks was given to Mr. and Mrs. F. B. Scott for their great services to the Sunday school.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MaNDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Councillor Greening, Mr. John Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS —The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—John Firn, in Cockhedge-lane, Saturday evening. fined 5s and costs; Anne Hodgson, in Naylor- street, tined 103 and costs; William Stokes, in Market- street, fined lOs and costs ;- Patrick Schofield, in Irlam- street, on Saturday night, ordered to pay costs ; James Donovan, in Dial-street, on Sunday morning. fined 5s and costs; Martin Ford, in Cockhedge-lane, on Sunday morning, fined 5s and costs. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TrESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 2-0. THE SWEARING-IN OF THE PEERS was at once proceeded with. Amongst the earliest were the Bishop of Newcastle, the Earl of Redesdale, the Duke of Bedford, the Duke of Leeds, the letlarquis of Winchester, the Earl of Bradford, the Earl of Yerularn, Lord Gerard, Lord Colville, Lord Elphinstone, and the Earl of Caithness. After. a shot t in- terval another batch presented themselves, consisting of the Earl of Lathorn, the Earl of Lytton, Lord Stratheden, Lord Napier of Magdala, Lord Boston, Viscount Bangor, lriscount Hardinge, and. Lord Dunsany. Subsequently, Lord Lamington, the Earl of Dartmouth, and a few other Peers were sworn in singly ; and then a batch of six, amongst whom were the Earl of Winchelser, the Earl of Galloway, Lord Balfour of Bernie, and the Earl of Kil- morey. After a further delay, the Marquis of Salisbury I came up to the table by himself and took the oath. The ' Premier, after shaking hands with the Lord Chancellor and the Clerk of Parliaments, at once left. At longer or shorter intervals there arrived the Duke of Buccleuch, the Marquis of Arlesbury and Lothian Avanland, Lord Suffield, Lord Henniker, the Duke of Newcastle, Lord Monson, Viscount Eversley, Lord Bary, the Marquis of Ripon, Lord Stanley of Alderley, Lord Monteagle, the Duke of Abercorn, Lord Crofton, the Lord Chancellor of Ireland (Lord Ashbourne), Lord Bishop of Peterborough. and the Duke of Norfolk. Lord Deramore (Sir J. Bateson), who was introduced by Lord De Roe and Bury, took the oath and subscribed the roll as a new peer with the usual ceremony. Lord Wolselev, introduced by Lord Hardinge and Lord Hood, also took his seat on being created a viscount. Lord H. Scott took his seat on being created Lord Montague. He was introduced by the Marquis of Lothian and the Earl of Home. Lord Colville of Cufross, introduced by the Earl of Kintore and Viscount Harrington, also subscribed the roll on being created a baron of the United Kingdom. Their Lordships adjourned at 4-20. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEIDNESDAY. This being the last of the days specially set apart for the swearing-in of members prior to the formal opening of Par- liament by Her Majesty, there was at two o'clock, when the Speaker took the chair, a good muster of those who had not previously taken the oath of allegiance. These included a substantial contingent of Irish representatives, many of whom had only just crossed the Channel for the purpose of taking their seats. Mr. Chaplin (Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster) was the first to take the oath and to shake- hands with the Speaker. He was followed by Mr. W. Etvart, Sir H. Selwin-Ibbetson, Mr. T. B. Potter, Mr. Spen- cer, and Mr. M•Lagan. Among the Irish members to whom the oath was administered were Mr. T. M. Healy, Mr. J. Dillon, Mr. I'. Harrington, Mr. Small, Mr. O'Hea, Mr. J. Leahy. Mr. J. Stack, Mr. D. Crilly, Mr. T. D Sullivan (Lord Mayor of Dublin), Mr. P. J. Power, Mr. E. Harrington, Sir T. ismond, Mr. D. Sullivan. Mr. J. Clancy, Dr. Tanner, Mr. J. Kenny, Mr. F.. Leamy, Mr. H J. Gill, 'Mr. T. NI ayne, Mr. T. P. Gill, Mr. W. Redmond, Mr. J. O'Coanor, Mr. W. J. Reynolds, and Mr. W. Murphy. Of the other members sworn during the first hour of the sitting may be mentioned the Marquis of Hartington and Mr. G. Dixon, Mr. P. Essle- mont, Mr. Joseph Cowen, Lord William Compton, Mr. Finch Hatton, Mr. Morgan Howard. Mr. Stevenson, Sir. F. Milbank, Mr. Pal ner, Lord Charles Bereaford, Mr. Puleston, and Mr. Mackintosh. About three o'clock, after a short lult in the busiraess, Mr. Parnell came to the table alone and took the oath, after which he shook hands with the Speaker in a.cordial manner, and remained for a minute or so in conversation with the right hon. gentleman. The unsworn members came up after this at appreciable intervals, and among the last to be sworn were Viscount Folkestone: Sir John Rarnsden, Sir Charles Tennaut, and Sir Rainald Knightley. At a quarter to four o'clock, on the motion of Mr. Akers Douglas, the House adjourned to next day. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The eleventh Parliament of the Queen was formally opened to-day by Her Majesty in person. The Queen was attended by the Prince of Wales and other members of the Royal Family and the great officers of State, whtlst the proceedings were attended with the usual ceremonies. The Commons having come to the bar, the Lord Chancellor read the Royal Speech in the terms following:— THE QUEEN'S SPEECH, MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEM, My relations with other Powers continue to be of a friendly character. The difference which existed when I last addressed you between ray Government and that of Russia on the subject of the bonndaries of Afghanistan has been satisfactorily adjusted. In pursuance of a convention which will be laid before you, the English and Russian Commissioners, with the full concurrence of my ally, the Ameer of Afghanistan, have been engaged in demarcating the frontier of that country. I trust that their work may tend to secure the continuance of peace in Central Asia. A rising in Eastern Roumelia has given expression to the desire of the inhabitants for a change in the political arrangements under which they were placed by the Treaty of Berlin. My object in the negotiations which have followed has been to bring them, according to their wish, under the rule of the Prince of Bulgaria, while main- taining unimpaired the essential rights of his Imperial Majesty the Sultan. Under a Convention which has been concluded with the Ottoman Porte, Commissioners have been appointed on be- half of England and Turkey to confer with his Highness the Khedive, and to report upon the measure required for secur- ing the defence of Egypt and the stability and efficiency of the Government in that country. Greatly to my regret, I was compelled in the month of November to eticlare War against Theebaw, the King of Ava. Accounts of hostility on his part against my subjects and , the interea!S of my Empire had, since his accession, been' deliherate and continuous. These had necessitated the withdrawal of my representative from his Court, and my demands for redress were systematically evaded and disre- garded. An attempt to confiscate the property of my sub- jects trading under agreement in his dominions, and a refusal to settle the dispute by arbitration, convinced me that the protection of British life and property, and the ces- sation of dangerous anarchy in Upper Burmah could only be effected by force of arms. The gallantry of my Euro- pean and Indian forces, under Lieutenant-General Sir Harry Prendergast, rapidly brought the country under my power, and I have decided that the most certain method of ensur- ing peace and order in those regions is to be found in the permanent incorporation of the Kingdom of Ava with my Empire. Papers on this subject will be immediately laid before yau. The time vrich has elapsed since I assumed the direct government of India makes it desirable that the operation of the statutes by which that change was effected should be carefully investigated. I commend this important matter to your earnest attention. A protracted negotiation respecting the rights of the Republic of France on the coasts of Newfoundland, under the Treaty of Utrecht, has been brought to a satisfactory conclusion by an agreement which will be laid before you and before the Legislature of Newfoundland as soon as it assembles. An agreement has also been made with Spain securing to this country all commercial rights granted to Germany in the Caroline Islands. Your consent will be asked to legislative measures ren- dered necessary by a convention on the subject of interna- tional copyright to which I have agreed. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS, The Estimates for the expenditure of the ensuing year, which have been framed with a due regard to efficiency and economy, will be submitted to you. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— I regret to say that no material improvement can be noted in the condition of trade or agriculture. I feel the deepest sympathy for the great number of persons in many vocations of life who are suffering under a pressure which I trust will prove to be transient. I have seen with deep sorrow the renewal since I last ad- dressed You of the attempt to excite the people of Ireland 'to hostility against the legislative union between that country and Great Britain. lam resolutely opposed to any disturbance of that fundamental law, and, in resisting it, I am convinced that I shall be heartily supported by my Par- liament and my people. The social no less than the material condition of that country engages my anxious attention. Although there has been, during the last year, no marked increase of serious crime, there is in many places a concerted resistance to the enforcement of legal obligatious, and I regret that the prac- tice of organised intimidatioa continues to exist. I have caused every exertion to be used for the detection and pun- ishment of these crimes, and no effort will be spared on the pedxaureatticolif my Government to protect my Irish subjects in the isbe e rofliberty. e legal rights y i n fo information otnh the e adsme enjoymentto a apprehend, rienhcleinvdi the existing provisions of the law should prove to be inade- quate to cope with these growing evils, I look with coy& dence to your willingness to invest my Government with all netlecsisles.isivial irlc,yibocephuonsiwcusiinroisl nt etdtr aht noe s acycootuue dn ft oi ebr syt or tafhnesfce ro Greatrui nr tsgß roittfoa nRu eiaper ert Quarter teunßstiainl Sessions and other authorities. A measure for the Reform of County Government in Ireland is also in preparation. These measures will in- volve the consideration of the present incidence of local burdens. A bill for facilitating the Sale of Glebe Lands in a manner adapted to the wants of the rural population will also be submitted to you; as also bills for removing the difficulties which prevent the easy and cheap Transfer of Land; for mitigating the distressed condition of the poorer classes in the Western Highlands and Islands of Scotland; for the more effectual Prevention of Accidents in Mines; for ex- tending the powers of the Railway Commission in respect to the regulation of rates; and for the Codification of the Criminal Law. I trust that results beneficial to the cause of Education may issue from a Royal Commission which I have appointed to inquire into the working of the Education Acts. The prompt and effective despatch of the important busi- ness which, in an ever-growing propertion, falls to you to transact. will, I doubt not, occupy your attention. In these and in all other matters pertaining to your high functions, I earnestly commend you to the keeping and guidance of Almighty God. The Address in answer to the Speech was moved by the Duke of ABERCORN, and seconded by the Earl of SCAR- ZoROUGH.—EarI GRANVILLE, in the course of his criticisms, referred to the reported seizure of Samoa, the arrangement made with Spain in regard to the Caroline Islands, the an- nexation of Upper Burmah, Sir H. Wolff's mission to the East, and the condition of the Balkan Peninsula. On the

question of Ireland he thought the paragraph in the Queen's Speech was not clear enough, and complained that no men- tion was made es to the means that were to be taker to pre- serve peace and order in Ireland.—The Marcpis of SALIS- BURY replied, and in speaking of the con,lition of Ireland said the circumstances were such that they required unam- biguous language from the Government. Such language, he said, had not been used by everybody. It had been no ; small addition to the responsibilities of the Government that they had had to face declarations of opinion or indications l of opinion from Mr. Gladetoqe operating with fatal effect upon those with whom they were dealing. He ad- mitted that the experiment of ruling Ireland with- out the reimposition of the Crimes Act had to come extent failed, but it had had every chance, and he still believed that the worst of the exaggerated symp- toms which Ireland now showed was due to the declarations in favour of Home Rule which were supposed to have been made by leaning statesmen in this country. The noble Marquis announced a change that ha'd. taken place in the' Government of Ireland, and said that practically it had been committed to the care of Mr. W. H. Smith, and there would be no faltering on the part of the Government when they had received his report.—The discussion was continued by Earl Spencer, Lord Ashbourne, the Earl of Kimberley, and Lord Cranbrook ; and the Address was ultimately agreed to unanimously. Earl ledesdale, having been reappointed Chairman of Committeee, their Lordships adjourned at five minutes to eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIRTFISDAY. _ _

It was appointed that the House of Commons should meet at ten minutes before two o'clock, but such was the anxiety to secure seats on the Opposition side of the Cham- ber that a number of the Irish members came down as early as ten o'clock. By noon every seat en the Opposition side was secured, and though there was not the same competition for places on the Ministerial side of the House, yet nearly all the seats were taken before the House met. The Speaker entered the House at a quarter before two, and prayers were said.

NOTES BY THE WAY. Askarn-in-Furness paid a visit to the Swinton ground, a good game resulting in the victory of the home team by one goal, two tries, and three minors to two minors. The ground was in wretched condition. The match between Bradford and Batley, on the ground of the latter, was witnessed by an enthusiastic concourse of 10,000 spectators, who were treated to a really grand game, which ended in a draw—Bradford one minor to nil. The game, as expected, was stoutly contested. Broughton, who journeyed to Halifax, went with a poor team, and thereby met with a crushing defeat at the hands of their powerful opponents; result at call of time being five tries and nine minors to nil.

Rochdale Hornets visited Broughton Rangers, but their ground being flooded Broughton generously offered their field, which offer was accepted. The Hornets had rather a weak team, which might perhaps account fer their defeat, a splendid game ending in a victory for the Rangers by one goal, oxe try, and two minors to one minor. Birkenhead Park met their old opponents, New Brighton, a good game resulting in favovr of New Brighton by one goal and three minors, to 'three tries and three tries and three minors. Birkenhead had by far the best of the game, and were rather unlucky in not placing a goal from one of their tries.
A most stubbornly-contested game was that between Warrington and Tottington, on the ground of the former, which ended in a draw slightly in favour of the home team by four minors to three.

The meeting to-day of West Lancashire and West Cum- berland, on the Warrington ground, is causing a lot of ex- citement, both teams being very strong. Runcorn met the Liverpool Old Boys, dn the ground of the latter, a very pleasant and excellent game ending in a draw—Runcorn one minor to nil.

Whines received a visit from Farnworth, the proceeds of this match going to one of the Widnea forwards who got hurt a short tir.ne age. Widnes had little trouble in defeat- ng them. Result :—Widnes one goal, one try, and two minors to nil.

At a quarter-past two Black Rod (Admiral Sir James Drummond) was announced. Having advanced to the table, he intimated that "the Queen commands the imme- diate attention of this honourable House in the House of Peers." The Speaker, preceded by the mace and followed by a crowd of members, then went to the Upper House to hear the Queen's Speech read. On his return in a quarter of an hour the sitting was suspended till four o'clock. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock, and intimated that members desiring to take the oath should come to the table. About 40 members thereupon came forward and were duly sworn in. At the same time an extraordinary number of members, including nearly every member of the Parnellite party, put down their names for the ballot, quite half an hour was occupied by hon. gentlemen in writing their names on the list. The Speaker proceeded first to read the customary sessional orders, which Were passed. The Pernellite members endorsed with art audible" aye" the order against peers of the realm taking part in any election of members of this House. NEW WRITS.—New writs were issued for Croydon, Mid- Armagh, and South Edinburgh. NOTICES, &c.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer gave notice that at the close of the debate on the address he will move certain resolutions relating to the procedure of the House, and ask that facilities should be given for the con- tinuous discussion of the subject. Sir R. Cress gave notice that on Monday he will ask for leave to introduce a bill to facilitate the sale of glebe lands, and Sir H. Holland in- timated that on Thursday next he will move for a Select Committee to inquire into the working of the Endowed Schools Act of 1869 and the amending Acts.— After nearly two hundred notices of motion cm various subjects had been given, Mr. BRADLArGIi gave notice of a bill to provide for the better cultivation of land. Amongst the amendments to the Address of which notice was given were one by Mr. Jesse Collings, expressing regret that no measures were announced affording agricul- tural labourers facilities for obtaining allotments, and one by Mr. Hunter, expressing regret that the revenue of India had been employed in the Burmese war without the sanc- tion of Parliament. New writs were ordered to issue for Carlow county and North Monaghan, Mr. E. D. Gray hav- ing electecl to sit for Dublin and Mr. Healy for South Derry. DEB.t.m ON THE ADDRESS.—The Queen's Speech having been read, Viscount Cueloet moved an Address to Her Majesty in reply.—This was seconded by Mr. HOULDS• WORTH, who, alluding to the proposed Royal Commission on the working of the Education Acts, said those Acts gave an immense poster to School Boards and had been worked in a manner very prejudicial to voluntary schools. The hon. member at some length justified the annexation of Burmah —Mr. GLADSTONE said that from the first his highest ambition had been, and continued to be, not to say one word to any man mingling in the question that could bring elements of wrath and passion into a debate on the government of Ireland. Nothing but looking at iewith can- dour and iustice would afford the smallest hope of solving it. He did not deny that the sub- ject had been his daily study, but his obj&ct had been to show where responsibility lay, and that was where the means of action lay there was no greater public calamity than to bring this question within the lines of party politics, and he would take care net to do so. He would wait for the plans of the Government, and although he should listen with great attention to all they would pro- pose he intended to reserve his freedom cf action. He hoped the House would get from the Government some conclusive statement of their views open the social condi- tion of Ireland. Whatever was to be done to Ireland should be done with all promptitude. Whatever the Government thought it should be, the House should know it.--Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Sir J. Kennaway, Mr. Harrington, Mr. G. lirodrick, and Mr. Parnell followed, and the debate was ad- journed.

div.head: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT BY THE QUEEN.
div.p: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT BY THE QUEEN.
PROCESSION AND SCENE IN THE LORDS.

The Queen on Thursday opened Parliament in person. Her Majesty left Buckingham Palace at .a quarter to two, and drove through the Mall, St. James's Park, the Horse Guards, and Parliament. I street. Unfortunately, the weather was very dif- ferent from that which is traditionally associated with Her Majesty's public functions. The snow which fell during the night and the morning, suc- ceeded by light rain, thawed rapidly, and the streets were soon reduced to a miserable plight, though the state of some part of the Royal route was not so bad, owing to the employment of men to clear away the snow. Notwithstanding these un- favourable conditions, however, large crowds of persons lined the route along which the Queen passed, and cheered Her Majesty with the utmost enthusiasm. The Royal procession consisted of seven carriages. The first six contained the officers of Her Majesty's household, and the Queen drove in the 1 seventh, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and the Duchess of Buccleuch. The Prince and Princess of Wales, with Prince Albert Victor, Prince George, and ! Princess Louise of Wales; the Duke and Duchess of ' Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, and Prince Christian and Prince Henry of Battenberg preceded Her Majesty to Westminster. Barriers had been erected along the route, which was kept by about poo police and 3,000 soldiers. Military bands were stationed at various points. A Royal salute from a battery of 'artillery was fired in St. James's Park I immediately the Queen reached the House of Lords.

As early as twelve o'clock, the ambassadors, dis- tinguished personages, and peeresses who have the privilege of being present on State occasions, began to arrive at the House of Lords. And long before the arrival of the Queen, which was fixed for two o'clock, every available accommodation was completely occu- pied. The scene was one of unique magnificence, which for interest and splendour cannot be rivalled in any other country in the World when the Sovereign of Great Britain, with her usual State ceremonies, in- augurates the session of her peers and the representa- tives of her Commons. The gorgeous decorations of the golden chamber, the antique costumes of the peers, the brilliant uniforms of the distinguished per- sons, and the rich a varied dresses of the peeresses, resplendent with diamonds, presented a spectacle of extreme interest and magnificence. The royal cortege did not arrive at the Victoria Tower until a few minutes after the appointed time, and after a short interval the royal procession entered the House headed by the Prince of Wales, who took his seat on the right of the thrones. The peeresses, on his approach, threw off their robes, and the whole of the distinguished assembly rose to their feet. Follow- ing the Heir Apparent came a body of State officials —pursuivants, heralds, and equerries, the Lord Privy Seal, the Deputy Chamberlain. The Prime Minister and the Duke of Portland, carrying the crown, imme- diately preceded the Queen, who looked pale but extremely well. Her Majesty, who wore a black velvet dress trimmed with ermine, and a long train borne by the pages of honour, was assisted to the Throne by the Prince of Wales, and the other mem- bers of the Royal Family at once grouped themselves in their places around the Throne above the Woolsack. The Princess of Wales and the Duchess of Edinburgh were unable to be present. • Her Majesty having signified her pleasure that he should be summoned, the Speaker, in his robes of State, followed by a crowd of honourable members, whose rush frosa one House to the other was somewhat tumultuous, after a short interval, appeared at the bar, and the Speech was read. The Speech over, the proceedings came to an abrupt termination. The Queen, having bowed ceremoniously to the House and to t'ee Speaker at the bar, was led from the Throne by Prince Albert Vic- tor. At the foot of the dais the Prince of Wales took Her Majesty's hand, Prince Albert Victor offering his to the Princess Beatrice. The Heir Apparent con versed with his Royal mother as they led the way from the House, followed by their attendants. In another moment the procession had disappeared. The whole function lasted exactly 22 minutes. A brief period enough, justifying perhaps the overt comment

SANKEY V. ItrNOORN OLD BOPS (IST TEAMS).—P,layed at Sankey on • Saturday. The visitors kicked off against the wind, Jefferson returning. The home forwards going with a rush, forced the visitors to save. After the kick-out the ball as returned by Harding, and J. Barton following up well got past the opposing backs and scored a try. Jeffer- son took the place kick, but failed to improve upon it. Harding now made a short run, but fell. This brought about half-time. Sankey kicked off, and the visitors' for- wards going with a rush, compelled Sankey to touch down. After dropping out, Sankey took the ball to the visitors' 25. and Aahurst passing to J. Barton. this player eluded the visitors backs and grounded near the touch line, but was ruled back. Nothing more happened up to the call of time, Sankey being the winners by one try (Barton), 12 minors, to one minor for Runcorn. Barton, Jefferson, Harding, and Woolev, backs, and Jones, Pemberton, Tongs, and Cowper, forwards, for the home team played a good game. RUNCORN v. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS.—Unfortunately the weather en Saturday was not as agreeable•as the visitors to Brookfield would have desired, a cold wind and drizzling rain being the order of things. A splendid game, however, was witnessed by a fairly large but enthusiastic crowd, and at the close it was voted by all to have been the fastest and best contested match 'played this season on the Brookfield enclosure. The game was maintained at high pressure throughout, both sides exhibiting an amount of vitality that was surprising, with a result that at the finish neither side could claim a victory, one minor—a touch down to Runcorn—being all that was scored during a game of two 35's. For the visitors H Speakman kthree-quarters) and the two half backs (H Hughes and H Andrews) put in some sterling work both offensive and .defensive, and in this trio the Old Boys found the nut hardest to crack; though the Iforwards exhibited little weakness. For the home team the whole of the backs put in a lot of useful work, Hickson especially shining; but the main strength was in the splen- did forward play, and here H Chapman, F Chambers, Walker, and Benstock showed wonderful power. Teams : Runcorn: T Woods, back; E Lunt, El Speakman, and John- son, three-quarters; H Hughes (captain) and H Andrews half backs; W Hughes,'. Wright, J. Lewis, J. Hoffman, J Dean, J Barnes, J Gatley, J Clarke, and W H Broady., forwards. Old Boys: F Hickson, back; 4 D Jones, M Perry, and W Jones, three-quarter backs; Munn and 0 N. Bell, half backs; Chapman, F Chambers (captain), S Charabers, Walker, Bullen, Henstock, Lockwood, Whyte, and Edmunsls, forwards. Mr A B Wilson, of Birkeiahead Park, was the referee. WARRINGTON v. TOTTINGTON.—This match was played

at Warrington on Saturday last, in the presence of alioat 3,000 people. The ground was in a rather slippery condi- tion owing to the recent frost and rain, which made good play very difficult. Fogg won the toss, and Warren started the leather, which was returned into touch in the home territory, where hostilities raged for a short time, until Dillon dribbled nicely to neutral ground. Ashton next put in a dribble, and a pass from Gilbert to Warren, and War- ren to Jolley, was neatly done. A dead ball and touch- down was soon afterwards credited to Tottington. The home team EIOW pulled themselves together, and by some good passing between the backs, and smart rushes by the forwards, play was taken to the visitors' goal. Here from a line up Frank Turner got over the Tottington line, hut , the ball was ruled back on the plea that it was not straightly thrown out. A dead ball was here registered for Warring- ton. Soon after the kick out a long shot by Coop added another minor in the visitors' favour. Half time here being called, the score stood, Tottington 3 minors. to Warrington 1 minor. Fogg started the leather, which Buxton returned well into the visitors' ground. A kick by Massey. followed well up by Povev, compelled Coop to touch down. Play for a short time was very even, both sides, working hard, but the ball being so slippery was very difficult to hold. A smart run and kick by Buxton invaded the visitors' goal, the ball being kicked dead. The leather being started, the home forwards made a determined rash to . the visitors' ground, and Speakman kicked over the line, Coop touching down. No side was shortly afterwards called. The game resulted in a draw in favour .of Warrington by four minors to three minors. The whole of the home team played a good hard game, and, for Tottington, Coop was, as usual, a good full back, his kicking being very serviceable. Dr. Worth- ington, Butterworth, and t.pencer also played a good game. Teams :—Warrington: Back, Buxton; three.quarters, Jolley, Speakmas. and Massey; half, Warren (captaia) and Gil- bert ; forwards, Ashton, Fair Turner, Povey, W. Dillon, S. Hough, Frank Turner, lieges, Nevins, and Savage. Umpire, Mr. T. Barnes. Tottington: Back, Coop; three-quarters, Dr. Worthington, G. Butterworth, and Fogg (captain) ; half, R. Hamlett and Barlow; forwards, Wilson, Leonard, H. Hatnnett, W. Spencer, W. :•methurst, G. Holden, J. Green, J. North, and J. Holt. Umpire, Mr. R. Wallwork. Referee, Mr. T. R. Sutton (Athletic News).

Kiddie, whe was disabled in a match at Roch- dale, was played on Saturday at Widnes in miserable wea- ther. The visitors had the benefit of the wind in the first half, but failed to score, Widnes scoring two minor points. In the second ball Corns got over, and Morris kicked a goal. Murray and Cordingly hereabouts put in some good work, but the Widnes forwards soon had the ball back, and Smith and Corns dribbled over,the first-named securing a try. Time was called, leaving Widnes winners by one goal, a try, and two minors to nil. , WEST LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWNS UNION.—The draw for the first round of ties in the above competition took place at a meeting of the committee held at the Goat Hotel, Liverpool, on Saturday evening, the following being the result :—Pagefield v. The first mentioned club in each case has chlhice of ground, and the round must be played off on the first Satur- day in March. RUNCORN (2IND TEAM V. Strrrox).—This match was played at Runcorn en Saturday. The home team won the toss, and on play being located in the visitors' quarters the home team scored several minor points in quick succession, Cawley, Davis, Faulkner, and Dolan having very bard lines in not getting over the line. On changing ends, the home team came with a rush, Sod carried the ball to the visitors' line, and the Newtonians were again compelled to save. After the drop out, Riley grounded the ball over the line. Faulkner was entrusted with the place, and landed a splen- did goal. The home team still had the best of the game, and just before call of time Clarke secured the ball and gained a second try, Faulkner again doing the needful. No other point was scored, and when time was called Runcorn ' were declared victors by two goals and ten minor points to Sutton nil. _ • _
