EARLE STOW N OLYMPIC V. PRESCOT (A TEAM). - This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday. The captain, centre forward,'and Hobins played well for the home team, but despite all their efforts, the home team failed to score, and a, call of time the Olympians were the victors by six goals to none. The visitors, who had mat- ters much their own way, played a good passing game throughout.

STOCXTONT HEATH Sr. THOMAS'S v. STRETFORD. -- The first teams of the above clubs met on Saturday at Stockton Heath. Stretford kicked off against a strong breeee, and very soon had to play on the defensive. owing to the home forwards' grand play. They, as usual, immediately took possession of the ball, and sent in shot after shot at goal, but were unsuccessful, owing to the splendid defence of the Stretford goal-keeper, who played a grand game, and was deservedly applauded by the spectators as well as both teams. This state of things continued until half-time was called and after a short interval ends were changed, when, with the wind in their favour, the Stretford men endeavoured to fol- low the example of their opponents, but were unsuccessful. Again, in spite of the wind, Stockton Heath were bent on scoring, which made their opponents once more play on the defensive. This kind of play lasted until the call of time, leaving neither side victorious, so that the game ended in a draw. The Stockton Heath goal-keeper had not occasion to handle the ball once throughout the game. PEASLEY Cnoss v. WIDNES.—This match was played on Saturday last at Widnes, and resulted in a victory for Teas- ley Cross by 4 goals to nil. In the first half the home team

The first of a series of Liberal Irctures upon political topics was delivered in Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday evening, by the Rev. W. Vause. the pastor of the local Methodist Free Church. Notwithstanding the inclement state of the weather, an audience of much intelligence and earnestness gathered and listened very attentively to the facts Mr. Vause had to put before them on; the subject of "Our National Expenditure. and, how we are robbed." Mr. W. Handley presided. In the opening address, the Chairman said he was very pleased to see such a good gathering on such an inclement night. If the audience had been much less they would have been quite satisfied at that experimental meeting. It was intended that the president of the local Liberal Association (Mr. James Handley, J.P.,) would have taken the chair, but he took it that the unpropitious state of the atmospheric elements had prevented him from attending; but he could assure them that his sympathies were with them. These meetings were originated for the purpose of keeping alive that Liberal feeling which found such strong expression on December Ist. (Loud applause.) They meant to keep up. that feeling. It was said that nothing succeeded like suc- cess.arThey succeeded on that day he had mentioned, and they must keep it up to that mark, and if possible go beyond it. It was thought at a recent meeting of the Associa- tion it would be an advantage to have monthly meetings of any Liberals, or all Liberals, in Runcorn, to discuss freely and openly subjects which would be to the front in the next session or two of Parliament, so that 'whether the election was near or far in the future they would have formed clear and decided opinions when that election took place. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Vance, who was cordially greeted, said it was one of the most cheering signs in coonection with our national life that the subject before them was fast becoming a topic of general conversation and discussion. There was no subject which would better repay examination on the part of the working and commercial classes than that of our national taxation. In connection with it there was so much that was mean and cruel ; so many instances of shameful oppression and cowardly plunder that it was impossible always to control one's indignation and to avoid giving utterance to one's pent no feelings with regard to our un- speakable aristocracy. (Hear, hear.) The people:were dis- covering how for ages they had been robbed, plundered, and bamboozled. If the people were wise there could only be one result—remedy—reform. (Applause.) The National Debt now stood at about £750,000,000. How had this monster assumed such enormous proportions. If they went back to the time of Cromwell they found there was no national debt. The country had often been at war both foreign and civil, but it had always paid Its way. After Cromwell's death came the restoration of the Stuart line in the person of Charles 11. During his first Parliament, called the Convention Parliament, an act was passed which changed the whole character of our fiscal arrangements, and paved the way for the creation of our National Debt. This Act of Parliament stood in history as one of tile vilest acts of robbery and oppression the world had ever seen. When William the Conqueror beat Harold the Saxon in 1086, he parcelled out the country among his various chiefs reserving, however, large estates for himself, which were celled crown lands. They must not think, however, that he made free gifts of the land to his barons. He gave them the land to hold upon certain conditions. These con- ditiens were sometimes very burdensome. In times of war for instance the barons had to bring and support so many men, according to the amount of land they held, for the as- sistance of the King. If the King were taken prisoner they had to provide money to ransom him. Moreover they had to raise large surds of money when the King's sons were knighted and provide dowries when his daughters were mar- ried. From this they were able to draw a:most important con- clusion, viz., the barons who received and held these estates on the above conditions were not landowners but landhol- ders. The land they held did not belong to them but to the Crown as representing the people. The land belonged to the people, and the barons rented it. This continued for about 600 years In the reign of Charles 11. it was enacted that all these obligations or conditions upon which they held their land should be abolished, and in lieu thereof ex- cise duties upon liquors, brewed or distilled, for sale should be granted to the King and his successors for ever. Thus by one act did they release themselves from the obligation and in full compensation, as they put it, for the rents which they refused to pay, grant to the King a tax upon the people After tbat the people paid the rent and the barons kept the land. No wonder that from such a disgraceful act of oppression many of the landholders themselves shrunk with shame, and that it became law by only a majority of two. The excise duties, however, would not meet the ex- pense. What must be done. Should they impose another tax upon the people, No ;that would be toe dangerous. The people would rise against it. The landholders must tax them- selves. So during the reign of William 11L-1692—they passed the best Act ever passed by a Parliament of land holders, and agreed to tax the entire land of the country at the rate of 4s in the £ yearly value. This tax upon land —"in short upon all real property whatsoever "—should have yielded £3,000,000 per annum. But it was enacted that the statement of value should be taken "not upon oath." Here, then, was a premium upon lying, a tempta- tion our landowners never could resist. A third of the tax went at once. The tax produced two instead of three mil- lions per annum. Nor was this the worst. It had been enacted that this tax should be upon the value of the land at a rack rent. But a few years afterwards an Act was passed declaring that the tax should be at 41 in the en the value in 1692. Besides which la illiam Pitt in 1792 was terribly in want of money for the prosecution of his wars, so he passed a bill for the redemption of the land tax at a very easy rate of purchase. Now see the effect cf this to-day. Land had risen in value in proportion to the commercial progress of the country, and our expenses had increased enormously. Had the land tax increased in pro- portion? Nothing of the kind. That tax which produced two millions when it was imposed in .1692, and which should produce about £40,000,000 according to the in- creased value of the land, produced 4 how mech did they think in 1880? £1,047,076! Out of every X they ought to have paid the handholders managed to put 19s 5d in their own pockets. Was there ever a greater fraud or a more shameful wrong? (Hear, hear.) The history of taxation in this country was a record of shameful oppres- sion and wrong. There was only one class of men in Par- liament, the aristocracy, and so long en they protected their own interests they cared not how they invaded the interests of others. If the taxes they imposed had been imposed directly so that the people really could know how cruelly they were wronged, a revolution would have been pro- duced in a month. But they taxed indirectly, and so they blinded the people. They taxed feed and clothing, and the people did not know that when they spent £5 or £6 a sovereign went really for the article they wanted and the other five to pay the taxes the landlord class refused to pay. By this system our trade and commerce had been fettered, and the poor of the land ground down and starved. The landlord cities spent money and they taxed; they taxed and spent money until there was hardly a thing an ordio- ary Englishman could eat or wear or do, without a great part of the money spent going to pay for the extravagance of our ruling class. Mr. Vause described haw the National debt had been created, and traced its gradual ac- cumulation up to its present enormous proportions. After sixty years of comparative peace and most cruel taiation, we have not reduced the debt 90 millions, or less than millions per year. At the same rate of reduction it would take 500 years to wipe off the debt still remaining, while at the same time we should have ta meet our ordinary ex- penditure and pay for any wars in which we might engage. . Altogether, six years ago, the National Debt had swallowed upwards of two thousand millions since 1800. At the

present time the interest on the debt amounted to nearly £30,000,000. We had our army and navy to sustain. To- gether they cost nearly £29,000,000. We had the expenses connected with the collection and manage- ment of revenue departments, the civil depart- ments, and other charges on the consolidated fund, and together these amount to £28,000,000. Therefore our total ordinary annual expenditure for the year ending March, 1884, was £87.000,000. len years before, 1874, it was £74,000,000, an increase of £13,000,000 in that period. At that rate of progress we should reach £100,000,000 an- nual expenditure before the century was out. But astound- ing as the figures might be we could have little or no true conception of the reckless extravagance and cruel injustice they represent until we come to examine in particulars the way the money went. Then we should discover the most • complete system of organised villany the world bad ever seen. We should see how British landholders, having frau- dulently obtained possession of the land, were far from con- tent; how they, having seized almost every seat in the House of Commons as well as every seat in the House of Lords, manipulate the laws so that the great weight of tax- ation might press upon the commercial and labouring classes and not on themselves, how although as much as possible they avoid the paying of the taxes, they were always in at the plunder; how they monopolised all the best offices, however incapable they might be of fulfilling the duties ; how the public service, the government, the army, navy, diplomatic service, the State church, enc., enc., were crammed with their friends arid relatives ; bow, for occupying these positions, many of which are sinecures formed for the purpose of cramming the pocket of some in- famous and fawning sycophant, they bad managed to rob the British taxpayer of scores and scores of millions. (Applause.) ' Mr,Tause, illustrating how the public service was crammed with the relations of our aristocracy, gave particulars show- ing that daring the thiry years 18150 to 1880 there were 25 relatives of the Duke of Devonshire filling 55 offices, and had received a total of £174,000. But while this single family have been taking from the public funds this enor- mous sum of money in pensions or salaries for doing some- thing or nothing, as the case might be. it must be remem- bered that they had been receiving at the same time still greater sums from the landed estates which they had stolen from the State. The Duke of Devonshire owned land in 14 different counties, amounting to above 193,000 acres. This brought in a rental of over £172,000. nearly £5OO per day. The Marquis of Hartineten owned 5,633 acres, a rental of over £6250; Lord eh esham 11,486 acres,a rental of £15,614. Here there was a family having an annual rental of nearly £200,000, equal to £6OO a day, and yet in addi- tion to this tremendous sum of money they crammed every possible lucrative nosition with one of their family or hangers-on, and in 30 years extract money from the public public coffees to the tune of £174,000. Nor was this the worst. They were a family notoriously incapable and com- mon-place. They had never possessed a clever man. ,Take, for instance, the Marquis of Hartington. He was, he (Mr. Vance) supposed, the most capable man they had produced. But what was he? He occupied one of the most responsible positions in the last Liberal Government and had a seat in the Cabinet. Why ? Because of genius or transcendental ability ? Yot at aIL He did not suppose he had the ability of an ordinary man of business. In commercial life he would never have made his way. But in politics, to he Liberal party the support of these great Whig families was thought to be in- dispensable, and the Duke of Devonshire must be concil- iated. In 30 years 21 of the relations of the Duke of Bed- ford bad received consiierably over £540,000. Besides that the Duke had a rental of £140,000, exclusive of land in London, which as a result of the trade and commerce of the country had become of fabulous value. His daughter was married a few days ago, and would tkey believe it this Duke with his vast income from his London estates, his other estates in eight different counties, actually purchased almost the whole of the bride's trousseau in Paris. What did they think of it in a time of anparalleled trade depres- sion, when business men were at their wits' end to meet the heavy taxation, this mean and selfish bloated aristocrat, this wholesale land robber, this runner away from taxation, this stick-up gilded pauper, would, to save his own pocket, take the trade from the men who, by their hard labour, sup- port him and his family, and give it to those of another nation. And this. forsobth, was the class who talked about and condemned Free Trade, who wanted a tax put upon corn again, so that the farmer might get more for his grain and pay more in rent to the greedy landlord. (Applause.) There were dukes 28, maiquesses 83. earls 200, total 261; and these families had crammed 3.391 relatives into 5,963 offices, and received over £48,181,202 But besidcs these there were 60 viscounts and 211 barons. These together with those above gave a grand total of families 532, rela- tives 7,991, offices 13,888, money received in 30 years, 108,614,632. A great part of the public service was inede for these persons. Sinecure positions were created, and most extravagant salaries were attached ; and the people were continually being deceived, bamboozled, and robbed. And this would continue until the people examined the question and rose up against it. Then it would be swept away, and the people would wonder why they were fools, and bore it so long. Why, with sons of their own every office should be crowded with those of another class, why the wealthy and idle class should alone be thought cepahle of doing the nation's business and receiving the cream of the public pay. (Applause.) We were a limited monarchy. Undoubtedly that was the form of Government preferred by a majority of th'e people, and for that reason, though not for many others, it was better we should have it than a Republic. Having a monarchy, it was proper we should pay a liberel amount to our reigning family. In this liberal frame of mind he asked them to look at the annual cost of our Royal family, and however good humoured they might be at the commencement they would gradually lose patience, until at last they would stand aghast at the reckless extravagance, the disgraceful extortion, and the paltry greed this part of our expenditure exbibited. Our queen was generally thought to receive about £385,000 per annum, but when there was added to that amount the expenses of the numerous palaces and other residences kept for her benefit; the outlay on the royal yachts, and other naval charges, together with the expenditure on royal escort, military charges, they would find the total amount paid on account of the sovereign to exceed £600,000. Then all her children were specially provided for. Time Prince of Wales received i`.40.000, charged on the consoli- dated fund ; about £65,000 from the Duchy of Cornwall; and £lO,OOO on behalf of his wife. Moreover, he monopolises five or six military appointments, for which he did nothing but draw the salary, and attend the Liverpool Grand National or the Lincolnshire Handicap whilst his regiments are fighting in Egypt. (Laughter and applause.) The total expense of the Royal family to the country was just about a million per annum. Surely there was room here for a vast reduction in our national expenditure? (Ap- plause.) With all the vast sums paid to our Royal family year by year they lost no opportunity to squeeze an extra £lOO whenever they could. (Hear, hear.) Even for the last German beggar a bill of special nation- alization must be hurried through Parliament, so that with- out a moment's delay Henry of Battenberg might be ap- pointed to a lucrative position in the army and begin. to drain the public purse. (Applause.) After ilealiug ev!th the great cost of the Royal yachts, Mr. Vanse said paying such vast Burns of money the least the people expected was some sign of anxiety on the part of the Sovereign for the national interest. But instead of considering that she exists for the nation's good she seems to consider the nation as existing for her own personal benefit. Mr. Vause, in illustration of this referred to her action during the crisis with Russia early in 1885, and other matters. During the last twelve months there had been three distinct and im- portant and public occasions on which our Sovereign re- fused to perform the duties for which she was paid and put the country to immense inconvenience. In conclusion he said hitherto the legislation had all been for the landlord class. Now the power had passed out of the hands of the landowners, and they cried out lest the new demo- cracy shetild use their new power to their own good. Don't allow cries about class legislation from those who for hundreds of years had been scheming and legislating for their own clue to prevent them from trying to equalise matters now they had the chance. (Applause.) There was only one way in which the new Democracy could make its power felt—that was by sending men to represent them pledged to strive after their interests. And the pledge required should be not a few vague sentences on a public platform a month before an election, but the record of the candidate's past life and a similarity of interest. He hoped the time had come when for a man to be connected with the landed, the fighting, or the aristocratic interests would make it impossible for him to be a Liberal candidate, and he advised them to always chose a local manufacturer or a working-man. If they did this they should soon see the last of the second great cause of all the evils of which he had been speaking—he meant indirect taxation. (Loud applause.) Mr. Leak and the Chairman made a few remarks upon the subject, and upon the motion of Mr. B. Kniveton, seconded by Mr. Jepson, a.cordial vote of thanks was ac- corded to Air. Vause for his able and instructive lecture.

div.head: ENOUGH EVEN FOR SCEPTICS. (Loncloa Christian Globe.)
div.p: ENOUGH EVEN FOR SCEPTICS. (Loncloa Christian Globe.)

Highly interesting accounts have appeared lately in a number of professional and other publications of the mar- vellous results attained in the cure of certain painful dis- eases (which have hitherto been classified as incurable), through the medium of an external remedial agent. These accounts are so well authenticated as to leave no doubt of their absolute truthfulness and the efficacy of the remedy. Upon analysis it 13 found that one of the princi- pal ingredients of the preparation in question is an oily sub- stance extracted from the leaves of a species of pine tree by a patented process. This may account for the fact that the remedy has become known as an oil—the trade mark being "St. Jacobs Oil," under wbich name it has been re- gistered in the Patent Office in this and other countries. Among numerous surprising cures we investigated and verified two in particular, either of which is suffizient to leave no doubt of the immense value of this discovery. One is the case of a man who has been treated at numerous London and other. hospitals for a number of years, where not only did he receive no benefit, but his case was pro- noanced incurable. Here was rheumatism of the most ag- gravated desAption, drawing up the joints and rendering the patient a helpless cripple. At one of the institutions in Derbyshire where he received treatment he enjoyed the benefits of all the advantages, baths, mineral waters, &c., at the command of the name, and after all was discharged as incurable. A friend's attention having been called to an article in a London newspaper upon the subject of this oil, a trial was suggested. The first bottle produced a marvel- lous change, and after two week's use he was cured and

On Saturday, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- Lire Railway, near Silkstone Station, the remains of a l:Ick burner, named Charles Harrison, were found strewed Z)out the line. It is supposed that he was caught, nocked down, and literally cut to pieces by a fast goods train.

The Key-note of Good Breeding.—"B" natural. The point any woman can appreciate.—Point lace. When is a fawning '' toady " like cinders F—When he falls in the dust before the great (grate). First friend: How can Mrs. Jones wear such loud colours? —Second friend: Why, don't you know? She's as deaf as a post. PHYSIOLOGICA.L.—" What are the last teeth that come?" asked a teacher of her clan. "False teeth, mum !" replied a boy on the back seat. A lady once said to Turner of one of his glorious sunsets,' "I never saw anything like this in nature." No, madam," he responded, 'but don't you wish you could?" Little Johnny, on being asked by his school-teacher if he knew what was meant by "at par," rep/tied, "Ma is always at pa when he comes home late. Six-year-old to grandfather Grandpa dear, we have come to wish you many happy returns of your birthday; , and mamma says, if you give us each half-a-crown, we are not to loss it on our way home. An Irishman angling in the rain was observed to keep his line under the arch of a bridge. On being asked the reason he said, " Och, sure the fishes will be after crowding there to keep out of the wet!" At a meeting in Whiteehapel a pertinent answer was given to a question asked by a candidate for Parliamentary honours. "What," said he, "did a Lord 'Mayor ever do for you ?" "Give you six moiths," was the reply. "Mrs. De Silva is so poetical r. observed Mrs. Brown to her husband. "She calls her new dresses 'dreams." "A very good name for them," responded Mr. Brown, "for her busband always speaka of the bills as 'nightmares." A barrister, in replying to his antagonist in court, said he had a keen rapier with which to pierce all fools and knaves; whereupon his opponent "moved the Court" that the rapier be taken from him, lest he should commit suicide. Mother: Why, you are surely not hungry after eating such a big dinner i—Sean : Not 'xactly huegry, but I've got an all gone feeling, just as lithe dinner wasn't there! Music-teacher: Your daughter, Mrs. Jones, has real musical talent. She ought to have a thorough training.— Mrs. Jones: That's just what I was telling Mr. Jones to- day; and we agreed to engage a competent teacher for her after she has finished her next quarter with you. EXCIIANGE OF COMPLMIENTS.—First lady (to bosom- friena) : "That dress suits you admirably. What a pity the material is so common !"—Second lady: "True. And spurs is a splendid material; you must be sorry it dose not aft you better !" When the superintendent of a certain Texas penitentiary said to a newly-arrived convict, "You have the privilege of , working at any trade you prefer," the prisoner replied, "I'd ' like to keep on drivin' cattle to Kansas." Another in the same institution wanted to be a sailor. Not long ago a Scotch lad ran away from farm-service, and, on being questioned by his friends as to the reason, he ' said he did not like the meat. "The farmer," he said, "had a sheep that deed, and I had to help to eat it. Then a calf deed, which I had to help to eat as weel. Thee the auld farmer's wife deed, and I was sent to a shop for a lot o' salt. Div ye think I was gann to stop to eat the anld woman? No likely! So I hooked it.* "You will have to watch for alligators very carefully at first," was the advice given to an invalid on his arrival in Florida; "but, after you have been here a few weeks, it won't so much matter." "Why not ?" was the question. "Why should I be more cautions at one time than another?" "Because," was the reply," after you have been here a little while, you will have grown too this to be an object of in- terest to alligators. They want only fresh arrivals." An "'eggshellent " joke, says the IV aval and -Ifiliigary Gacette, was perpetrated by the Sirdar of Candahar upon some English visitors who were proud of their marksman- ship. He made them shoot at a hen's egg hung against a wall, which baffled their aim until the thread was cut, and , the egg fell to the ground without breaking. They then found that the shell was blown, and the wind of the bullets ' had saved it from being struck. Among the replies to an advertisement of a musical com- mittee for "a candidate as organist, music-teacher, fsec.," was the following one—"Gentlemen,—l noticed your advertise- ment for an organist and music-teacher, either lady or gentleman. Having been both for several years, I offer yen my services." "How does it happen.,, Bridget, that there are as many feet of gas charged for this month as last, when Mrs. Blossom and myself have been out of town three weeks "Shure an' I can't tell, sorr, eavin' that, whin the gintiermus came to Ink at the mayther, there was six fate of coal and wood on top of it, an' he obearved that I needn't bother wid it— he'd take a Ink at the pracaydin' figgers. Maybe he added the six fate of wood an coal—l don't know !" At a recent trial in Ireland a witness who had been as- saulted and considerably damaged about the head-piece was being examined. "And were you stunned when you were knocked down ?" "Was I what, yer honour ?" "Stunned." "Shure an' I don't know what ye mane, yer honour." "Were you rendered insensible ?" "Shure an' what is in- sinsible, at all, at all ?" Counsel was shrugging his shoulders in despair at the stupidity of the witness, when a juryman arose and asked to be allowed to interrogate him. "Did they kill ye now, Pat?" said he. "Shure, an' they did intoirely, yer honour !" answered Pat.

• &MINK; HIM A LITTLE OF HIS OWN SArC2.—ln Limerick an hotel-keeper said to a customer who was com- plaining about the bad times, "You're a landlord, sir, and must put up with the times, and make a reduction to your tenants of fifty per cent." This was before dinner. After It came the bill, amounting to eighteen shillings. "Here, waiter," said the diner, "is half a sovereign ; give your master nine shillings and keep the change. He is an honest fellow, and must.put up with the bad times !" A three year-old girl was taught to close her evening prayer, during the temporary absence of her father, with "and please watch over my papa." It sounded very sweet, but the mother's amusement may be imagined when the child added, " and better keep an eye on mamma, too!" "I understand that Mr. Wilson has retired from business," remarked the bill collector to the clerk. " Yes, sir," replied the clerk. "I wonder whet is to be dine with this little bill of mini? " "I don't know, sir," answered the clerk. "I think—" "Where can I address Mr. Wilson? If he doesn't pay I sue him. Where is he to be found ? " "I can't say, sir. Be—" "So he has gone away, has he, without leaving his address? The old schemer." "Yes, sir. Be is dead." A GOOD ScrGauFrrios:—Some men find it difficnit to grow old gracefully. Colonel Yergeris one of them. Last Sunday his little daughter caught him at work on his own head with a band razor and a pair of tweezers. "Papa, what are yon doing to your hair ? " she asked. "I am pul- ling out the white hairs, Mollie?' "Why don't you pull the black ones out? you will get through quicker. There ain't half so many black ones as there are white."

PROLONGED -TORTURE. "In '72," said somebody to a G 143, Delnoerat correspon- dent, "I was a green young country boy, and had commenced studying law in Attica—that little place we jest named. In the summer-time a friend of mine, who knew I was hard up, suggested that I go out to his farm and spend a couple of months while he and his wife made a visit te Philadelphia. I was only too glad to do it. He lived about four miles from Attica, half the way over a turnpike that had been disused—a lonely, but rather pretty location. '4 The only other person there was a farm hand. Thee wasn't much to do and I had a high old time. One day, I remember it was 'boiling hot—in July, I think—the hired man went to a picnic and left me alone on the farm. To. ward noon I got a diabolical toothache. It was the jump- ing kind; felt every moment or two as if somebody had hit the nerve with a tack hammer, and I went raving about the place has a madman. I tried everything I could think of until I recollected all of a sudden that there was a small bottle of whisky on the pantry shelf. I rushed in, grabbed the bottle, and took a swig. As I sat down I glanced at it, and to my unspeakable horror read the word 'laudanum' on a big black label. It struck me instantly that I had got the wrong bottle, and also that I had a strange taste in my mouth. They kept a lot of medi- cine and odds and eneis in the pantry, and that accounted for the mistake. "For a moment my brain was in a whirl, and then I col- lected my thoughts ann rapidly surveyed my chances. I did not know exactly how much opium there was in the laudanum, but realised that I had oertainly swallowed enough to kill a dozen men, and my only hope lay in obtain- ing prompt me' .cal assistance. I thrust the bottle in my pocket to iicate how much I had taken, and ran for the barn. "There was only one horse on the place—an old, wind- broken, dirty-white bag of bones, that hadn't seen out of a walk since the year one. The way I slung the harness on to him was a caution to snakes. My hands trembled so that I could scarcely fasten the buckles, but I finally got our rattletrap of a two-seated buggy hitched up and started for town. "I didn't stop to shut the gate. I just leaned over the dashboard and hammered the old horse with the whipstock until he broke into a scared gait, half-run and half-trot. In a moment or two he got used to the licking, and it was almost impossible to keep him going. If Berg had seen me,• I would certainly have been in the penitentiary to-day for cruelty to animals. I smashed him over the back until great welts stood out like furrows oa a plow field, and howled, and raved, and swore. It seemed to me we mailed along so slowly we were scarcely moving at all, and the minutes sped in diametrically opposite ratio. I would have got out and walked, but dare' not trust my legs for the dis- tance.

"Meantime I felt the poison working in my system. A deadly lassitude crept over me. I had read of such things, and I felt them in all their magnified horrors. It seemed, In some strange, inexplicable way, as if I had a dual ex- istence, one weakly, eager to lie down and sleep, come what might, and the other fired with all the energy of despair to rea, the town. No tongue can tell the battle I fought be- tween these two.impule.es.

"I loeked with indescribable anxiety for teams on the road, but there was little travel on the turnpike I have de- scribed, and none at all that day. I passed several farm- houses, it is true, but the people were all in at dinner, and I .dare not take the time to hunt them. My life hung on the momenta. - _ .

"BY this time I had lost all volition. The whip dropped from my nerveless hands, and the reins slid into my lap. It is needless to say the horse fell into a very slow walk. Occasionally he stopped and appeared to be ruininating. I tried to yell at him, but, although I desired to make a noise with an intensity of will that was agonising, my tongue seemed chained, and I uttered no sound.

But last night the police took concerted action, and at the doors of the-Gaiety, the Avenue, Drury- Lane, and Exeter Hall constables were successful, and brought in their men. These raids always have a geterrent effect. There is a scare. "The profession" abandon their old haunts, business remains dull for a week or so, and then a new centre is formed, and the thieving recommences. The public will at least be glad to hear that for some little time to come the theatre exits will be safe. M. Van Beers has had this year less success than last. The Salon Parisian was an experiment last season, and had novelty to recommend it. The pub- lic were caught by mysterious arrangements of light, eccentricities of framing, and a general tricki- ness of accessory. The works exhibitga were won- ful in execution, but in subject not what English people were accustomed to. This year the salon has gone further in the same direction. One may not quite hold the Horsley theories of the nude and yet object very decisively to the suggestive. M. Van Beers is, comparatively speaking, a young man with 1 a great sense of colour and an almost uncanny facil- ity of execution. All his landscapes and a few of his figure subjects show him to have the stuff out of which great artistic triumph may come. But he is not sufficient of a giant to corrupt English taste, 1 and the public verdict .has on this occasion been i plainly given. .

LONDON, THURSDAY. Londoners have so few spectacles that it was a little hard to find the skies dark and lowering to- day when the Queen went to open Parliament. The snow, which fell between two and three this morning, had melted, leaving the streets in a pitiable condition. There was a cold bleak wind, ' and some threatening of rain. Nevertheless the people had assembled in hundreds of thousands along the route from Buckingham Palace to West- minster Bridge by which the famous eight cream horses would presently go. Enterprising persons having desirable points of view along the route had put up wooden platforms, and were rewarded by unbounded custom. According to the experiences of these gentlemen there is nothing and nobody draws like the Queen, a favourable view of Her Majesty's attractiveness fully borne out to-day. , Going down to the House about an hour before the Queen was expected, I noticed that every stand was filled to its utmost capacity. There was a great show of policemen on foot and on horseback, also of soldiers. The route was, in - truth, guarded as if conspirators lurked in every cellar, and assassins were promiscuously posted at the open windows. The Queen's nervousness at appearing in public decidedly increases. ' She has, since she came to the throne, made many passages through London; but never were such extraordinary pre- cautions taken in the matter of police and military arrangeasents as were carried out to-day. The muster of judges was notably 1 small, their lordships being for the most part on circuit. They wore their gowns and wigs, some with white tippets and others with dark blue 1 cloaks laced with gold. Both bishops and judges ' had a considerable advantage over the unhappy 1 noblemen penned up upon the benches nearer the ' bar. They, like Sterne's starling, "could not get ' out" if they had wanted, and if they had got out ' could not get back. The bishops and the judges had free circuit in the limited space open to anyone, and went about gaily chatting with Royal princes or with the ladies of their-acquaintance. The first of the Royal Family to arrive was the Duke of Edinburgh, who did a good deal of hand- shaking. The Duke of Connaught arrived shortly afterwards, both hiding their uniforms, under the cloak of the peer. Prince Teck, in colonels uniform, appeared next crossing before the Throne with swaggering stride, betokening the bold sabreur. At a quarter to two a sudden rise and a buzz of whis- pering announced the arrival of the Prince of Wales. His Royal Highness, who, by the way. is getting s balder than ever—was in most gracious mood and made at least a dozen peers and as many ladies happy by shaking hands with them. Xwo or three bishops betrayed a strong desire to bring themselves within the light of the royal countenance. and finally succeeded in their object. The Prince ' lounged over the rail at the end of the bench on the ' Opposition side and talked with all the ladies with- ' in his reach. As he turned to one or other to make salutation, the lady rose and curtsied which, as Mr. Pepys said, " was pretty to see." All this time the Throne had remained tenantless, half hidden with a mantle of Royal crimson and velvet heavily trimmed with gold lace and lined with white satin. At two o'clock the ladies began to take off their opera cloaks and shawls; a hun- dred white shoulders flashed out into the gaslight—' a good deal of some of them; the curtain was drawn back from the doorway to the left of the Throne, leading into the ante-room; and visions were caught a of plumed knights and men-at-arms passing to and ' fro. Suddenly the buzz of whispering incessantly kept up in the House was silenced by a blare of trumpets. The ladies with one accord rose to their feet and finished the work of divesting themselves of their outer wraps. The Prince of Wales crossed over from the corner at which he had been standing, and took up his position on the right of the Throne. The curtains over the doorway was dropped, and the whole audience remained standing in momentary expectation of the entrance of the Queen. It was at this moment a splendid sight; the fair women, the flashing jewels, and the manifold military uniforms. ~ At ten minutes 'past two, the curtain of the door- way on the other side of the Throne was drawn back and there entered a procession of heralds clad in gorgeous cloth of gold, who bowed low to the Prince of Wales as they passed, and halting again before the Empty Throne did it obeisance. Im- mediately after, came the Queen, looking, if the truth may be told, a little "dumpy" in the brilliant procession of which she was the central figure. She wore a dress that seemed black, though I am told by a lady that it was a dark blue. A few white , ribbons relieved the dullness of the costume. - She wore a crown of diamonds on her head, whilst the famous Koh-i-noor blazed from her throat. At an almost imperceptible signal from the Queen, the audience resumed their. seats; the Commons were sent for; they came with a mighty rush; the Lord Chancellor read the Queens speech; whereupon her Majesty rose and returned, having opened Par- liament without opening her lips. ' There has been this week quite an unaccountable • ~ . display of energy on the part of the London police. I suppose they were so busy with the dogs lately that they got a taste for action, and they were cer- tainly much better employed in concentrating their forces on pick-pockets. We have had thia -winter a recrudescence of pocket-picking, especially at theatre doors. No doubt the opening of Parliament has brought a number of thieves to town. Displays

ICE ACCIDENT: Two CHILDREN DBOWNED.—A terrible ice accident cccutrad on Saturday afternoon on a pond at Annesley Park, Notts, the seat of Mr. John Chaworth-Mus- ters. Frosty weather bad caused the formation of a ;beet of thin ice upon the pond. Some children finding their way into the park began to slide upon the ice, but it gave way, and five then fell into deep water. Help- WAS obtained after a little delay, but only three of The children were saved. CONCERT AT ST. BEDE'S APPLETON, WIDNES.-04 Tues- day evening a miscellaneous concert took place in the new school-rooms, Appleton. Although the weather was un- favourable, there was an excellent attendance. The fol- lowing artistes took part in the entertainment: Misses Jameson, Hewitt, Messrs. Morrison, Heyes, Finn, Scott, and St. Mary's Catholic Choral Society. Special mention is due to Miss Jameson for her rendering of the well-known songs, "When other lips" and the ‘. Circas!ian's dream," both of which procured encores. Mr. Morrison, who sang in capital style deseivedly gained the recalls which were awarded him. Mr. F. Scott (of Runcorn) brsnutht the house down by his singing of two comic songs. Miss Hewitt was not in her usual good voice. Mr. F. Hayes and Mr. Finn also sang .in a pleasing manner. The St. Mary's Catholic Choral Society sang three glees in a manner which elicitedconsiderabie applause. Mr. Finn and Master F. N. Mercer gave two finished performances on the pianoforte. Misses Culleen and Johnson ably accompanied the singers. At the conclusion of the concert the usual votes of thanks were passed.
