JAQUES.
LABOUR AND TRADES COUNCILS. Sir,—You have been kind enough to insert several letters
'rom me on labour questions. I ask for your further indul-

gence on this subject. li•therto my object has been to point out the necessity that exists for the complete federation of the whole of the labour classes, and I have urged, along with this, the great desirability of union for employer and employed. A case has just arisen in this town, in which a body of men, num- bering between fifty and sixty, have been refused admit- tance into what is known as the " Warrington Trades Council." lam compelled to draw attention to this case, sir, inasmuch as in your last issue I find a short report of the mere meeting of this Council. A short sketch of their doings would have been interesting to your readers, who are no doubt chiefly working-men, and therefore interested in labour quest:ons. The rejection by the Trades Council of the body of men to whom I refer may result at an early date ix consequences none will deplore more than the present writer, but the decision will no doubt be accepted as final, and independence of action will be claimed and acted upon by the poor discarded ones. The question may be asked—What do we expect to gain by forming strong cembinations of labeur ? The answer to this is a wide one ; but we may take it for granted that the good resulting from such combination will depend very much upon the intelligence by which they are guided. It is not for me to urge the federation of labour for the mere purpose of .enforcing unfair conditions upon employers. Such a policy could be but the outcome of ignorance, and would result in disaster. I rather urge it for the purpose of creating a means whereby the power possessed by work- men can be used for forwarding such negotiations and equitable settlements, as can only be the outcome of an equality of interests. To make this clearer, the interest of the workman lies in having plenty of work, and in being well paid for it. The interest of the employer lies in the full empl yment of his machinery, and in receiving such interest, or profit, as will repay him for all rieks he may run by investing his capital in trade. The interests here are equal, or mutual. I suppose very few people expected that with the advent of a new Government we should witness a sudden revival of trade. There might be a few, who, pinning te.eir faith to a Fair Trade policy, thought by returning a Tory majority they were deing something towards bringing about a better state of things. These poor deluded people have lived to see their hopes dashed to the ground, and possibly they may think it woith their while now to listen te the *Cassandra-like wet flings that have been thrown out during the past twelve months. It is needful that work- .men should realise that England is not now the workshop of the world. Nations that were once our largest custo- mers now manufacture for themselves, and are actively leaving their own shores in search of customers. The eplestion for us, as workmen, to ask is—how are we placed in the competitive race ? Are we fairly handicapped with these foreigners in our efforts to :produce, and in our methods of distribution? We must answer, certainly not.

Working-men, by being strongly combined, could insist upon manufacturers helping them to bring about a reform in our land laws. Instead of paying enormous sums of money to landowners for the right to get the earth's minerals, we ought to be able, after paying a nominal royalty, to get these ores, and dispose of them for the national, instead of the individual, welfare. I must tell the various sorts of ironworkers in Warrington that before the metal he has to manipulate reaches his hands it has already been taxed by one who toils not neither does he spiie "to an extent that would sufficiently repay him for his labour. This applies to production. With distrinution the question is so large that it is beyond the scope of anything less than a Royal Commission. I saw in the papers a short time ago a statement to the effect that Messrs. Nettiefold, of Birmingham, intended to remove their Want to some part of the Welsh coast. By this they expected to reduce their yearly railway charges by an enormous amount In one of your contemporaries there has just been published an account showing the cost of conveying iron girders from Antwerp to Birmingham ; the sea and land carriage via Grimsby is 163 8d per ton. For less than half the mileage, viz., from Birmingham to Grimsby, the manufacturer has to pay 203. Is it not clear from this that neither landowners, nor vet railway share- holders, are alive to the fact that- they are conspirieg together to bring down the English workman to the level of the Continental workman. Here we have the railway company encouraging German manufactures by subsidy, and we have landowners claiming to tax the products of nature by the exaction of royalties. English workmen must understand that the wages paid in Germany would not have the same purchasing power in England that they have in Germany. The same economic forces that enable the Germans to produce cheaply enable them to live cheaply, and yet it is as sure as fate that un- less action is taken in the direction to which I have pointed not only our foreign markets will be lost to us, but our home markets also. Ere this state of things arrives, we shall, as workmen, have found the lower depths. By some twist of the social kaleidoscope we find that German wire manufacturers are joining in partnership with English manufacturers, and are insisting upon the right to dictate and arrange snch terms as to them seem agreeable. No defence can be made, because mutual benefit has not been kept in view ; and I take it that in this trade at least, in consequence of sheer stupidity, the metto for the future will be—" Each man for himself, and the devil take the hindmost."

div.head: ?Centro to the gditor.
div.p: ?Centro to the gditor.
THE READING ROOM.

Sir,—l have paid several visits to the reading room in Bold-street, but have never been able to find a current issue of any London daily paper, or even of a provincial daily newspaper. Is not the good old town of Warrington a little behind hand in this respect? One can enter news- rooms in smaller places, and places of far less importance all over the conntry, and find copies of the leading London I and provincial journals, and a number of weeklies and tech- nical publications to boot. In days of such fast progres- sion, what's the use of going to a reading room to pick up a few days' old newspaper, when, perhaps. the character of public events has completely changed. The present state of things may suit a few of the old people, but it is not likely to very much advance a knowledge of passing events amongst the younger and more numerous class.— , Yours, A REMINDER.

div.head: GAS DEPOSIT SYSTEM.
div.p: THE GAS DEPOSIT SYSTEM.

Sir,—Pleise allow me to say a few words on the practice of the gas authorities in Warrington in demanding a deposit from householders whose houses they supply with gas. I see that the subject was brought forward at a recent meet- ing of the Town Council, and that some of the members, I believe the Mayor included, justified the mode of dealing in question, and it was also said that the gas officials were very careful as to whom they required deposits from. It is all right to exercise caution to prevent being swindled by migratory families, but to me the question resolves itself into one of principle. A friend of mine occupying a good position took a house in the town, and an official of the Gas Committee, he informs me, came to take away the meter immediately he had entered the house, without allow- ing him time to communicate with the gas authorities. MY friend says that according to the rules of the Gas Com- mittee persons who barn gas without communicating with the officials first are liable to a penalty, but in his case no Lime was given for him to do so. lie resented this treat- ment, and dispensed with the use of gas while occupying that house. I believe •be now uses gas without paying the deposit. I think that the principle of demanding deposits is contrary to all business customs, and places gas consumers at a disadvantage. What would be thought of a private trader who tried to introduce such a practice, and refused to supply goods on credit without prepayment of a deposit? —Yours, <kn.,. PRO LEST.

div.head: STREEI NUISANCE.
div.p: A STREEI NUISANCE.

Sir,—When, under cover of darkness, I timidly ventured to drop my little note on the above subject into your cipa- cions letter box the other week, I little thought the letter of so humble and obscure an individual as yours truly (if it should he so fortunate as to obtain insertion)•would create such a flutter amongst the offending chipped potato caterers. That there was some ground for my feeble complaint is moved by the readiness with which the .potato prowlers hasten with so much vituperation to deny-mv assertion. I fancy when " John Plinston " wrote his epistle he must have been suffering from the irritation of a journey to the Museum in order to consult " Webster " to spell his way through my short letter. I all sorry " John " had need of a dictienary, and still more sorry that he htd not one of his own ; but I regret most of all that the " chipped potato " business is so dreadfully dull that he cannot afford to buy one.

_ lam not in want of any pity from' " Pol 6 Cat," or any- one else, as I am neither young, untravelled, nor an " ex- quisitely sensitive plant," but a person of ordinary feelings, and somewhat accustomed to the " vulgar contaminAtions of every-day life." It was not, therefore, with any desire to " rush into print " that I wrote you, Mr. Editor, but with a view to rendering some service to my fellow-townsmen irry stopping, if possible, an undoubted nuisance, and it is to be hoped that, notwithstanding the flat,eriog mariner your cor- respondents speak of Inspector Norman for having hither° let them alone, the worthy Inspector will do his duty, and thus relieve those whom providence has gifted with a slight sense of smell.—Yours, J. G. R.

ALDERMAN BURGESS AND FE MALE • DRUNKENNESS. Sir,—What a wonderful genius for analysis Alderman Burgess must possess. On several occasions, by his search- ing analyses of the motives and prejudices of people who have objected to the smells from Longford depot, he has conclusively demonstrated to his own satisfaction that the odours complained of were really not at all of the character it was said they were, but that, on the contrary, in sweet- aess and wholesomeness they were little short of the balmy gales which the poet says come from "Araby the blest." But even in the analytical line be excelled himself at the com- plimentary dinner to the Mayor last week. He had a list of 148 different females who had been charged with druuken- ness during the year in Warrington, most of whom, accord- ing to the Chief Constable, were "girls and young women." But Alderman Burgess doesn't like this way of putting it ; he is jealous of the fair name of the " girls and young women" of Warrington. Lie therefore sets his analytical genius to work, with the result that in less than live minutes the whole list vanishes into thin air. But how does he do it ? With true analytical instinct he eliminates. First of all he leaves out all the delinquents who are above 25 years of ago, then he fixes die standard at 1$ years of age, and leaves out another batch, and finally he comes down to 16, with the happy result that not one is left. The honour of Warrington was certainly never before so ingeniously vin- dicated. But it is to be feared there is a fatal flaw in the Alderman's argument which the ladies themselves, although no doubt anxious to say the best they can for their own sex, will be the first to fix upon, and that law is in the limits which have been fixed upon as to age. It can safely be said that if the decision was left to a jury of ladies the unanimous verdict would be that both Alderman Burgess and the Chief Constable were making an unwarrantable as- sumption when they hid it down that a female after com- pleting her twenty-fifth year had for ever passed from the hopeful regions of young womanhood.—l am, sir. yours, I Le., TEMPERANCE.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

Sir,—ln your reports of the meetings of the School Board the clerk is reported to have said," The effect of the operations of the School Board have been to put a great deal of money into the pockets of the managers of denomi- national schools." The clerk of course knows perfectly well that not one penny of the money from denominational schools goes into the pockets of the managers. For the in- formatioh of any of your readers who may be inclined to believe the statement of the clerk. I may say that the ac- counts of the denominational schools have to be kept as carefully as those of the Schoel Board. They have to be audited and presented with the vouchers to Her Majesty's inspector, and a balance sheet sent to the Educational Depart- ment in London. If one penny bad been misappropriated, the managers would lose the Government grant, without which the schools could not be carried on. Many hundreds of pounds have come out of the pockets of the Anpporters of the Wesleyan Schools, but not one penny has ever gone into them.

It is a great pity that men in authority should make random statements calculated seriously to injure the char- acter of the managers of the denominational schools, who have been making provision for the education of the children of the town during the last 30 or 40 years at a very considerable outlay both of time and money. Another random statement of the clerk's is that the Edu- cation Department would object to a "sliding scale" of fees, and that "it would be idle to press upon the Depart- ment a proßosal to which they would not give their con- sent." At the Widnes Board Schools the fees rise from 2d in the infants' school to 6d for standards 5 and 6. It is rather strange, too, that the clerk himself advocated a slid- ing scale, 2d for standard 1 and 3d for standard 2 and up- wards!

It is disappointing to those who have been long working in connection with denominational schools to find so little consideration shown towards them. Perhaps when the cost per head of educating the children in the Board schools is ascertained, the advocates of very low fees will not find themselves quite so popular with those who have to pay the rates as they would like to be. In the Widnes Board schools the fees were fixed at a higher rate than in the denomina- tional schools, and I believe they have since raised their fees to the same level.—Yours respectfully,. Runcorn, 21st January, 1888.

div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.
AGED PERSONS TREAT AT RUNCORN.

For the third year in succession the aged people of Runcorn were entertained to an excellent meat tea at the Public Hall on Wednesday evening, The committee of the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion were again the hosts, and the gathering was an unqualified success. Formerley all persons who had reached the age of 60 years and upwards were admitted without charge. Age was the passport. On the present occasion, however, those who were in the sere and yellow-leaf of life and in good cir- cumstances were expected to pay a fee of one shilling—a decision at which no one will cavil. Notwithstanding the inclement state of the wea- ther, and the extreme difficulty of locomotion at least 650 persons of venerable age assembled in the hall. Mr. Peck at reduced charges kindly con- veyed those who were unable to walk. Every ar- rangement had been made for the reception and comfort of the old folk by a committee consisting of Messrs. Meredith, F. J. Norman, W, Shaw, and W. Pownall (secretary.) The work of demolishing the good things provided was quickly begun. The by no means light duty of "cutting up" was per- formed by Mesdames Coventry, Walker, W. Pownall, Cook, Brown, Kniveton, Howard, Leatherwood, Stringer, Millington, Pownall, Dawson, Peacock, and Bowyer; Misses Owen, Peacock, and Bowyer; whilst the wants of the guests wore atten- ded to at the tables by Mesdames Beckett, Lake, Marwood, W. Shaw, W. Pownall, C. Pownall, Coventry, Longshaw, Rogerson, Kniveton, Bowyer, , Howard, T. Cooke, Dawson, Hankinson, Walker, Randle, Le Couteur, Meredith, Percival, Hodgson, Johnson, Bellamy, Marsh, Millinger, Blair; Misses N. Handley, Peacock, and Barclay. A large number of the "Young men acted as waiters. The com- mittee had to acknowledge kindness from Mrs. Meadowcroft, Mr. Hankinson, and Mr. J. 0. Jack- son, and the trustees of several chroThes and chapels. A large quantity of the provisions con- sumed had been the gift of tradesmen in the town, and the donations of money, collected by Messrs. F. J. Norman, Nickson, Meredith, Smith Coventiy, and the secretary, amounted to about £3O, an increase upon the amount subscribed in previous years..

After: tea the tables were cleared away, and an entertain- ment followed. Mr. S. C. Beckett, president of the Associa- tion, eccupied the chair, and he was supported on the plat- form by the Revs. T. M. Armson, G. Wood, J. D. Thomas; Messrs. John Simpson, J. E. Meredith, J. Johnson. H. Handle, S. Coventtv, J. W. Lightlenta, B. Kniveton, F. J. Norman. James Higgins, W. Pownall (secretary), and a number of ladies. , The Secretary read a letter from Mr. J. Brundrit. J.P., regretting his inability to be present, and hoping the old people would spend a pleasant evening. Letters were also read from the Duke of Westminster, who enclosed £3, Lord Egerton £1 Is, Mr. J. T. Brunner. M.P., £B, Mr. John , Brooks, M.P., XI is, and Mr. W. H. Verdin £1 Is. The Chairman said be was very pleased to come before his aged friends at the commencement of another year. He believed that this treat would now become an annual one— in fact he was sure it would. and they would agree with him when they heard his reasons for thinking to. The commit- tee that bad been appointed to wait upon the gentry and tradesmen of the town spoke very highly indeed of the reception they bad received. In some cases their visit's had been anticipated. They had been so delighted with the previous entertainments to the old people through their kindness that they thought it would be better to have-it an annual treat. The donors had been more generous this Year than any other year, showing that the old people met with sympethy and kindness from those oatside the Y M.C.A. Tbe young men were delighted to cater for them, and on their behalf he gave them a Iraity new year's greeting. (Applause.) The Rev. G. Wood, after wishing all present " A Happy New Year and very many of them." (Applause.) Said he believed it was possible for old people with all their aches and pains to feel supremely happy—happy in this present life, and happy in their prospects of the life to come. There were two chief changes through which we all derived hap. piness. One was the innocent gratification of our bodily senses, and the other was in the enjoyment of Divine favour and fellowship Tyro of these senses had been very gener- ously catered for and gratified that night. The ssnse of taste had been very well feasted, and he could only wish that everyone of those dear old friends could have as good a meal every day of their lives. (Applause.) One of their great revivalists used to say that he did not think anybody could get cenverted with cold feet. (Laughter.) H 3 ',Mr. Wood) did not think anybody could be very happy with an empty stomach. There was another sense that thing g dare to get et saaywsaoyme o fromf those was being liberally gratified—he meant the sense of sound —by their musical friends. present felt it a very nice squalling grandchildren—(loud laughter)—and from their to wr blea uiagnnhndot ecvre(),n—ctal vocal d hmusic. Buts ca;e l scolding these i r bodilydeaaur l' regaledt eSensesrsin "wio afi wt h instrumental ours r e umei i. fled in this fashion, and yet they might not be permanently happy. There was another element in our nature which craved for satisfaction. And he should like every individual to carry dot of that hall something which would make them permanently happy. These bodily senses would all perish by and bye in the dark and silent tomb, but the soul had its senses which must be catered for and gratified. Life to him would be a very one sided thing—happiness would be a very imperfect thing—unle s the moral ail(' religious .-xceptions were not catered for ar d gratified. The Gospel was a feast a feast in which they were all invited to share. Geld Himself had become the caterer for us in this respect. It was- prepared for everyone of us. We might be the if* NiGho.d. Everyone of them might have a free ticket iukeest is of h admitted them to that entertainment, with- out money and without price. They might sit down in very good company at this feast with Abraham. Issec, and Jacob. By-and-bye, at the marriage supper of the Lamb, we might listen to music infinitely superior to any they

would listen to that night—the music of the celestia I harpers harping with their harps. In the language of holy l writ, " Come to this feast, for all things are now ready:" He could only cherish the hope that the feast of that even- ing would find its issue and counterpart in the feast of the Gospel and in the feast above in relation to everyone of them. (Applause.) he entertainment consisted of selections by the Volun- teer Band, and songs by Miss N. Handley; Messrs. R. Moore. R. Morris, T. Cooke, J. Graham, L. Coventry, J. E. Lon,,shaw, and A. Fox. The cnmic sketches of Mr. Graham provoked much merriment. The Misses Wood and Miss Jukes, and Master C. Le Couteur contributed piano- forte duets, and Mr. Wilson a concertina solo. Miss Howard and Master C. Cooke gave a duet, and Miss C. Littler re- cited. Mr. B. Kniveton gave a Lancashire reading ; Miss F. Handley ably officiated at the piaao. During an interval that person was presented with a bag of fruit. Advantage was taken of the interval by Mr. Bonkem, one of the guests, to return thanks for the agreeable manner in which they bad been entertained, and he paid a tribute to the late Mr. Norman, Yr he was president of the Association at the time of his death. The proceedings, which. commenced wi,h " God Bless the Prince of Wales," a reference to his pas- sage through the town in the afternoon, concluded with the National Anthem, the old people having appar- ently greatly enjoyed themselves. All those who suffered from infirtnity were taken home in cabs. The large quantity of provisions that were left after Wednesday evening's feast was distributed to about 40 poor persons on Thursday morning. The beef and bones un- used were handed to Mr. W. Shaw, of the Mersey Missions, who yesterday at noon provided a good number of children ' with a capital soup dinner. The committee of the Y.M.C.A. are considering the necessity of forming themselves into a 1 central relief organisation in order to provide means to alleviate the distress existing in the town.

div.head: JOHN SIMPSON.
div.p: JOHN SIMPSON.
COERCION IN IRELAND.

E.4ir,—Can it possible that coercion is once again to be r sorted in the government of Ireland? If rumour be true. more than one of our leading statesmen have more than half made their minds to fall back upon this stale and discred- ited device. It is certain that if dukes and lords, whether they be Whig or Tory, are to have their way we shall soon again have Irish prisons filled with men who have never been indicted for any offence; " sentences of death " in the shape of evictions, put in execution on the roadsides, and in -the already partially depopulated villages of Ireland, with the aid of English bayonets ; and we shall also have the inevitable reprisals of cattle maiming and midnight murder. But the question is—are dukes and lords, and those people who have, by the legalised robbery of their not so very remote ancestors, been put in a position to extract a luxurious living from the poor peasants of Ireland, to still dominate the policy of this country ? If whit we are so often told be true, that political power has passed into the hands of the working classes, it seems hardly credible that coercion can again be taken up until a good deal more has been done to satisfy the demands of the Irish people. _ _

iistory informs us that in a former age the arts and cul- ture of this country, such as they were, were derived from Ireland. I am inclined to think that in ages to come it will be the opinion that Ireland in this nineteenth century took the lead in an equally praiseworthy direction. We have won political equality; what we now want to win is social equality—not the unnatural equality of communism, eut the equality of like opportunities of acquiring dietinc- tion and fortune. The very first step towards this social equality is the abolition of the privilege conferred on a section of the community in times past, of living, like perpetual pensioners, on the produce of other people's la6our ; and it is this first stop which the Irish people are struggling so -tenaciously to make. There are increasing signs that the masses of the people of Great Britain are beginning to look ' upon the Irish problem in this way. For when the agri- culturists of Wales begin to find their burden too heavy, who is it they will turn to for advice ? To Michael Davitt, the founder of the Lind League, and of all the Irish leaders, the most genuine democrat. Nothing could be more suggestive of the way in which men's thoughts ate inclining than the fact that they turn to Davitt in prefer- ence to others. Mr. Parnell may 134 the politihl leader of Ireland, but Mr. Davitt is certainly the leader of the social

div.head: LATEST NE Ws.
div.p: LATEST NE Ws.

Mr. Balfour. M.P., is still unable to attend to business. Earl Granville had a further interview with Mr. Glad- stone yesterday. Summonses for a Cabinet Council to be held to-day (Saturday) afternoon were issued yesterday. MURDER IN NORFOLIC.—At Norfolk Assizes, at Norwich, on Friday, John Thurston, aged 30 a labourer, was convic- ted and sentenced to death for the murder of Henry Spring. all, at Hingham, on the sth December. The Central News understands that the Local Govern- ment Bard, Dublin, have despatched an inspector to Innisbhoffin and other islands on the north-west coast of Ireland to report upon the condition of the islanders. DEATH OF MADAME MOUREZ.—Madame Monrez. who was sentenced to six month' hard labour in connection with the Armstrong case, has died in Millbank paison. The cause of death is stated to be disease of the kidneys, but an in- quest will he held. THREE MEN DROWNED.—Four men belonging to Dun- cannon were bringing a fishing yawl from Fethard to Water- ford on Thursday evening, and in rounding the Hook in Waterford Lower Harbour the boat capsivd. Two of the men, brothers, named Penn, and another man named Butler, were drowned before assis.ance arrived.

THE QUEEN'S RETURN TO OSEORNA. The Queen left London on Friday morning on her return to Osborne. Her Majesty. who was looking very well, drove from Bucking- ham Palace at half-past tea in an open carriage te Victoria Station, escorted by a detachment of Horse Guards. There were only a few people along the line of route, in response to whose salutations Her Majesty frequently bowed. Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg and Lady Southampton wera in the carriage with Her Majesty, and the Royal suite followed. A crowd had collected around the main en- trance to the station, and greeted Her Majesty with cheers. The Queen, who arrived at the station a few minutes before the appointed time, was received by the leading officials of the Chatham and Dover and South-Western Railways, and proceeded at once to the special train amid the salutations of the spectators privileged to be on the platform. The train started at 10-40 for Portsmouth.

div.head: MURDER OF A FRENCH PREFECT.
div.p: THE MURDER OF A FRENCH PREFECT.

PARIS. FRIDAY.—Tee Seed this morning says that Madame Barreme, after long hesitation, has denounced one of her relatives as the murderer of her husband AiINE EXPLOSION AND LOSS OF 35 LINTS. NEW Yonn, FRIDAY.—An explosiOn has occurred in a mine at Newburg, West Virginia, causing the death of 35 persons. Terrific storms have prevailed on the Pacific coast by which San Francisco has suffered some dama2.-e. BULGARIAN MISSION TO TURKEY.

Sone,— -M. 'runoff, Minister for Foreign Affairs, starts this morning for Constantinople, charged to treat with the Ottoman Government on the question of the union of Bulgaria and Eastern Roumelia. Gadban Effendi, by pei mission of the Porte, will accompany M. Tsanoff to the Turkish capital. FATAL FIRE IN FRANCE.

PARIS, YRIDAY.—A terrible fire broke out during the night at a cabinet manufactory at Belleville. Before the fire engine arrived it spread to the adjoining houses, which -are inhabited by workpeople, and before Vie inmates could all be roused the flames had reached the staircase, which was of wood, and cut off their escape. A terrible scene occurred. No means of rescue was at hand. Two men were burned to death and five others terribly injured.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. Lord HARRIS, replying t') the Marquis of Ripon, said he had telegraphed to Lord Dufferin as to the alleged cruelties by British officers in Burmab, also directing that strict inquiry be made.—The Marquis of SALISBURY moved, the Earl of KIMBERLEY seconded, the Earl of Limnnicir sup- ported, and the House carried, a complimentary vote on the death of Sir William Rose, clerk of the Parliament. The House adjourned at 25 minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. There was a full attendance to-day. NOTICES. &c.—Mr. P. RYLANDS gave notice that when the Chancellor of the Exchequer proposed to give facilitiesfor con- sidering near rules for procedure, he should move that con- sideration of those rules be postponed until remedial measures for Ireland had been considered.—Lord R. CHURCHILL, re- plying to Dr. Cameron, said he was not surprised that ques- tions had been asked respecting the ghastly scenes reported to have taken place at Mandalay. He could not believe any officer wearing the Queen's uniform could allow such proceedings to have taken place. He did not believe the statem •nt could be true. He had telegraphed to the Vice- roy and the Chief Commissioner at Mandalay, and, if there was the slightest truth in the statement immediate action would be taken.

DASATE ON THE ADDRESS. The adjourned detate on the Address was resnmed.—Mr. SEXTON referred to the recent speeches of the Prime Minis- ter, and contended that the wor.is of Lord Salisbury could have no other interrretation in the minds of intelligent men, and they bad no other purpose, in his own mind, but to convey to the country that his administration were, ready to consieler the claim of the legislative independence of Ireland and in the settlement of the question to consider, at least as a general, guide the concession of the claims of the people of Hungary for independence. He charged the present Government with having first excited hopes in the mind of the people of Ireland, and then, when the result of the polls was known, of turning round and putting language into the mouth ef the Sovereign totally opposed to those hopes. Ha in very strong langu'age said Irish members would by every means fight the proposal of renewed coer- cion far Ireland. In his view the beet way to bring about a better state of things than at present existed in Ireland was to confide the power and responsibility of Irish law to Irishmen. (Loud cheers from the Irish members.) Refer- ring to the late election, he said there never was a national verdict more conclusive than that given its Ireland, and it was for Mr. Gladstone, who, lee an- ticipated, would soon be responsible for the con- duct of affairs, to determine whether he would imitate the folly of the present Government. (Cheers.) —.I he ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND defended the language used in the Queen's speech regarding Ireland, and denied that it was unconstitutional, or that it went beyond what the exceptional circumstances of the time called for. Government in Ireland was, he said, going from bad to worse, di,content increasing, prosperity diminishing, and in face of all this the power of the National League was ex- tending. It interfered with individual liberty of action, not only between landlord and tenant, but in every relation in life. He insisted that boycotting meet be dealt with In a firm and decided manner, and if ordinary law WAS insuffi- cient then repressive measures were justifiable, and the Government would shrink from no responsibility calcu- lated to give good government for Ireland.—Mr. LABOUCHERE said, as far as he understood the last speaker, coercion was necessary because the law was not strong enough to deal with boycotting, but the Chancellor of the F,xcequer had told the House that offences of that character had been suc- cessfully dealt with by the ordinary law. He considered the national demand for Home Rule ought to be conceded and he denied that it meant separation from England. He maintained that the integrity of the Empire would net be injured if there were a dozen Parliaments in different parts of the kingdom.—Mr. WARING warned the House not to judee from the conduct of the Parnellites in the House the course they would take, if they were in a position to con- trol the Government in Ireland.—Mr. H. Cosnlat declined to be a party to give Government further poeuer of coercion in Ireland.—Colonel DAWNAY believed the Government would adopt a wise course as regards Ireland if they would protect the Loyalists and break up the National League. [LEFT SITTING. j

div.head: WARP INGTON.
div.p: WARP INGTON.

NOT ILL, BUT DRUNK.—On Wednesday evening a man named Patrick Milroy was found lying on the pavement in an insensible condition. A gentleman proffered to pay for a cab and the man was taken to the infirmary, when it was discovered that he was drunk. He was brought up at the Police Court for that offence on Thursday, and was dismissed with a caution.

MISSIONARY MEETING.—On Wednesday evening the Rev. Mr. Watson, missionary frornNew Zealand, lectured in Holy Trinity School, in support of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. The Rev. S. Wilkinson occupied the chair. Mr. Watson has never been in England until the last few months. A most interesting and instructive lecture was given, in which was pointed out the progress of missionary work in New Zealand, the means, and manner, and incidents connected with the landing of the first missionaries, and how the conversion of the Maori people was brought about. Mr. Watson pointed out that 30 Maori clergy were clergy of the English church. A vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer on the motion of the Rev. E. C. E• Carleton, seconded by Mr. Westbrook. Mr. Watson acknowledged the same, and, replying to a question which had been asked him, said that they in New Zealand were not Protectionists, though they did tax some imports; but it was a strange fact that the Protectionist party with them were the Radicals, whilst the Free Traders were Conser- vatives. A vote of thanks was passed to the chair- man, and the meeting closed. THE POTATO MACHINE CONTROVERSY.—At the sitting of the Borough Court on Monday, a cir- cumstance cropped up with regard to the odours emanating from the chipped potato machines which are perambulated in the principal streets of the borough on an evening, and which have formed the. subject of a discussion in our corremondence columns. David, Samuel, John, and Sarah Ann Plinston were summoned for allowing potato ma- chines to stand a longer time than was necessary in Horsemarket-street and Market-street, on the 9th instant. Evidence was given by P.C. Bruen and Inspector Berry to the effect that the machines had on the day in question been kept in One place for such a time as to cause an obstruction, and the latter remarked that the stench from the chipped potato machines was something dreadful; he had received several complaints.- Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk) was engaged at the court at the time, and said that he did not think there would be any complaint were it not for the smell. Several com- plaints had been made to the Sanitary Committee. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that he believed that one family paid Bs. or 9s. a week as toll for their potato machines. The police were expected to remove obstructions from the streets, and he asked what were they to do. Mr. Whittle said the fact of paying toll did not allow people to cause obstructions. In answer to the Mayor, one of the defendants said that he thought the smell might be reduced, and the cases were thereupon adjourned for a month to ascertain if that could be done.

TKE SUDDEN DEATH OF 117A-D-FTS-31-AN-.--- Jr, W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest, on Saturday, at the Crown and Sceptre Inn Butter- market-street, relative to the death Of Mr. Joseph Henry Woods, chemist, Buttermarket-street, the circumstances surrounding which were reported in last issue.—tederick Fairhurst, who had been em- ployed as errand boy by the deceased, with whom he lived, said that on the previous Thursday morn- ing, shortly after ten o'clock, he went to the bed- room of the deceased with a cup of tea, in accord- ance with a regular custom. He found deceased on the floor, near the bed, as though he had just dropped off it, with nothing on but his shirt. De- ceased was quite cold and appeared to be dead. He informed Mr. Sasson, the assistant, and Dr. Joseph was at once sent for. Deceased had been subject to , fits, and witness had many a time seen him in a fit. He thought deceased had a fit the week before Christmas. Deceased was not sober when he went to .bed the day before he died. The deceased. generally took a sle,eping draught, which the assis- tant mixed. .The housekeeper, who, lived in the house, died on the Monday morning previous, and was to be buried the day witness found deceased. Mr. Woods was upset by her death.—Dr. Joseph said that he had known deceased for twelve years and had attended him seven years, generally for epileptic fits. He saw the body on Thursday, and be- lieved that deceased died from epileptic convulsions. In the bottle produced there was nothing potent.-- James Kirk Woods, 30, Church-street, chemist, said that the deceased was 35 years of age. James Gerard Sasson, the assistant, said that the mixture for deceased was made up by himself. Deceased eid not keep any drugs in his bedroom: The key of the shop was kept by witness.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance -ss ah the medical evidence. OTINTY COT:MT.—A sitting of the Wanington County Court was held before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes on Thursday.—F. W. All wood, grocer, sued a man named Wells, a boarding-house keeper, or the sum of £l4 12s 3d, for goods sold and deliv- ered. Mr. Yearsley apPearecl for the plaintiff, and stated that defendant, in 1884, married a Miss Bul- lock, who had traded 'with plaintiff previous to her marriage. She afterwards said that in future de- fendant would himself order goods, and goods to the amount claimed for had been supplied.—De- fondant repudiated his responsibility, but admitted that he took a share of the profits delved from the boarding-house business.—His Honour found for Plaintiff for the amount claifned.—Samuel Pen-in, Kingsley, near Frodsham, sued George Pritchard, signalman and farmer, of Fearnhead, near Warring- ton, for the sum of £2 10s, alleged to be due for articles sold. Plaintiff was represented by Mr. Burton (Runcorn), and Mr. Jenkins defended. The case for the plaintiff was that in 1883 he gave up housekeeping and took lodgings at the house of the defendant, furnishing his own room. Some time afterwards defendant agreed to buy plaintiff's fur- niture for £5. He had, however, only paid ..E2 5s.— His Honour, after hearing evidence, gave judgment for plaintiff for £2 ss, and allowed defendant -..C1 lOs on a counter claim.—The case of Samuel Welsby v. John Kelly, which was part heard at a prei:_ous sitting of the Court, was resumed. Plaintiff is a shopkeeper at Stockton Heath, and he claimed OES 7s 7d as balance for bread supplied to defendant, who now lives in Wartington. Mr. H. J. Longipn appeared in support, and called witnesses proN ing the delivery of the bread from Mr. Davies's bakeiy, and the balance owing. Mr. Browne, for the de- fence, produced defendant's book, and said the claim had been paid with the exception of about £2, and that the quantity of bread charged had not been delivered. He also called witnesses to prove this.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

THREATENED 4TRIKE AT OLDHAM.—:geetillaS of a e branches of the Oldham Spinners and Twiners' Association were held on Wednesday eveninz. The principal meetings, at Oldham, disapproved the recommendation of the Council that the operatives should accept the reduction demand 1 by the employers. and declared their readiness to enter upon another strike. A final decision, however, will not become to fore few days.

RUNNING INTO A STMAM TRAM.—On Thursday morning an accident, resulting in serious, if not fatal, injuries to a driver employed by Mr. Strickland. brewer, Nelson, occur- red on the Burnley and District Tramways, about midway tietween Burnley and Padiham. The lorry, which the in- jured man was driving ran into an engine as it came round a curve in an opposite direction, and he wrq thrown violently on to the footpath, the lurry also passing over his body.

SPAIN. AND THE POPE. Maaaross, TrtSDAY.---At a Cabinet Council held last night, Senor Segasta read a letter of condolence from the Pope to the Queen-Regent upon the death ot King Alfonso. His holiness also expressed satisfaction at having contri- buted to bring about a settlement of the Caroline Islands question. The Pope, after wishing prosperity to the Regency, and offering to assist in strengthening it within the limits of his spiritual mission, concludes by sending his blessing to the Queen-Regent and her daughters. SPANISH EXPEDITIONS. MADRID, TurnaDAY.—The Spanish Government has de- cided to appoint governors and establish garrisons at Yap, in the Carelines, and at Baubelthonap, in the Pelew Islands. An expedition will also be sent to that part of the Archi- pelago where the German gunboat Albatross planted the German flag during the Yap incident. Another expeditien will visit the Spanish possessions on the West Coast of Africa. SERIOUS WORKMEN'S RIOTS IN PENNSYLVANIA. Nizw YOWL, TriIIRSDAY.—Riots have occurred among the Hungarians on strike in the coke manufacturing districts of Pennsylvania. One min has been killed and several others have been fatally injured in resisting the sheriff's posse, which. intervened to restore order. A number of women joined the rioters. A feeling of insecurity prevails in the district and citizens are arming in self-defence. THE FIRE ON A DUNDEE STEAMER. NEW YORS, THIIRSD&Y —The tire which broke out on board the steamer Crystal, from Dundee has been subdued. The damage by which the ca.ro chiefly suffered is estima- ted at 10,000 dole.

I "At last—it seemed ages—Attica came in sight. I braced every . ery nerve for a final effort. We nearly it slowly, the old horse sauntering along, and occasionally pausing to nibble a tempting bunch of grass. It was there that I registered a ; mute oatk to flay him alive if he ever pulled through. We entered t.)27 the main street, and I counted the seconds as we approached the post-office, over which was the doctor's rooms. At last we were there, then an awful fact suddenly dawned on me. I was unable to move, unable to speak, powerless to attract attention, and, sir, as I hope to be saved, that infamous horse deliberately walked past the doctor's i straight through the town and out the other side." He paused for a moment. and looked silently out of the: window. "You have probably read of mariners," he went on, I " starving, desperate, famished, who are tossed on a raft in i mid-ocean and see a great ship sail pass them on the hori- i son. Well, I felt something the same way, only worse, as • speechless and motionless I sad dying like a graven image , on the buggy seat and saw the .town disappear behind my back. There were few people on the streets—yon know; how it is in a ,country place at noon—and those who saw tie supposed I was only drunk. "I don't know whether it was absolute despair that partly broke the spell, or whether I swooned, but anyhow I fell out of the buggy at the sdge of the town, and upon this the horse made its very first exhibition of energy and ran off. They carried me back to the doctor's office and laid me on the floor. I was still unable to talk, but I feebly motioned to my pocket, and they took out the bottle. The doctor un- corked it, smelled it, and remarked that he was sorry to see me intoxicated. This made me so mad that I found strength to gasp out I— " You old idiot, oarft you see I'm poisoned. That's laudanum 1' " ' It's nothing of the kind,' he said, 'it's whisky.' " ' Look at the label, you maniac 7 I shrieked. He turned over the bottle. "'That's an old label,' he said, 'and crossed out. I filled the bottle myself with whisky. What's the matter with you, anyhow?' "I felt my symptons suddenly disappear. When I found the door' I disappeared, too. I afterward hunted up a big coloured man, and gave him a quarter to kick me, and—. But here's Lafayette, I see. Tills is any stopping place. Good day." I 1
